c.3: The consecration for hoisting the banner (*dhvajārohaṇapratiṣṭhā*), the collection of sacred bathing sites (*tīrtha*) perfumed with black incense, and the powder festival (*cūrṇotsava*). p.5a, l.1: c.1: The ritual for the great sacred site (*mahātīrthavidhi*), the silent offering (*maunabali*), the festival of the Preceptor (*ācāryotsava*), the beating of the drum (*bherītāḍana*), and the *vināyaka*-drumbeat (*vināyakatāla*); c.2: The ritual for the festival of the devotees (*bhaktotsavavidhi*), the consecration of the Field Protector (*kṣetrapālapratiṣṭhā*), and the [sacred] utterance—[the utterance] 25; c.3: ... In due order … and I invoke Rudra; by the sequence of differentiation, the courtesans, wearing the dress of Śūdra-Draviḍas, with paramours in full force … [and] a water-pot in hand, [perform] the release; from the Praśasta. In the middle of the stage, according to this sequence, she who obstructs the jars in the cardinal directions. [The remainder is blank. Page 6a is blank. Page 6b, f1, l.1: … may there be auspiciousness).
(Meditation verses—[appears to be an incomplete verse]—which those who know the Vedānta of Brahma speak.)
Salutation to Him who is the Supreme, the Primal Matter, and likewise the Puruṣa; the Liberator, the Emergent Cause, or the Lord—to that Vighnavināyaka, salutations!

I worship Gaṇapati of the deep river, who wears swaying bee-adorned earrings, who bears an ocean of compassion, whose eyes are like full-blown lotuses, who is a wish-granting tree for the worlds that bow before him, and whose sprout-like tusk destroyed the rutting elephant-demon Madana.

I take refuge in the son of Gaṅgādhara, whose temples are drenched with streams of rut-fluid, who is like a cloud of ichor flowing from his cheeks, who is a mountain-elephant for the bees wandering about in search of fragrance, whose neck is agitated, and who is served by Gandharvas, Siddhas, Asuras, and Kinnaras. (3) [He is] accompanied by the songs of the swarms of intoxicated bees, which are drawn by the drinking of the ichor flowing from the slopes of his own temples.
Gaṇapati, with his ears motionless against his neck, brings about the destruction of obstacles. 4.
(Bherīpūjā / Beating the Drum) — In the center, on the right and left sides of the drum, reside the gods Śambhu, Viṣṇu, and Padmaja.

All the *kīlas*, the Mothers, the hide, and the serpent are located in the pair of [sides] wrapped in leather; and the two deities Moon and Sun are situated in the space above those who dwell upon the earth and in heaven.

For the welfare of those dwelling on the mountain slopes, and for the sake of the pacification of the enemies of the gods, I now strike this drum. (5) To proclaim [my] victory over the entire world, and for the protection of living beings, I strike this drum—the drum that initiates the festival of bloodless [compassion] day after day—before the daughter of the noble Himālaya mountain, as a teaching for deer and birds. (6)
O you who are the embodiment of Brahmā, Indra, Nārāyaṇa, and Rudra, standing before this Subduer of Cities, I now beat the great drum for the delight of both quadrupeds and bipeds upon the earth. (7)

The satisfaction of the eighteen host-deities in the world of moving and unmoving beings through the *sūtra* and *hita* offerings; the bathing of the image of Indra; the service of the sin-removing holy ford of Śiva; and the hoisting of the banner and the beating of the drum. (8)
In the evening of the night, at another time, the sixth hour at the end of the day is the [proper] time for the Vidyā.
Thus, when applied according to the rule at its own time, the drum for the procession, consecration, and festival should be struck.
(9) In the application of sacred sites frequented by sages, it is hidden elsewhere, joined with the count of the poor.

May Śrīkaṇṭha, who has shattered his enemies, protect for a long time; may Bhava be the preeminent one to be honored on the paths by the foremost among the hosts of Piśācas and Bhūtas. May the virtuous prosper, may cows yield abundant milk, and may the social orders shine, fully complete with manifold riches.
May the sky yield abundant rain, and may the earth be rich with excellent crops;
may the world, free from grief and well-informed, long remain victorious, having attained its purpose through the Śaiva scriptures.

In that glorious and great festival, dedicated to the rite of protecting the *jagatī*, Govatsa was initiated; a resident of the sacred precinct (*sthalavāsin*), he was intent upon performing service to Paśupati.
May the deities Śrī, Padmodbhava, Bhāratī, and the others, as well as Hara, Ādijā, Gaṇeśa, Skanda, and the lotus-eyed one, come at the command of Caṇḍa.
That [place], which always bestows joy upon the curious,
was for the sake of service ascended by the venerable Govatsanātha, whose head was bowed in the midst of the festival of the sacred ford.
O Kūrma, let there be a proclamation with the sounds of the jhallī, maddala, tāla, and kāhala, with the noise of the ḍhakkā,
ārdra, and muṇḍubhi, and with the lute, flute, drum, conch, and kettledrum!

In that [city], which was like a great mountain range adorned with rows of palaces as lofty as the king of banners—banners made of various silken cloths fluttering in the gentle breeze that dispelled the fatigue of the coming and going of herds of elephants eager for the opportunity to prostrate themselves, as inferred from hearing the sharp sound of many drums amidst the music of the performance of the rites for the glorious ear-ornaments; and which possessed broad, long, and charming streets lined with rows of mansions.

Upon trees embraced by charming creepers such as *yūthikā*, *mallikā*, and *mālatī*, he beheld the supreme pleasure garden (*sarodyāna*). In the waters of the lake, which were overflowing with the intense fragrance of various blossoming flower-clusters (*mañjarī*), he gazed upon the waves of the Yamunā and the winds; and in that place, which was rendered fragrant and delightful by the spray from the ripples of the river and frequented by the gods, he experienced a blaze of wonder at observing the various artistic wonders of the pavilions, gate-towers, ramparts, and other structures visible within.

In this royal capital, the city of Śrīmad-Govatsanātheśvara—a place where the courtyard floor is made beautiful by the mass of jewels adorning the Rudra-dancing girls who perform songs and dances amidst the tumultuous clamor of the assembly; a site for all auspicious sacrifices where curiosity is aroused by the playful diversions of those who have mastered the Vedas and are ever-engaged in sport; and a venue for a great festival that increases the kingdom’s prosperity, longevity, health, power, and good fortune—I hereby issue this proclamation by the sounding of kettledrums and conchs. 11.

He whose independent mental resolve is worshipped by the feet of all the foremost gods, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva; who possesses eternal and stainless knowledge regarding the reality of all existing things throughout the three divisions of time—past, future, and present; who perceives the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) consisting of phonemes, words, mantras, principles, worlds, and kalās; and who is as beautiful as a ruby lamp within the temple of the circle of fire situated in the center of the moon.

He who delights in the sport of bestowing the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation upon his devotees; who, with a stream of compassionate nectar, removes all poisons by the mere touch of his own throat from which the venom has fallen away; whose tips of tusks, white as autumnal clouds, serve as ornaments for the jewels they pierce; who is the supreme Boar who lifted the circle of the earth; whose lotus feet are the object of the vision of Padmanābha; who is eternally pure like a flood of nectar and the essence of crystal; who wears a garment of hide; and who possesses five faces, ten arms, and fifteen eyes.

In his right hand [he holds] a spear, a trident, a mace, a sword, and a serpent; in his left hand he carries a *pināka* bow, a shield, a sword, a water-pot, and a noose like a lotus stalk. His lineage is graced by a white and tender sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). He stands upon a proud bull as his mount, amidst the shattered great mountains and the Mandāra groves, which resound with the tinkling of wind-chimes that fill the quarters of space. His matted locks are crowned by the peak of Mount Meru, and he is adorned with the deer-mark and the crescent moon.

[He] whose forehead-eyes blaze with the pair of earrings from Hindukuṇḍa; who has swallowed the five-arrowed god of love with the fire of his gaze; who delights in looking with compassionate side-glances that consume the moon, fire, wind, water, earth, the sacrificer, and the self; who is the very body of Rāma’s purpose; who has protected the circle of the fourteen worlds; and who is skilled in fierce play that is the cause of the origin of the worlds and the beings within them.

May Mahādeva, the Supreme Lord Śiva—the blue-necked one, knowable through the Vedānta, composed of the Vedas, and devoid of old age and birth—who grants fearlessness to the world, be present upon the central petal of the divine trident, the weapon of Śiva, and bestow his grace.

From the lamentation of Kāpaṭa, the multitude of gods, led by Bṛndāraka, [praised] the Lord who is the source of the meters; whose lotus-feet are the golden peaks of Mount Meru; whose chest shines with a sacred thread equal to the flow of rivers; and who, by the expansion of his wings, surpassed the excellence of the garland of waves from the Ocean of Milk, pervading all that is moving and unmoving.

May Brahmā—the lotus-eyed lord whose intellect is steadfast in discerning the entire range of meanings, from the subtle to the gross, the near to the far, and all else, as if they were held in the palm of his hand; whose four arms are adorned with a book, a rosary, a water-pot, and a deer; who possesses eight eyes and four faces graced by a cluster of white lotuses; who dwells at his own will in the celestial abode and is devoted to meditation upon Śiva in his heart—having established his presence upon the right petal of this divine trident, the weapon of Śiva, may he render it auspicious.

Nārāyaṇa, the crusher of Naraka, whose feet are Kṛṣṇa, who [treads upon] the entire surface of the earth including Krauñca, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and sword; he who, by his own power, has opened and caused to emerge the multitude of all cosmic eggs from his city and region; he whose vehicle is the wind-god Māruta, the elephant Airāvata, and the bird Garuḍa, as manifested by Lakṣmī.

By whose path, like that of a rutting elephant, the earth—sunk in the ocean of all the waters of the cosmic egg beginning with the birth of Brahmā—was rescued by assuming the form of the Boar; and whose conduct was characterized by the great waves of the deep ocean of his incarnation, while his unbearable valor caused the golden breast of Hiraṇyakaśipu to burst open at the tips of his claws, thereby producing a profusion of blood that created the hue of twilight and formed a thick sandalwood paste upon the firm breasts of Lakṣmī.
Having established his presence upon the left petal of the divine trident of Śiva’s weapon, may he grant his grace. 3.

Her eyes are like lotuses fallen under the rays of the young sun; her pair of beautiful, reddish, and restrained eyes are fixed upon the moon; her face and hips are like the cave that serves as the pure seat for the supreme yogi; her belly is the source of the jars of the nectar of breast-milk; her palms are like blue lotuses and sprouts; she is the embodiment of supreme bliss.

O beloved of the Lotus-eyed One who sits upon the elephant throne, having shaken off the filth from your lotus-like hands, you are adorned with an ear-ornament; [you are] beautified by a mass of pearls arising like a flood of moonlight, lovely as a cluster of lilies upon your lotus feet.

May the goddess Umā—the blue-locked one, who accomplishes her devotees with the nectar-like side-glances of her compassion; she whose compassionate skill provides wealth for the sake of both body and soul; she who is worshipped by hosts of gods such as Indra; the sole sovereign lady of the world whose footprints have subdued all; she who possesses beautiful manes born of a supermundane nature; she who is ever united with the lion-vehicled Lord; the beloved of the Supreme Lord; the Blessed Goddess—having made her presence within the leaf-cup in the midst of the divine trident, grant her grace! 5.

The daughter of the King of Sindhu, who was adorned with a crown, armlets, and ear-ornaments set with nine kinds of jewels; whose slender body was embellished by a girdle of refined gold; whose chest shone like a honey-filled Madhava-thana; who was radiant with the auspicious banners and marks of victory preceded by all prosperity; who was sprinkled by the ocean of the mass of her own fame—manifested through supreme generosity like a pair of living Jīvakas, a wish-granting cow, a kalpa-tree, and a cintāmaṇi gem.

May she who dwells in the lotus situated within the reality of the Lord of Knowledge—counted foremost among the elephants [of the quarters] skilled in the excellent qualities headed by radiant beauty—who, having established her presence upon the left petal-ridge of the divine trident of Śiva’s weapon, bestows grace. 6.

[He is] one who, having entered [the state of liberation], has brought rest to the multitude of travelers at his side through the joy arising from the consolation produced during the time of sport upon the slopes of Mount Meru, Mandara, Niṣadha, and the Kulācala ranges; he whose obstacles are fanned away by the breezes from the triple city, and who, though established in the excellence of virtues, is solely intent on the protection of all the worlds, including the directions and the netherworlds (pātāla).

[The river] flows with the playful splashing of the ears of elephants—tremulous from the sport of plunging into the pure waters consisting of the meditations upon the hearts of the foremost sages, headed by Brahmā, who hold in their hands the *vālavyajana* (fly-whisk), the goad, the rosary, and the water-pot; it is graced by the wind [blown] from the flapping of those ears; and it is adorned by fragrant jars and other vessels, as well as by the moon, the stars, and the planets, which serve as its seat, spread out like fresh, pale-red lotuses and goads.

May Gaṇeśvara, the Lord of Obstacles, who possesses a great torrent of ichor flowing from his temples—fanned by the wind from his trunk and filled with the divine wine of the gods; who rides upon the powerful elephant named Ripunitata that emerged from the Khara forest; who restrains millions of thunderclouds; who is the master of all the Gaṇas; and whose face is like a jar [shaped] from the divine trident of Śiva’s weapon—may he, being present here, bestow his grace. 7.

...whose universal form is a magnificent mass of rays with the color of saffron, and who displays on his left and right sides a great power consisting of light that appears like a lake of water; (p. 13a)

...who is saluted by the entire host of beautiful celestial women with their hands extended holding a bell, arrow, sword, bow, axe, noose, vajra, cock, shield, bow, and a handful of peacock feathers; whose neck and mouth shine intensely like a fresh mass of water-laden clouds; who possesses a charming and most auspicious dance like that of a dancing peacock; who is a moving necklace for the cheeks of the multitude of beautiful celestial women; who is the moon of the moon-like face of Candrikā, saluted by the entire assembly of beautiful celestial women; who is eternally youthful, possessed of strength and prowess, the king of all sciences, and the Swan (Haṃsa).

May the one whose range of action is like that of a lotus among the six-faced [Kārttikeya], who is the source of sustenance for the entire world, who consists of palaces for the honey-bees of all beings, who removes the suffering of the twelve great lotus-eyes, who is Kārttikeya, the protector of the celestial realm, the capable Lord Kumāra, the six-faced commander-in-chief of the army, the destroyer of the host of asuras, the incomparable hero Subrahmaṇya, having established his presence in this place where the divine trident of Śiva’s weapon shines, may he grant his grace. 8. (p.13b, f8a, l.1)

[He is] the one who, at the time of the churning of the nectar (*amṛta*), assumed the form of Mohinī—delighting the hearts of all people and captivating the twelve minds of the gods and demons—and who was born from the body of Gaṅgādhara; he is skilled in fulfilling the desires of those devoted to his own worship through his expertise in the conclusion of all faultless branches of knowledge; he is adorned with a quiver filled with nectar; he possesses a form that destroys the suffering of those who bow before him and bestows fearlessness; and his bowstring is a swarm of bees settled upon his golden bow.

May the Great Teacher, who is beloved by the speed of the majesty of his arrows—fragrant with the essence born from the Sindhu river; who has made the multitudes of gods, asuras, and sages, including Hara, Hari, and Viriñca, his subjects through the glance of his collyrium-like eyes; whose body resembles the deep red of the *japā* flower; and who is like a fresh seed-pod for the tree of saṃsāra—having established his presence at the tip of the divine trident, the weapon of Śiva, may he grant his grace. 9.

Savitṛ, the bestower of consciousness upon all worlds, the cause of the increase and waning of the moon’s rays, the source of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and Atharva Vedas, possesses the power to create, sustain, and otherwise transform the causes of time—beginning with the morning, midday, and evening; the seasons; the movement of the fierce-rayed sun; the two eyes, face, chest, tail, and other parts of his body; and the supreme state of the *paramahaṃsa*—down to the *nimiṣa*, *lava*, *kalā*, *kāṣṭhā*, *ghaṭikā*, *muhūrta*, day, night, fortnight, month, season, solstice, year, *yuga*, *kalpa*, and so forth.

His own nature is protected by his independent power, abiding within the essence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva; he has attained the state of being the sacrificial fire for all offerings, and is likewise established as the object of worship for those who dwell in disciplined restraint. He is skilled in bestowing gifts, a wish-fulfilling tree that completely fulfills the aspirations of those who worship him with their own devotion. Like the peaks of the Golden Mountain, he circumambulates the single wheel proclaimed by the Sole Lord, having purified the single path; thus, the entire circle of the world is rendered auspicious by his circumambulation.
May Brahmā, the sun whose form is present [here], having established his presence within the center of the divine trident—the weapon of Śiva—grant his grace. 10.

May Candra—the support of the life-breath of all the world, the illuminator of the seven worlds, beloved by the eyes of all people, the delighter of all beings, the lover of the night with his white rays, the lord of all medicinal herbs, the nectar-filled maker of the night, the true portion of the third eye of Atri, and the crest-jewel—having established his presence within the divine [disc] of Śiva’s weapon in its western part, grant his grace. 11.

Naked, adorned with serpents, dark as a fresh rain-cloud, with a pair of lotus-like hands shimmering with a skull-cup, having the immeasurable one (Viṣṇu) as his vehicle, possessing a blue beard and hair, in the form of a youth, decorated with a garland of skulls and ornaments, with tawny eyes and terrifying fangs, adorned with a garland of the heads of the Lord of the Gods severed in battle, wearing all kinds of jewel ornaments, the Guardian of the Field (Kṣetrapāla), having established his presence before the divine trident—its upper and lower parts [adorned]—may he grant his grace. 12.

May Caṇḍeśvara—the fierce one of fierce prowess; the commander of the army of the Wielder of the Broken Axe (Śiva); he who gazes with compassionate side-long glances; he who holds a chisel as a weapon in his hand; he who wears the remains of the offerings worshipped by the entire host of Gaṇas; whose food is what has been offered; who has attained the lordship of the Gaṇas through the destruction of his own father for opposing the worship of Maheśvara; and who bears a sharpened axe—having established his presence at the base of the divine trident-staff of Śiva’s weapon, may he grant his grace. 13.

May Lakṣmī—the abode within the constant embrace of Mukunda’s arms; she whose bodily beauty is like a mountain stream with twin waterfalls from the peaks of the slopes near her jeweled crown drenched by streams of nectar poured from golden jars held in the hands of Gandhasindhura, who resembles a mountain; she whose mass of hair is like that of Indra; she whose lotus-feet are worshipped by the gods of Indra; may she, seated upon the tip of the first petal of the divine trident-wielding Śiva’s weapon-lotus, grant her presence and bestow her grace. 14. (p.15b, l.1)

She who is the soul of all that is moving and unmoving; she who is skilled in the creation of the vast manifold universe (*prapañca*); she who is the cleverness of the four-faced Brahmā; she who is Brāhmī; she who is Maheśvarī, the playful consort of Śaṅkara—the Earth, Water, Sky, Wind, Fire, and Moon; she who is Kumārī, whose form is fashioned as Kārttikeya; she who is Vaiṣṇavī, who delights the faces of all gods, demons, and Viṣṇu; she who, by the grace of her lotus hands adorned with the plow, pestle, boon-granting gesture, and fear-dispelling gesture, has accomplished the destruction of the host of enemies.

May Cāmuṇḍī—the sovereign of wish-fulfilling creepers who brings about the destruction of the power of Mada at the end of the eon; whose innate majesty gladdens all objects of sense; who is the great Indra to the entire world; who possesses a divine trident as her weapon; and who dwells upon the tip of the southern petal of the lotus—having established her presence there, may she grant her grace. 15.

O Goddess who destroys the destruction of those in distress, who bears the conch, discus, trident, mace, and sword; O You who remove the pride of the demon Mahiṣāsura—O Durgā, who dwells on the mountain slopes, who possesses great joy, and who holds the auspicious divine trident and lotus upon the tip of its northern petal: having made Your presence here, grant Your grace! 16.
Mahādeva, Śiva, Rudra, Śaṅkara, Nīlalohita,
Īśāna, Vijaya, Bhīma, Devadeva,
Bhavodbhava, and Kapālīśa— thus is Rudra proclaimed as the eleventh.
May these eleven Rudras be present here.
(17) Vaikartana, Vivasvat, Mārtāṇḍa, Bhāskara, Ravi, Lokaprakāśaka, Lokasākṣin, and Trivikrama. (18)
May Āditya, Sūrya, Aṃśumālin, Divākara, and the others—thus the twelve Ādityas—be present here. 18.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, and Cāmuṇḍā—these are the Seven Mothers. May these Seven Mothers be present here. 19.
May the divine Nāsatyas, the Aśvins—the deities Vinibhadra-aśvin—be present as the presiding deities of the Aśvinī constellation. 20.
Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Agnilocana, Pratyuṣa, and Prabhāsa—these are proclaimed as the eight Vasus. (Verse 3) May these eight Vasus be present here. 21.

May the gods, the Daityas, the hosts of Dānavas, the seven types of Rākṣasas, the multitudes of Bhūtas, Pretas, Piśācas, and Kinnaras, as well as the Nāgas, Vidyādharas, Gandharvas, Guhyakas, Pitṛs, Yakṣas, and Kiṃpuruṣas—these Siddhas together with humans and sages, numbering eighteen groups—be present here. 22.
May Īśa, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta—the deities of the Heart, Crest, Head, Eye, and Weapon—be present as the deities of the inner enclosure; may they be well-disposed.
(23) May Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, Kalavikaraṇī, Balavikaraṇī, Balapramathanī, Sarvabhūtadamanī, and Manonmanī—these nine Śaktis—be present. (24)
May the eight Lords of Knowledge—Ananta, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Ekanetra, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śikhaṇḍin, and Śikhaṇḍī—be present here. 25.
May Nandi, Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgin, Vināyaka, Vṛṣabha-skanda, Devī, Caṇḍa, and the others—the lords of the Gaṇas—be present here. 26.
May these ten guardians of the world—Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Kubera, Īśāna, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu—be present here. 27.
May these ten weapons—the vajra, the śakti, the staff (daṇḍa), the sword, the noose, the goad, the mace, the trident, the lotus, and the discus—be present as the ten weapons. 28.

May the eight auspicious signs—the mirror, the full water-jar, the bull, the pair of chowries, the śrīvatsa, the svastika, the conch, and the two lamps—be present here as the eightfold auspiciousness. 29.
Asitāṅga, Ugra, Caṇḍa, Krodha, Amṛtabhairava, Kapāla, Bhīṣaṇa, and Sāhmāra—may these eight Bhairavas be present here. 30.

[Salutation] to the illustrious one, [who dwells within] the entire world of moving and stationary beings—humans, wild animals, beasts, birds, reptiles, as well as gods, demons, the best of sages, *siddhas*, *vidyādharas*, *yakṣas*, *rākṣasas*, *garuḍas*, *gandharvas*, *kinnaras*, *kiṃpuruṣas*, *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, *siddhayoginīs*, *ḍākinīs*, *śākinīs*, *brahmarākṣasas*, the hosts of planetary spirits, the stars, and all [creatures] including men, deer, cattle, fowl, and serpents; and within the worlds of earth (*bhūrloka*), atmosphere (*bhuvarloka*), heaven (*svarloka*), great light (*mahāloka*), the world of men (*janoloka*), the world of heat (*tapoloka*), and the world of truth (*satyaloka*); and within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), the egg of Brahmā, the egg of poison, the egg of Rudra, the egg of Viṣṇu, the egg of the egg, the outer egg, and the netherworld (*atala*).

The seven netherworlds beginning with Vitala, Nitala, Sutala, Rasātala, Talātala, and Mahātala; the eight great nāgas beginning with Ananta, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Koṭaka, Padma, Mahāpadma, Śaṅkhapāla, and Gulika; the great mountain Meru; the Himavat mountain, the Naṣadhā mountain, the Krauñca mountain; the great mountains such as Udaya, Asta, Malaya, Mandāra, and Kailāsa; and the seven oceans of salt, sugarcane juice, wine, clarified butter, curd, milk, and pure water, together with the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Sarasvatī rivers.

The Tuṅgabhadrā, Godāvarī, Kāverī, and Śoṇa rivers; Vyāsa, Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, Viśvāmitra, Bharadvāja, Bhṛgu, Mārtaṇḍeya, Hari, Yajñavalkya, and Vālmīki; the assembly of the nine planets, the ten guardians of the directions, the eleven Rudras, the twelve Ādityas, the eight Vasus, and the hosts of thirty-three crores of deities; the fourteen worlds, the fifteen lunar phases, and the sixteen vowels—these constitute the mantra of the feet, the great mantra, and the secondary mantra.

[It is] the path of *huṃ*, *phaṭ*, *svāhā*, *navaṣaṭ*, and *pavaṣaṭ*; of pleasure, pain, and the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; of the manifest (*vyakta*), the unmanifest (*avyakta*), the great principle (*mahat*), the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), the elements, and the senses; of that which is called the organ of speech, feet, hands, anus, and genitals; of speaking, coming and going, giving, excreting, and sexual bliss; of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell; of hearing, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose; and of the vital breaths—*prāṇa*, *apāna*, *vyāna*, *udāna*, and *samāna*—as well as the *nāga*, *kūrma*, *kṛkara*, *devadatta*, and *dhanañjaya* winds, and the channels *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *suṣumṇā*.

Śrīkaṇṭha and Pārvatī, together with the Nandā, Hastijihvā, Lampūṣā, Kuhu, Śakunī, Hālāhala, Viṣa, Amṛta, all worldly objects—both visible and invisible, eternal and non-eternal—the partless word and its referents, prose and verse, the systems of the Buddhists, Āhikas, Vaiśeṣikas, Naiyāyikas, Mīmāṃsakas, Cārvākas, Vāṇīyas, Bhavatas, Vātsyāyanas, the forms of words, the eighteen Smṛtis, the many Purāṇas, the Dharmaśāstras, the Tarkaśāstras, the Śabdaśāstras, and the Śaivāgamas.

For the sake of the auspicious service at the holy site of Navadinadhvajārohaṇa, [this is dedicated] to Śambhu—the Lord of the illustrious Govassāna—who is accessible through devotion to the Blessed One, who bestows the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation, who is the eternal bliss and auspiciousness residing in the hearts of the sages, the bearer of the Gaṅgā, the Leader of the Gaṇas, the one free from passion, the Three-Eyed One, and the Beloved of Pārvatī; and to Caṇḍeśvara, the commander of the army of Śaṅkara, who has come here for that purpose.

With drums, lutes, flutes, *bhaṇavālaka*, *kāhala*, kettledrums, cymbals, clay drums, *muraja*, *jhallari*, conchs, tabors, and other such instruments—in this secluded place, amidst the sounding of these drums, I perform the proclamation: "Homage to the glorious Gurus! The drum-beating is complete. May there be auspiciousness for Śiva! Homage to the Guru! (Navasandhi, p. 19b, f14a, l.
1) I bow to the divine Bull, whose form is white in color, who possesses sharp horns, whose feet are the Vedas, the joy of Śambhu, and the vehicle of the Lord—white as the moon and the jasmine.

I salute Nandin, the giver of dharma, who delights [the world], who is always surrounded by the foremost of the gods and by the chief Gaṇas led by Śailādi, who is constantly praised with hymns, whose deep-sounding roar from his throat causes the earth and the worlds to tremble, and who is the protector of the faithful. He resembles a rampart formed by a multitude of mountains beautified by the slopes of the mountain forests, which are draped in accordance with the timing of the ocean tides, and adorned with necklaces, armlets, and jeweled crowns of millions of glorious golden gems.

To Śambhu, who delights in many [forms], whose pair of lotus-feet are forever bowed to by the daughter of the mountain (Pārvatī), who is like the youthful orb of the sun to the lotus-face of the Mountain’s Daughter, and whose four feet—which are the Vedas and the very essence of Dharma—are the abode of Viṣṇu; [and] to the Lord of Bulls, who has made the quarters of space tawny with masses of thick, golden dust raised up from his hooves, and who is accompanied by the divine dwellers of the atmosphere, the earth, and the netherworld, such as the Puṣkalāvartaka and other great clouds.

Together with all the hosts of gods, for the sake of serving the auspicious festival of the Navadinadhvaja-ārohaṇa at Tīrtha, let the people come to Vṛṣabheśvara—the Blessed Supreme Lord Śambhu, who holds the power of creation, maintenance, destruction, and concealment of the entire world and heaven, and whose glorious Govatsanātheśvara has been protected by Caṇḍeśvara, the commander of Śaṅkarasena.

... with musical instruments such as the *samā*, clay drum (*mṛdaṅga*), lute (*vīṇā*), flute (*veṇu*), *śivatāla*, *kāhala*, kettle-drum (*bherī*), large drum (*maddala*), *murava*, *jhallarī*, conch (*śaṅkha*), and *paṭaha*, I cause the great sound of the assembly of drums to resound. ... ॥

The Bull, the celebrated one, the celebrated one with celebrated broad arms; endowed with the mountain-bow of the essence of the hooves’ center; O fierce one who protects the world; Indra, flower after flower; where? where? the Bull, the Bull, the coiled one, the coiled one—this is the banner of Śiva’s vehicle; the circular *maṭhi*; the most auspicious wild beast of the forest; by the cow of the mountain-pass; for the sake of the goal of those whose birth is laughed at by the planets; the bliss of enjoyment, the particularity of the word of ultimate reality.

That which is the sound of the five great notes, the dance, the offering of flower-petals, the passion, the pure *varālī*, and the five-fold beauty within the leaves—to you, the divine Brahmā, homage! To you, the lotus-born, homage! To the Lord of Causes, homage! To you, the four Vedas, homage! I salute the four-faced god, Brahmā, the lotus-born, the Golden Womb (*Hiraṇyagarbha*), the Creator, the Grandfather of gods and asuras, who delights in milking the honey that flows from the Vedic scriptures of his glorious lotus-face.

(1.5) Salutation to You, the sole abode of Dharma, the self-existent Lord of the entire universe, whose majesty is like that of lightning, bees, enemies, the Gaṅgā, the snowy peaks, and the moon; who is beloved by the lady of speech; who creates the joy of those bowed down by their devotion and who is the life-breath of all living beings—to You, the Brahman, I bow. Indeed, Brahmā has the luster of golden color and eyes like the sun; ... [he is] four-faced and two-armed, with a water-pot in his left hand, and in his right hand he holds the gesture of granting boons (*varada*) and a rosary.

O Hara, mounted upon the swan, with matted locks crowning your head, you who are the servant of the Lord of the Gods—may you be served! O Śiva, come quickly on this day of festival; may you hasten to our assembly. You who have entered the essence of all that is moving and unmoving—the entire multitude of gods, asuras, humans, beasts, cattle, birds, those born from eggs, those born from moisture, and the rest of the beings included within the three worlds, along with the dense networks of trees, mountains, and all other entities—O Śeṣaka... O Hiraṇyagarbha, Pitāmaha, Prabhañjana, [and] Kṣīroda-dadhi...

In the midst of a golden necklace, which was adorned with smooth drops of perspiration born from passion for the ocean’s shore and which clung to her breasts—smeared with thick saffron and sandalwood paste made pleasant by the gentle breeze—the Supreme Lord, Prajāpati, the Creator, the Source of the Universe, Viriñca, the progenitor of all the world, [was seated] upon the lotus-born Brahmā, who had arisen from the navel-lotus of Viṣṇu, whose lotus-feet were massaged by the gods delighted by the light of day.

He is endowed with the four faces, the lotus, the Vedas, and the specialized knowledge resulting from the investigation of the Vedāṅgas; he is encircled by the perfection of exertion and possesses the eight great powers (*aṣṭamahābhūtaya*): *aṇimā*, *mahimā*, *garimā*, *laghimā*, *prāpti*, *prākāmya*, *īśitva*, and *vaśitva*. He is the protector of the manifold world, the one who speaks, whose brow is adorned with three lines, and who is the source of the divisions of time—*lava*, *kāṣṭhā*, *ghaṭī*, *muhūrta*, day and night, fortnights, months, solstices, years, and kalpas—and who is seated upon a lotus throne in the lotus posture.

"Let Brahmā—the Lord who effects the creation, maintenance, destruction, concealment, and grace of all the worlds and heavens, and who is fond of the five notes beginning with *brahma* and *tāla*—come here together with the entire host of deities, at the command of the Supreme Lord (*Parameśvara*), which is observed by Caṇḍeśvara, the lord of the Middle Quarter and commander of Śaṅkara’s army. Thus, [the drummers] played the mṛdaṅga, vīṇā, flute, bhaṇava, tāla, kāhala, bherī, maddala, muraja, jhallarī, conch, and paṭaha drums.

With various musical instruments, I here make this proclamation with the sounding of the *bherī* drum: "O Beloved of the Lotus, Supreme Cause of Causes, Primordial Four-faced One, Beloved of Sundara! Beloved of Sundara! O Hiraṇyagarbha, Grandfather—[this is] uninterrupted by the dancing and the rhythmic gestures (*nirṅgita*) of the *bherī*, *maddala*, *muraja*, *jhallarī*, conch, *kāhala*, and *gadha* drums. This is known as the great *tāla*; it is known as the *Tattadbrahma-tāla*. The *veda* is the *pañcapaṇa*; the dance is with feet together; or the song is the time.

To the Lord of the Vedas, accompanied by musical instruments, sacred knowledge, and rhythmic beats; who holds a water-pot in his hand, whose vehicle is a swan, who is together with his limbs, weapons, and retinue—along with Śakti, and adorned with all ornaments—I invoke Brahmā in such a form.

I perpetually bow to Mahendra, the supreme lord of the gods, the bestower of boons, the illustrious one; to Indra, whose form is the thunderbolt, the destroyer of Vṛtra—homage, homage! To him who is the lord of sacrifice, who possesses mountains, kunda flowers, sandalwood, and nectar, [and] whose mount is Airāvata surrounded by hosts [of attendants]; to him who has abandoned pride in mounting the shoulders [of his elephant], who is the delight of the gods in Mandāra groves; to him who sports with playful abandon, while his beloved Gautamī, with her firm, high, and beautiful breasts, embraces him tightly—I bow always to that great Indra.

Indra, dark-bodied, with eyes [wide] from sudden joy, holding the thunderbolt, mounted upon his elephant-vehicle, accompanied by the moon and surrounded by gods and lords of sages—may Hara, who is to be served by the Lord of Gods at his command amidst the sound of kettledrums, dancing, and singing during today’s festival, quickly come to you. May he arrive swiftly!

[He who is] the lotus in the nectar-water of the beauty of his own body, upon whose pair of feet the rays of the rubies from the crowns of all the celestial women are arrayed; [he who is] more charming than the garlands of *pārijāta* flowers being offered by the sandalwood forest deities of the thousand-eyed Indra; [he who is] the beloved of those whose gait is measured in equal time-steps; [he who is] the cause of the creation, maintenance, destruction, concealment, and grace of the entire world and the splendor of heaven; [he who is] the Lord of the Eastern Quarter, protected by the command of the Blessed Supreme Lord.

I grant that great favor to Caṇḍeśvara, the commander of Śaṅkarasena, so that he may not go together with all the hosts of Indra—those who increase the glory and desire [of the gods], who possess beautiful forms, who pervade the universe, and who are swift—as well as with the hosts of the Indras. I perform this for him.

The great sound of the Lord of the Gods, who stands at the beginning of the *prakrama* [meter] and has caused the expansion of the formless Lord, which is desired by the gods and causes the destruction of the three worlds; which was made before the city of Indra and before the city of Śiva; "O Indra, we fear this Veda"—the forest of leaves, the dance on the tips of the arms, the song accompanied by musical instruments with equal rhythm.

O Lord of Devas, to him who has a vajra in hand, whose mount is Airāvata, who is accompanied by his limbs, his weapons, and his retinue, who is endowed with his powers, and who is adorned with all ornaments—to such a one, I invoke Indra. *Namaḥ* to Indra! I present this *bali*: these perfumes, unbroken grains, flowers, incense, lamps, excellent garments, ornaments, and other decorations—these are all the ritual services (*upacāras*). *Namaḥ* to Agni, to the one of fierce form, and to Vaiśvānara.

To you, who are the form of universal withdrawal, the life-force of the world, the embodied one—to that very you, the seven-flamed fire who pervades everything, whose body directly bears the form of the Lord himself; by whose banner alone, shimmering like a ram, the entire world is offered as an oblation to the flesh-eaters, even while it is being consumed.

Since [the world] consisting of moving and unmoving beings, beginning with the flesh-eaters (*kravyād*), has been withdrawn into that Supreme One—O Agni, red-bodied, with a radiant face, endowed with the seven tongues and the rest, offered into the garland of flames, joined with the crest of fire, mounted upon a ram, bearing a golden lotus, a spear, and a *tomara* weapon, beloved of the power of Svāhā-Agni—may you, together with the various winds, quickly come to this blazing crest! Hail! May there be well-being for the entire assembly of world-protectors, together with cows, Brahmins, and kings, who are full of auspicious countenances. (p. 24a)

[This is] the abundance of the dharma of the established sectarian division, the abundance of the lineage, the abundance of virtuous conduct, the abundance of all dwellings, the abundance of material wealth, the abundance of the patron, the abundance of cattle and buffaloes, and the abundance of female and male servants—belonging to the Guru, the Supreme Lord, the Blessed One who has been realized through forceful means; [it concerns] the establishment of the rules arising from the abundance of the subjects, the propitiation, the offerings, the mudrās, the specific exertions, the daily festivals, the monthly festivals, the annual festivals, and the great festivals such as those of the Vedas.

O Vaiśvānarā, whose form is pure, who possesses the power of the submarine fire (*baḍavāmukha*) within the thick golden enclosure, whose weapon is the strength of the bearer of oblations (*havyavāha*), who is the pacified, self-controlled, primordial command, and the vision of the Fire-god; O Svāhā, O Svadhā, you who consist of the essence of the offered light, who dwell in the lotus-hand of Pavana, Mitra, and Śaṅkara, who are the sanctifier of the self and the complete gratification of the hosts of gods, whose nature is the sacrificial offerings to gods and ancestors (*havyakavya*), who are beloved by the Lord of Kollī when the sounds of the Vedas are bound with honey and offered as oblations, and who reside in the city of Tejavatī.

"By the command of Caṇḍeśvara, the commander of Śaṅkarasena, who is obeying the decree of the Supreme Lord—the author of the creation, maintenance, destruction, concealment, and grace of all worlds and heavens—come together with the entire host of Agnis led by Śampati of the South, East, and Center! Thus, at his order, I cause this proclamation by the sounding of drums to be made here with the music of mṛdaṅgas, vīṇās, flutes, vaṇavas, tālakas, kāhalas, bherīs, maddalas, murajas, jhallaris, conchs, paṭahas, and other instruments."

The blood, the blood of the stringed [instrument]... the blood of the stringed [instrument]—the blood produced by the eye, the jaw, the house, and the hand—the blood; the crest-jewel of Nandi’s matted hair—ḍama ḍama ḍaṃ—krikitaṃ krikitaṃ—the Gaṅgā, the water, the high pride, the high pride of the water—the swift movement of the gait, the swift movement of the gait, the measure of the wrestler—the womb within the hollow of the protection-house—the womb—the darkness of the hands at the waist of the protector—the increase, the increase—the burning bestowed upon the thunderbolt.

Haṃ kricataṃ kricataṃ – O supreme teacher of the gods, on the rugged slope of the curved bank of the celestial river, on that ruggedly fashioned slope of his stride, [I perform] this dance: the fifth, the *āṅkoli*; the song is the *varāli*; the instrumental music is the *baddhāvaṇa*.

To the Lord of Splendor, who holds a spear in his hand, whose vehicle is a ram—to him with his limbs, his weapons, his vehicle, his retinue, accompanied by his Śakti, adorned with all ornaments—I thus invoke Agni.

Mounted upon a buffalo, bearing a banner of smoke and holding a staff and a noose—wrathful, the terrifier of the world, with three eyes, and possessing a staff-like body like Time (Kāla)—accompanied by hosts of *bhūtas* and *pretas*, by the command of the Lord of Gods whose body is impure: "Be served by you who have become knowers of the *hara-utsava*; come together quickly! Homage to you, Dharmarāja; homage to Vaivasvata; homage to Yama, the god; homage to you, O All, the witness of all!

He who is free from the fear of merit and demerit, and from the fear of what has been done or left undone; whose weapon is a fierce and massive staff; the ornament of the family of Caṇḍāśoka; who is adorned with various vows unto the end;

whose banner is beautiful with the rope of a great buffalo upon a mountain-like base of elemental beings; who resembles a joyful dark cloud that shatters [all things]; he who is ever beloved by those who have performed their duties.

Victory, victory to you, O eye of the world’s welfare! You who have abandoned forest-dwelling, O refuge of the deities, compassionate toward devotees who have sought your protection, abode of mercy, O Śāntāka, O Śāntāka...

"Let those who come for the purpose of serving the auspicious rites beginning with the mounting of the banner and ending with the *tīrtha* [ablution] of the venerable Govatsanātheśvara Śambhu—the ancient Puruṣa, whose lotus-like pair of feet are bowed to by the supreme lord of the gods, Paśupati, who is the bestower of boons in the forms of water, fire, the sacrificial fire, wind, and space; who holds the young moon upon his crest, which is dear to all the gods; and who is the self-born Lord—be provided with water."

The son of the thousand-rayed one (the Sun), accompanied by the Lord of the Southern Quarter, Dharmarāja Vaivasvata, Citragupta, Mitra, the parasol, and the fly-whisks; he who possesses the skill to traverse the three worlds while occupied with the thought of refining the dharma and non-dharma of all people; the illustrious [name] whose vehicle is the buffalo; together with Bhṛṅginī, who dwells in the city of Yama and protects the entire world—[these were] united in the *tāla* [dance].

"Let them come together with Kauśika, Svarapriya, the Seven Mothers, and all the hosts of Dharma-dwellers from the heavens, the atmosphere, the earth, and the netherworld"—this is the proclamation by the beating of the drum made by Caṇḍeśvara, the commander-in-chief of Śaṅkarasena.

Resembling a *sārisārisūri*, resembling a *sāri*, with water resembling the appearance of a *liṅga* and *kāka*; resembling "kaha kaha," resembling "kā kā," [he] offered to the Lord of the Pretas a sharp sword that was like a jar of wine filled with living beings—a sword skilled at warding off those various jars—[an offering] consisting of the Vedas, the fragrance of the earth, fearlessness, a merchant from Kauśika, a dance marked by staff-like feet, the music of Rāmagiri, and the surface of the earth [offered] by Bhṛṅgin.

To the one with staff in hand, whose vehicle is a buffalo, together with his limbs, weapons, vehicles, and retinue, accompanied by his spear, adorned with all ornaments—to Yama of such a form, I invoke you. Homage to the one devoted to the Śarabha, the Lord of the Daityas; homage be to you—the Lord of the Rākṣasas, the Great Stirrer... [mahāmīrite]... ॥

I bow to the Lord of Creatures (Paśupati), who causes fear even to the hare-marked moon, who is surrounded by Vetālas, Bhūtas, and other spirits, whose mouth is like a fire blazing with flames, and who has formed a stream of essence from blood; he whose body is pierced by faith, who is red and clad in red garments, the protector of the world, the remover of all hair [or sins], the terrifying one who destroys the fear of birth, old age, and impure karma for those dwelling therein—the instruction that subdues the young.

"Let them come together with the entire host of the Nairṛtas—those who possess the splendor of the *lakṣa*, the self-nature, the protectors, the sword-holders, the hair, the wrestlers, the palm-tree banks, and the sound of the *bhrāṣa*; those who are beloved by all the worlds and heavens; those who maintain the creation, preservation, and destruction [of the universe]; those who uphold the command of the Supreme Lord (*Parameśvara*); and those who dwell in the southern, western, and central quarters, as well as in the divine realm of Nirṛti, the atmosphere, the earth, and the depths of the netherworld (*pātāla*). Thus, at the command of Caṇḍeśvara, the commander-in-chief of Śaṅkarasena, let the various drums, lutes, flutes, cymbals, and trumpets proclaim [this].

I perform the *mārava-jhallarī* dance. [O Goddess] whose playful glance is the second eye agitated by the pair of eyes on the chest-ornament of the protector; who, O Sarabha, bears a straight lordliness that devours the hearts of those who have been humbled; whose lotus-face is praised for its wandering, heavy dance performed with the play of moving eyebrows; who possesses a dark-blue neck-jewel with trembling sheaths, which, though black and fierce, is a devourer of the sluggish Kali-age and a source of delight. That very [neck-jewel], dark-blue with trembling sheaths, is a devourer of the sluggish Kali-age and a source of delight.

He considers this Veda—[performed] with a mind of self-conceit, with the *iccaparṇa* [leaf], and with the *naṭṭa* dialect; the dance is accompanied by the triple song of serpents, with the *malāhāri* rhythm. To him who has blood-red eyes, who is mounted upon a corpse, who holds a sword in his hand, together with his limbs, his weapons, his vehicle, and his retinue—to him who is accompanied by his spear, adorned with all ornaments—I thus invoke Nirṛti. Homage to the one with golden horns! Homage to you who hold a noose in your hand! Homage!

I take refuge in Varuṇa, the wise and supreme lord known as Pracetas, who is eternally worthy of homage; he whose palace is ever-expanding and variegated with red hues, who bears the noose as his weapon, who is the treasury of the waters, the clay-soldier, the wondrous one whose banner is the crocodile, and who is surrounded by beautiful, singing, and playful women of exquisite form.

In which all the moments were satisfied by oblations of various forms of *trai-mantra* and *sarpis* (clarified butter) issuing from the mouths of distinguished sages who were experts in the entirety of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas; and in which there was an abundance of rain, free from the calamities of Indra, Āditya, and Parjanya, arising from the various species of trees such as the *candana*, *nāga-keśara*, *aśoka*, *sajjigita*, *kadamba*, *punnāga*, *mallikā*, *mandāraka*, *kunda*, and *kuravaka*.

Nandyāvarta, pāṭala, lotus, panasa, karṇikāra, bhṛelā, lavaṅga, lāmajjaka, bakula, prāsantā, śamyā, arka, śatapatra, bilva leaves, bandhūka...ṇa, dhūrdhūra, kunda, arka, kumuda, kuravaka, nīlotpala, ...ja, santānaka—[these] leaves, flowers, fruits, roots, and [the four kinds of food: solid food (bhakṣya), soft food (bhojya), food to be licked (lehya), and food to be sucked (coṣya), as well as perfumes and flowers.

For the purpose of serving the auspicious festivals from the "Climbing of the Banner on the Ninth Day" (Navadinadhvajārohaṇa) onwards, [this is offered] for the propitiation through the elaborate presentation of offerings—including incense, lamps, ghee, honey, clarified butter, special sugar-candies, jaggery, sesame, mung-bean rice, lentil soup with rice, pure rice, *vilopa* side-dishes, *takola*, betel, lotus-like hands, the three *jātī* flowers, the three *bhallātaka* fruits, the three pungents, the charming citron, and divine side-dishes—to Mahādeva, who is the bow of meditation for the multitude of worshipful offerings, who is honored by all the worlds, the illustrious Govatsadādhāśvara Śambhu.

Hiraṇyaśru...gāvaruṇa-paśupati—whose hand is turned back, whose splendor is endowed with nine *tālas*, who is beloved for his voice and desire—[and you] who dwell in the city of young women! Together with the hosts of gods who protect the command of the Blessed Supreme Lord—the author of the creation, maintenance, destruction, concealment, and grace of the entire world—come along the path! Thus do I issue the command of Caṇḍeśvara, the commander of Śaṅkara’s army.

I praise that Veda, which is a fortress for the house-dwelling crane, a difficult-to-traverse mountain whose slopes are graced by the playful movements of the Sandhyā river; where the lotuses of the feet of the Lord—beautiful and continuous upon his slender body—move like the Vindhya range; whose neck is adorned with jewels... [and] who, together with his friend, again displays the pride of the Mind-born God (Kāma); who sports in the ocean tossed by the palms of his hands; who is the very essence of that sport in the ocean moved by his palms; whom I, bowing as a Brahmin, praise—[this is] the dance of the Parṇaśrī-rāga, performed with curved gestures and song.

O Kuñjarī—[this] music in nine *tālas* [is for] Varuṇa, the Lord of the West, who holds a noose in his hand, whose vehicle is a makara, together with his limbs, weapons, vehicle, retinue, and powers, adorned with all ornaments; such as he is, I invoke him.

Salutations to the Wind, the soul of all principles, the primordial and illustrious one who exists under various names such as Prāṇa and others; I bow to Vāyu, whose form is manifold, who bears fragrance, whose body is the most excellent river, and who consists of the essence of existence. He is the eternal stage for the multitude of living beings and all creatures, the deer-marked banner, the protector of the three worlds including Indra, Upendra, and Pitāmaha; O Lord, be gracious and grant your supreme self to all without exception.

The primary cause of the birth, prosperity, movement, and destruction of all specific objects—both moving and unmoving—that constitute the entirety of the universe; born of space, the cause of the destruction of the cities of the wind-god through the force of his flames; born of fire, the cause of the stability of bodies divided by the various names of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth which pervade space; possessing the quality of sound residing within; endowed with the power of consciousness that expands at the time of the dissolution of the internal organs; the wind for the lotus-faces of all the assembly of sages; the hollow of the sky.

The earth was shaken by the movement of his hands and feet, stirred by the wind from thousands of young reeds; his fingers, like lotus-stalks, propelled the ground. The ten-headed Rāvaṇa was reduced to a pool of blood flowing from his feet, hands, face, neck, shoulders, and trunk. As the sound of the chant rose, [he fell before] the cause of the moving and unmoving world, who is radiant, whose nature consists of the parasol, ornaments, and mantras...

I compose [this work] for the venerable Govardhananātheśvara, who honors the entire world. [I praise him whose] body is lofty like the gait of an elephant in rut; [whose] lotus-feet are shaken by the breeze fragrant with the humming of bees; who is adorned with earrings that serve as ornaments for his nearby shoulders; and who, with the sound of his *ḍamaru* drum—*ḍama-ḍama*—which hangs from the celestial tree, causes the surface of the earth to tremble, and with his moving small bells... [his face] beautiful with a lotus... [Note: The ellipses indicate the damaged portions of the manuscript.]

O you whose supreme dance is suited to the tumultuous clamor appropriate for the assembly of celestial nymphs; O you who possess manifold qualities gathered within your hanging bodice; O you who sport simultaneously upon the surface of the earth at the shore of the Vedas—at that very moment, simultaneously upon the surface of the earth... [the various [beings]...]

With palms joined in the ten-syllable *tāla* gesture, red as a ripe pomegranate, dancing with the grace of a serpent—O Keśin, I invoke Hari, the Lord of the Banner. I invoke the Wind-god (*Vāyu*) in such a form: together with his limbs, weapons, and vehicle; accompanied by his retinue and his powers; adorned with all ornaments. I bow to Soma, the gentle one, the lord of the moon, whose form is nectar, who serves as the crest-jewel of Śiva, and who is the cause of the world’s prosperity.

I bow to the one who possesses the speed of a yogi through contemplation, the vehicle of great bliss that brings flowers, the staff that eternally pervades this entire universe by means of the sequence of treasures, the lord of protection, the crest-jewel of the moon, the dear friend and refuge of the wish-fulfilling gem, who dwells within all hopes, a treasury of virtues, wondrous, and bearing diverse weapons.

...the great time that determines the end of the world, which, due to its vast internal expanse, causes the entire universe—including all gods and asuras—to whirl in a great, slow rotation; which, from behind the various musical performances rendered agitated by that expanse, is endowed with a massive form that serves as an ornament for the crest-jewel of Śiva’s matted locks, resembling the softness of Lakṣmī’s sister (the Yamunā)...

I perform [this] for Caṇḍeśvara, the commander of Śaṅkarasena, who comes for the purpose of serving the auspicious evening rites at the holy ford beginning with the flag-raising on the ninth day of the lord Śambhu, the glorious Govatsanātha—the increaser of the vigor of Cupid, whose cause is gentle radiance, consisting of sixteen digits, the path of the play of white luster, whose entire body is marked by the movement of the steps of his beloved Svarapriyā, the destroyer of poison, the lover of Rohiṇī.

Today, [he is] white like a blooming night-lotus, possessing a magnificent and auspicious splendor; his eyes are fixed upon the entire creation situated within the white lotus of his own heart. He is eternally exalted by the assembly of perfected and renowned sages, eternally pure, eternally marvelous, abundant, variegated, and praiseworthy for a long time—beautiful with various such praiseworthy qualities. May Soma offer this Veda as a cow of plenty.

With the *varṇa-rāga*, the *gauḍī-tāla*, the *ḍaḥ-karita-tāla*, the dance, the *āṅkucita* [gesture], and the *parṇa-tatkeśi* [rhythm]. I invoke Kubera, who is mounted upon his horse, together with his limbs, his weapons, and his spear, adorned with all ornaments—Kubera in such a form, I invoke.

Salutations to Śiva, the peaceful one, the distinguished one who possesses eight forms—to Īśāna, upon whom all things depend, for the destruction of the hair [of ignorance], the tranquil one. I repeatedly praise you, the three-eyed one, who bears the terrifying ornaments of Śrī, whose weapon is the sharp axe, whose lofty banner is the preeminent bull, who is risen from the sacrificial pillar, radiant, smeared with ashes, accompanied by Pāṇḍurāga, resembling a joyful dark cloud, self-controlled, and the subduer of Kṛtānta.

Ever [established], he is one who is immovable in his restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), perfected in the meaning of all the scriptures, and who—like a medicinal tree of the nectar of yoga—is the burner of Tripura, whose eyes are flowers for the multitude of those devoted to Someśvara, Kālamukha, Sundarakaṅkāladhara, and Bhairava, and who has severed the bonds of the entire mass of hair, the slaughter of animals, pride, intoxication, envy, passion, hatred, and the attainment of the states of *sālokya*, *sāmīpya*, *sārūpya*, and *sāyujya*, as well as the constant practice of right conduct and all forms of pain and terror.

For the purpose of serving the auspicious festivals beginning with the Navadinadhvajārohaṇa at the holy site of Śrīmad-Govatsanātheśvara—Śambhu, who is Īśāna, Tryambaka, and Trailokyanātha—the venerable [king], whose lotus feet are praised by the entire host of celestial beauties, who bears the emblem of the bull, who is rich in fame, and who is dear to Kālapāṇi and Svara, [acts] for the sake of the Lord, the Supreme Sovereign, who effects the creation, maintenance, destruction, concealment, and grace of all worlds and heavens, and who is protected by the command of the Blessed One.

"May they come together with all the hosts of deities, beginning with Īśāna, who delight in the directions beginning with Īśāna"—by the command of Caṇḍeśvara, the commander of Śaṅkara’s army, I shall cause the proclamation of the drums to be made day and night with musical instruments such as mṛdaṅgas, vīṇās, flutes, bhaṇavas, tālakas, kāhalas, bherīs, maddalas, murajas, jhallaris, conchs, and paṭahas.

I worship Him who is saluted by the lotus-born [Brahmā], whose ears are like conch shells, whose beautiful feet possess the tinkling of small bells, whose throat is like a conch, who is white as a lotus, whose face is like the orb of the moon, whose abode is the peak of the White Mountain [Kailāsa], who dwells in the ocean, who is praised by auspicious waters, and who removes [all suffering]. The Veda says: "He is the Lord of all sciences... [I worship Him] whose hands are the school of letters, whose feet dance upward, and who is celebrated with graceful song and instrumental music.

*Karitālam*: To Īśāna, the Lord of the Trident, whose vehicle is the bull, together with his limbs (*sāṅga*), his secret consort (*sapīṭha*), his vehicle (*savāhana*), his retinue (*saparivāra*), accompanied by his power (*saśakti*), adorned with all ornaments—to Īśāna of such a nature, I invoke you. These offerings of perfume, unbroken rice, flowers, incense, lamps, food, betel, and other ornaments—these are all the services; may there be auspiciousness. *Śrī gurubhyo namaḥ*. (The remainder is blank; page 33a is blank; page 33b, f28a: *hariḥ om*, *śubham astu*). ... *Om iti digbandhaḥ*. Meditation (*dhyānam*):

Having performed the *ratnāmbhodhi* austerity and restrained the vital breaths (*prāṇāyāma*), on this meritorious lunar day distinguished by such specific qualities, [this is the record] of the illustrious Sadāśiva—the embodiment of Śiva who consists of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) comprising letters, words, mantras, principles (*tattva*), worlds, and kalās; whose nature is both with and without parts (*sakala-niṣkala*); and of the illustrious Govatsanātheśvara, the one known as the lotus-mouth of Tatpuruṣa, the initiator of the tradition of the true lineage of practice belonging to the illustrious Govatsanātheśvara.

For the sake of the increase of security, stability, longevity, health, and sovereignty for the Prince—born under the asterism Amogha in the [such-and-such] lunar mansion—as well as for the King together with his family, his kingdom, and his treasury; for the sake of attaining an abundance of elephants, horses, buffalo, and other livestock; and for the sake of obtaining many virtuous sons endowed with beauty, good fortune, and long life, [this is] dedicated to the illustrious Lord Govatsanātha.

For the sake of pleasing the deity Govatsanātheśvara, [this festival] called the *utsava*, preceded by the hoisting of the banner for the glorious Govatsanātheśvara on the ninth day, shall be performed; and on the twelfth day (*dvādaśāhne*), during the *iṣu* [month], as circumstances permit, there shall be the offering of the sprout of the banner for the Lord of the Festival (*utsaveśvara*)—namely Candraśekhara and others—the worship of the Lord of the Festival, the offering of food, the worship of the *liṅga*, the trident, the bull, the cloth, the water-jar, the drum, the bull-sacrifice, the fire-oblation (*homa*), the oblation for heaven (*svargāhuti*), and the consecration of life (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*).

At the base of the banner (*dhvaja*), for the purpose of hoisting the banner, its constituent expiatory oblations (*prāyaścittāhuti*), the sprinkling [of water], the offering of the *mūlabali*, the beating of the drum (*bherītāḍana*), the recitation of the *Utsaveśvara-stotra* and the *Annaliṅga-raudrapāśupata-mantra*, the invocation of the trident (*triśūlāvāhana*), the beating of the drum, the traditional benedictions for the kingdom, the mantras of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), the minister, the offering of the festival sprouts (*utsavāṅkurārpaṇa*), the tying of the auspicious thread (*kautukabandhana*), the consecration (*saṃskāra*), the worship of the Lord of Sacrifice (*yāgeśvarārādhana*), the Śiva-sacrifice (*śivayāga*), the fire-oblation (*homa*), the offerings to the deities of the directions, the circumambulation, and the sounding of the conch on the day of the festival... [line 2]... the sounding of the trumpet (*dhāṇeṇe*).

At that time, while performing the respective rites for the festival of Utsaveśvara—including the bathing, water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), the special food offering (*viśeṣa-naivedya*), the royal services (*rājopacāra*), the hunt procession (*mṛgayātrā*), the binding of the auspicious thread (*kautuka-bandhana*) for Naṭeśvara, the festival of Naṭeśvara, the binding of the auspicious thread for the sake of the sacred ford (*tīrtha*), the powder festival of the auspicious thread (*kautukatīrthacūrṇotsava*), the great sacred ford (*mahātīrtha*), the full-oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), the sacrifice of Yāgeśvara, the consecration with the ritual jar (*kumbhābhiṣecana*), the great bathing (*mahāsnāna*), the hoisting of the banner (*dhvajārohaṇa*), the offerings to the guardians of the world and their vehicles (*lokapālavāhana*), the silent oblation (*maunabali*), the festival of Gaurī, the sacrifice of Caṇḍa, the flower sacrifice (*puṣpayāga*), and the various rituals of the daily festival (*nityotsava*).

As an ancillary part of that, first, for the purpose of purifying all the materials—such as the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*), the celestial chariot (*vimāna*), the gate-tower (*gopura*), the temple (*prāsāda*), and the implements of sacrifice—in accordance with the method taught in the *Śrīkaraṇāgama*, I shall perform, together with the Śiva-brahmins headed by Caṇḍeśvara and the Pramathins, using substances produced from the primordial source (*sambhavasthiti*), the recitation of the *svasti* and *puṇyāha* mantras, distinguished by Mahādeva. May there be auspiciousness!
(The Ritual of the Śiva Festival).
Now, we shall explain the sequence of the ritual for the Śiva festival.

On the day preceding the appointed date—whether it be seven or nine days prior—one should begin the rite of depositing the sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*). In the evening, one should collect the earth. Accompanied by a trident, a bronze vessel, a jar, three water-pots, a spade, incense, lamps, jaggery, plantains, coconuts, perfumes, unbroken rice, flowers, cloth, and betel leaves, the Guru, together with his attendants and devotees, should proceed from the village toward the east or the north, to the bank of a river, the shore of a lake, or to a garden or forest.

Having approached a pure location on a cleared ground measuring three cubits, and having sprinkled it with water while reciting the *astra-mantra*, one should place a trident in the east and a spade in the south; then, sitting oneself facing east, having restrained the vital breaths (*prāṇāyāma*), [one should perform] the *maha*... on an auspicious lunar day distinguished by such specific qualities.

On the day preceding the day specified for the flag-hoisting ceremony (*dhvajārohaṇa*), intending to perform the collection of earth (*mṛtsaṃgrahaṇa*) as a constituent part of that rite—for the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord, for the attainment of the fourfold human goals consisting of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, for the pleasure of this deity, and for the propitiation of the deities—[the officiant], together with the great assembly, first [proceeds] for the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the purification of the ritual materials (*dravyaśuddhi*), and the purification of the self (*ātmaśuddhi*).

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) that "I shall proclaim the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) distinguished by Mahādeva," and having again performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) at the conclusion of the *puṇyāha* rite, one should make the resolve: "On this auspicious lunar day, characterized by such specific qualities, I shall perform the collection of earth and its worship as an ancillary part of the raising of the banner for that deity. Then, in the east: *oṃ hāṃ śivāstrāsanāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ śivāstramūrtaye namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ śivāstrāya namaḥ*. In the south: *oṃ hāṃ kuddālyāstrāya namaḥ*.

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the embodiment of the Kuddālī weapon. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Kuddālī weapon. Having thus worshipped and offered incense, lamps, and so forth, one should demarcate a square area in the center measuring one *aratni* in extent. Having sprinkled it with the Astra-mantra and veiled it with the Kavaca-mantra, one should spread seven blades of *darbha* grass in the directions starting from the east, and place the sixfold arising seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*) in the center. [Recite: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the seat of Bhūdevī. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the embodiment of Bhūdevī. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Bhūdevī. Now, the meditation (*dhyāna*).

One should meditate upon Viśvambharā, who has feet like the lotus of the dawn, a dark-complexioned body, and is enchanting; who holds a wish-fulfilling lotus in her foremost hand, possesses blue lotuses, and is beautiful with red ornaments; who wears a jeweled crown and variegated garments, and has sought refuge [in the Lord]. Having consecrated the beloved of Kaiṭabha’s enemies through the ten purificatory rites beginning with invocation, one should display the Kundalī and Śūla mudrās.
(Is this the *Aṅkurārpaṇa-vāstupūjā*?)

Having dug [the earth] with the *māmo...ṣat khaṇḍa...* mantra, having sprinkled it twice with the *gāyatrī* mantra, and having filled a bronze vessel (*kāṃsyapātra*) three times with soil using both hands holding *kūrca*-grass, having covered the soil with *kuśa*-grass, cloth, and flowers, and having placed rice and unbroken grains (*akṣata*) into the excavated ground and leveled it, one should offer an oblation (*bali*) consisting of eleven types of food—or of rice—to Indra and the other world-protectors (*lokapāla*), as well as to the *balākṣetrapāla*, and then [place it] upon the head of the attendant.

Having carried [the materials] and established them in the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*), one should designate a space of twelve squares in the north-western corner (*vāyavyakoṇa*). Having placed the *somakumbhapālikā* there, and having performed breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) in front of the three *puṇyāha* jars on that auspicious lunar day, one who intends to perform the worship of the *somakumbhapālikā*—beginning with the collection of earth that night and ending with the hoisting of the Lord’s banner (*dhvajārohaṇa*)—should first, as a preliminary part of that rite, for the sake of purifying the sacrificial pavilion:

Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "For the sake of purifying the *somakumbha* and the *pālikās*, for the purification of the ritual materials, and for my own purification, together with the great multitude of people, I shall cause the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be proclaimed by Mahādeva," and having further performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) at the conclusion of the *puṇyāha* rite, on this lunar day, one should make the resolve: "I shall perform the worship of the festival of Īśvara, the *gaṅgasoma*, the *kumbha*, and the *pālikās*. Then, having offered the sixfold seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*) to the *somakumbha*: "Oṃ hāṃ sāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Soma; Oṃ sāṃ, obeisance to the form of Soma; Oṃ sāṃ saṃ, obeisance to Soma. Now, the meditation (*dhyāna*):
White in color, with two eyes, and seated upon a white lotus;
he has two arms, is adorned with a crown, and is embellished by a halo of light.

Having meditated thus according to the ritual procedure—Kṛttikā on the right side and Rohiṇī on the left side—in the center of the lunar jar: *Oṃ sāṃ, homage to the body of knowledge; oṃ sauṃ, homage to the eyes*. Having consecrated [it] with the ten purificatory rites beginning with the invocation and having assigned its limbs: *Oṃ śrīṃ śrī, homage to Amṛteśvara*. And in the fourth [position], *oṃ bhūḥ, homage to Brahmā; oṃ bhuvaḥ, homage to Prajāpati; oṃ suvaḥ, homage to the Lord of the World*.

Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ, obeisance to Caturmukhā. (L. 4) In the four *pālikās*: Oṃ bhuvaḥ, obeisance to Vasudevā; Oṃ bhuvaḥ, obeisance to Parjanyā; Oṃ suvaḥ, obeisance to Ari...dhā; Oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā, obeisance to Pūṣottamā. In the four *khaṇḍikās*: Oṃ haḥ (bhuvaḥ), obeisance to Sadyojāta; Oṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva; Oṃ suvaḥ, obeisance to Aghora. (P. 38a, l. 1)

"Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ — obeisance to Tatpuruṣa. Having thus worshipped, one should wash the ten grains with milk. Having consecrated them with the *brahmāṅga* mantras according to the verse "yā jātā," having sprinkled them with the *astra* mantra, having shielded them with the *kavaca* mantra, and having rendered them nectar-like with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should divide that seed into twelve parts. During the four *śarāva* measures: [recite] "brahmajajñānam"; during the four *rāsi* measures: "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ"; during the four *ghaṭikā* measures: "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ."

Having sown the seed-syllables "yo rudro" in each of the four small jars with the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā* and the four verses beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇā*, he should purify [the area] with the *pavamāna* hymns and the like; then, having covered it with *bilva* leaves or *arka* leaves, he should offer milk-rice (*pāyasānna*). [The] altar...

...having prepared a sacrificial altar (*vedikā*) measuring one cubit (*hasta*) in length and breadth in either the east or west for the purpose of worshipping the site (*vāstupūjā*), and having leveled the ground (*sthaṇḍila*) in its center—having established the grid of the *āmoka* site—there, before the three *puṇyāha* jars, having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), on this lunar day—for the sake of removing the fault of contact with the perimeter of the temple during the raising of the banner of the Lord, [this is done] until the end of the year in the temple by the king’s adversary.

Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) thus: "For the purpose of avoiding the impurity of deep sleep, urine, persons, and stains; for the purpose of avoiding the impurity of contact with dogs, chickens, pigs, and the like; for the purpose of avoiding the impurity of malevolent planets (*duṣṭagraha*); for the purpose of avoiding the impurity of excrement from *caṇḍālas* and others; and for the purpose of increasing the longevity of the patron (*yajamāna*), I shall cause the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) distinguished by Mahādeva to be proclaimed together with the great people, for the sake of pleasing Śrī Īśvara, the God of Gods," then, at the conclusion of the *puṇyāha* ceremony, once again—

Having restrained the breaths (*prāṇāyāma*) and made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "On this lunar day, I shall perform the Vāstu-pūjā as an ancillary rite for the hoisting of the flag of the Lord," one should offer the sixfold seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*) upon the Brahmakumbha: "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the seat of Brahmā. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the form of Brahmā. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Brahmā. Now, the meditation (*dhyāna*):
Four-faced, four-armed, endowed with eight eyes, resembling molten gold, with a slightly smiling countenance.
Adorned with four crowns and holding a *kūrca*, a *yūta*,
and a *kamaṇḍalu*, one should meditate upon that form of Brahmā and join it to the *brahmakumbha*.

Oṃ hāṃ huṃ, homage to the one whose body is wisdom (*vidyādeha*). Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, homage to the eyes. Having consecrated [the deity] with the ten purificatory rites beginning with invocation (*āvāhana*), and having offered incense, lamps, and so forth, [one should worship] in the six squares starting from the east: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Marīci; Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vivasvat; Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Mitra; Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Dharādhara. In the two-by-two compartments of the southeast, [one worships]: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Āpa.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Āpavatsa. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Savitṛ. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sāvitra. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Indra. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Rudra. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Rudrajaya. In each of the single squares beginning with Īśāna: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Īśāna. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Parjanya. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Jayanta. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Mahendra. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ravi. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Satyaka.

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vṛśākapi! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Antarikṣa! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vahni! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Pūṣan! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vidhātṛ! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Graha-kṣata! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Māyā! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Gandharva! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Bhṛṅgarāja! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Mṛga! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Nirṛti! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Dauvārika!

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Sugrīva. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Puṣpadanta. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Varuṇa. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Asura. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Śoṣa. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Roga. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vāyu. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Nāga. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Mukhya. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Phallāṭaka. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Soma. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Mṛga. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Aditi.

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Bheditā. On the four tridents beginning with Īśāna: homage to Śārāmyā (Carakyā); homage to Vidāriṇī; homage to Pūtanā; homage to Pāparākṣasī. In the four directions beginning with the East: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Skanda; Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Aryaman; Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vijñābha; Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Balipiñcha. Outside, in the four directions beginning with the East: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Āditya; Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Soma.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bhauma. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Budha. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Guru. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śukra. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Chāyāputra. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Rāhu. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ketu. Having thus worshipped the deities of the site (vāstudeva), having offered incense, lamps, and the water-offering vessel (pādikā), and having established the fire that carries the hymns (sūktavaha) in front of them, one should offer a six-fold seat (ṣaḍutthāsana) there with the words: "Obeisance to Brahmā."
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the seat of Brahmā. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the form of Brahmā. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Brahmā. Meditation:
[One should meditate upon him] as having four faces, four arms, and endowed with eight eyes;
resembling molten gold, with a face slightly smiling.

Having joined the four-fold [vessel] together with the *daṭṭa* [ladle], and taking a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) with the *dṛtaśruvā* [ladle], one should meditate upon the form of Brahmā and unite it within the fire. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*). Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, salutation to the eyes. Having consecrated [the fire] through the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*) and other purifications of the site, one should offer fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), sacrificial porridge (*caru*), milk, sesame seeds, and rice grains with: Oṃ hāṃ hrāṃ hrāṃ, salutation to the heart.

Having offered one hundred and ten oblations for each of these preliminary limbs (*aṅga*), and having omitted the *vyāhṛti* at the end of the substances—(p. 41a, l. 1)—[one offers]: *oṃ hūṃ hāṃ vāstoṣpate brahmaṇe namaḥ*.

"Svāhā!"—having offered one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) in this manner, and having thus offered the oblation of clarified butter to that deity, [he offers to]: Marīci, Vivasvat, Mitra, Dharādhara, Āpaḥ, Āpavatsa, Savitṛ, Sāvitrī, Indrajaya, Rudrajaya, Īśāna, Parjanya, Jayanta, Mahendra, Vivasvat, Satyaka, Pṛtyaśaka, Antarikṣaka, Vahni, Puruṣa, Vitala, Agra, Hagra, Kṣita, Yajamāna, Gandharva, and Bhṛṅgarāja.

Mṛga, Nirṛti, Dauvārika, Sugrīva, Puṣpadanta, Varuṇa, Asura, Śoṣa, Āroga, Vāyu—the chief of the Nāgas, Phalguṇa, Soma, Agni, Aditi, Diti, Marīci, Vivasvat, Mitra, Dhara-dhara, Skanda, Aryaman, Vi...bhāva, Pilipiñcha, Āditya, Homa, Maṅgala, Budha, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Śani, Rāhu, and Ketu.

Thus, [regarding] the sequence for the bull-sacrifice (*vṛṣayāga*), having offered three oblations at a time—concluding with a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) using the root mantra—with ten kinds of *darbha* grass, or *vrīhi*, or *tṛṇa* grass, or other materials bound into a bundle, one should perform the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*) inside the temple, in another location, or on the path of the chariot. Having performed the daily obligatory rites as prescribed in the ritual sequence, one should avoid [the sacrifice]. Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for the planting of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) and the worship of the site (*vāstupūjā*).
(The Procedure for the Bull Sacrifice:
