Now we shall explain the procedure for the bull sacrifice (*vṛṣayāga*). On the eastern, western, southern, or northern side of the flagstaff (*dhvajastambha*), having smeared [the ground] with cow dung—either on the left or as desired—one should cause a multicolored design (*raṅgavallī*) to be made; on the right side, [an image of] Umāskandeśvara.

To its side, to the east, is Caṇḍeśvara; or [alternatively], to its side, to the west, is Annaliṅga. To the northeast is a trident, and above it, three feet high, is a banner-cloth. Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) on its northern side—in those two [locations]—having placed nine jars for each, and having established the fire to its side, and having placed a drum in the northern region, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) there in front of the three auspicious jars (puṇyāhakalaśa).

Being about to perform [the following]: on this auspicious lunar day, being about to perform the worship of Umā and Skanda, the propitiation of Caṇḍeśvara, the worship of the *anna-liṅga*, the propitiation of the *astāra* and the *kalaśa*, the worship of the banner-cloth (*dhvajapaṭa*), and the *homa* which is its constituent part; being about to perform the worship of the trident (*triśūla*) within that, the beating of the drum, the invocation of the guardians of the quarters (*dikpāla*), and the offering of the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) as a subordinate part thereof; first, for the sake of purifying the temple and for the sake of purifying the materials...

Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) thus: "For the purification of the site, for the purification of the ground, for the purification of myself, for the purification of the parasol, fly-whisk, fan, banner, and other items, as well as the sword and ritual materials, and for the fulfillment of the desired fruits of the patron’s wishes, I shall cause Mahādeva—along with the hosts of Pramathas headed by Caṇḍeśvara—to proclaim the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*)," and then, at the conclusion of the *puṇyāha* rite, having again performed the regulation of the breath (*prāṇāyāma*), [one should perform] the worship of Īśvara on this lunar day endowed with such qualities, ending with Umā.

Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) "I shall perform [this]," and having offered the sixfold seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*) to the Lord of the Festival (*Utsaveśvara*): "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Somaskandeśvara; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form (*mūrti*) of Somaskanda; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Somaskanda. Now, the meditation (*dhyāna*):
"They are blue and pale-white in color, two-eyed and three-eyed."

Wearing garments and deerskins, adorned with golden earrings, known as Maṇi and Raktakaṇḍa, decorated with crested crowns, endowed with divine ornaments, possessing various beautiful and equal splendors, Skanda and Nandi, seated upon a divine jewel-throne—[the practitioner] should meditate on Somāskandeśvara, who bestows the fruits of desired wishes. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the one whose body is knowledge (vidyādeha). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the eyes.

Having consecrated [the deity] with the ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) using the root mantra, and having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the limbs with *oṃ hāṃ*, one recites: *Oṃ hāṃ somāskandeśvarāsanāya namaḥ |* *Oṃ hāṃ somāskandamūrtaye namaḥ |* *Oṃ hāṃ somāskandāya namaḥ |* "Triyambakaṃ yajāmahe... [recited] for Rudra, in the fire—may it be so. Then, having offered the sixfold arising seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*) to Caṇḍeśvara: *Oṃ hāṃ caṇḍāsanāya namaḥ |* *Oṃ hāṃ caṇḍamūrtaye namaḥ |* *Oṃ hāṃ caṇḍāya namaḥ |* Now, the visualization (*dhyāna*):
He has one face and two eyes, is adorned with a crown and a jeweled casket,
holds an axe in his right hand, and has his left hand resting on his hip.
Having meditated upon that Caṇḍeśvara, whose right foot is in the lalita posture and the other is drawn up, she arrived for the sake of Śiva and Pārvatī.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Caṇḍeśvara, whose body is knowledge. Having offered incense, lamps, and so forth, with devotion to the Annaliṅga, one should offer the sixfold seat for the Annaliṅga: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śiva as the Annaliṅga. Oṃ hāṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śiva’s form as Food (Anna). Now, the meditation:
I worship the pure Annaliṅga, adorned with the luster of pearls, resembling the moon, endowed with celestial splendor, the bestower of strength upon living beings, and the bringer of victory.

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vodanin, whose body is the Vidyā; Oṃ hām hauṃ, salutation to the food and the eyes. Having consecrated [the deity] with the ten purificatory rites beginning with invocation (āvāhana), [one prays]: "May I become the king of those who possess food, those who possess fragrant boiled rice, and those who possess curd-mixture (āmikṣā). Having offered incense, lamps, and so forth, and having gone to the tip of the trident of Amitri, one offers the sixfold seat for the trident: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the seat of Śiva’s weapon (śivāstrāsana); Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the form of Śiva’s weapon (śivāstramūrti); Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śiva’s weapon (śivāstra). Now, the meditation (dhyāna):
The ocean of Soma, square, circular, and in the form of Meru, as well as the staff-like [form], established by Rudra, Brahmā, and Mukunda;
the face in the form of three lines, which shatters the pride of the Daityas, is terrifying yet bestows desired objects and cherished aims.

One should constantly meditate upon the trident that brings about auspiciousness, illuminated by its own radiance and adorned with its causal [emanations]. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the eyes. Having consecrated [the deity] with the ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) beginning with invocation (*āvāhana*), one recites: Oṃ hāṃ, huṃ phaṭ, salutation to the seat of the weapon (*astrāsana*). Oṃ hāṃ, huṃ phaṭ, salutation to the embodiment of the weapon (*astramūrti*). Having offered incense, lamps, and other offerings, and having extracted fire and wind with force, the Sun and Śiva enter the trident.

The sacrificer [is blessed] with progeny and cattle. Having offered a seat made of six [materials] to Vṛṣakumbha—*Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Bull-seat; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Bull-form; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Bull*—then the meditation: [He is] three-horned, large-eyed, the proclaimer of the Vedas, most exalted, endowed with the resonance of the *ghaṇṭikā*, and adorned with gold and red [gems].

[One should worship] the Veda, who is the direct embodiment of Dharma, the form of Śiva, the Lord of the Bull: *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Bull whose body is knowledge*. *Oṃ hauṃ, salutation to the Eyes of the Pure One*. *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Bull*. Having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites, [one should worship] around the ritual jars—in the jars starting from the east: *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Nandin*; *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mahākāya*; *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Dharmāṅga*; *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Cokṣa*; *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Viṣṇurūpa*; *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Gaṇakartṛ*.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Svajaṅgha (Svajaṅghā). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vedapāda. Having thus worshipped and offered incense, lamps, and so forth, one should perform the worship of the Brahmās. And here, in the jars of the world-protectors (lokapāla), [one should offer]: Oṃ hāṃ brāṃ, obeisance to the seat of the world-protectors; Oṃ hāṃ brāṃ, obeisance to the form of the world-protectors; Oṃ hāṃ braṃ, obeisance to the world-protector. Now, the meditation: I worship the Lord of the Worlds, who brings happiness to his subjects—Indra, Agni, Yama, Nairṛta, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Kubera, and Īśvara.

Oṃ hāṃ brāṃ, salutation to the eyes. Oṃ hāṃ brāṃ, salutation to Brahmāśva. Around [the central deity] in the jars: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Indra; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Agni; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Yama; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Nirṛti; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Varuṇa; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vāyu; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Kubera; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Īśāna; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Brahmā; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu. Having thus worshipped.

Having offered incense, lamps, and so forth—and here, having offered banners, cloth, and so forth—having placed that cloth upon the eastern cloth, and having consecrated it with the *kūrca* grass using the mantra "May the waters purify," [one recites]: "May the waters purify the earth; may the purified earth purify me. May Brahmaṇaspati purify; may the purified Veda purify me. Whatever food is left over, or whatever ill-deed is mine—may the waters purify all that in me and grant me freedom from the acceptance of gifts."

Saying "svāhā," one should cast a golden image of a bull into the water; immediately thereafter, having placed the golden image into the midst of milk within a vessel filled with milk, and having placed a cloth over the vessel, one should recite the *svasti-mantra* for a trusted person. Then, one should recite the *nārāyaṇa* [mantra] to the north, [reciting]: "May you swell on all sides like Soma, the source of strength; may we be in the gathering of nourishment; born from the waters."

Immediately thereafter, having placed [the image] in a vessel filled with grain and having recited the mantra *apavitrah pavitrah*, [one should recite]: "Whether impure or pure, or even if one has reached any state whatsoever, whoever remembers Pārvatīśāna is pure both internally and externally. Following that, having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) beginning with "the black bed of bliss" (*kṛṣṇādi-sukhaśayyā*), and having recited the mantra *āśuśāna*, the Guru should place the cloth as before upon three supports and proceed toward the tip of the trident.

The invocation of the trident (*śūlāvāhana*): Having recited the prose passage beginning with "Śiva, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Pārvatī, Vāṇī, Rāmā," and so forth, one performs the invocation and other rites for each [deity], such as Muktā, and having offered incense, lamps, and other offerings.

Having gone near the drum and offered incense, lamps, and so forth, and having taken a nearby vessel or a mango leaf, one should strike the drums with the mantra "Śrīmadyatra" and, taking Caṇḍeśvara and Utsaveśvara, go to the vicinity of the pillar. Having sprinkled the pillar with water, having consecrated it with the waters from the ritual jar, and having adorned it with perfumes and flowers.

Having recited the prose hymn (*gadya*) beginning with "Brahmā-Viṣṇu-Gaurī," and having recited the prose hymn of eighty-eight benedictions (*svastyaṣṭāśīti-gadya*) beginning with "I bow to the one whose body is the Bull (*Vṛṣabha-deha*"), and having performed the hoisting of the banner (*dhvajārohaṇa*), and having offered the food offering (*naivedya*), incense, lamps, and so forth, and having performed the auspicious night-rite (*maṅgalārātrika*), one should go to the vicinity of the sacrificial pedestal (*balipīṭha*). There, one should invoke Brahmā; having sprinkled [him] with the waters from the Brahmā-pitcher (*brāhmakumbha*) and having offered the oblation (*bali*) to Brahmā, and having performed the meditation (*dhyāna*) on Brahmā’s hand-drum (*tāla*) and other attributes, [one proceeds] to the east.

Having gone to the direction of Indra, having sprinkled [the site] with the water from the Indra-pitcher, having offered the Indra-oblation, and having recited the Indra-verse; the Guru, having gone to the direction of Agni, having sprinkled [it] with the water from the Agni-pitcher, and having offered worship, oblations, incense, lamps, and so forth, having recited the Tattāla-verse; having performed the sprinkling, worship, and so forth for the southern, northeastern, and eastern directions, and having had the dancer perform the *tāla* and *taṭi* gestures, he should go to the vicinity of Nairṛti and perform worship with the water from that pitcher.

Having offered the *bali*, having offered incense, lamps, and so forth, [performing] the meditation on "the eternal universe" (*śāśvadviśva*), and [reciting] "if unknown" (*ajñātā ceti*)—with the *tāla* known as the *mallatāla*, like a dancer, amidst the sound of musical instruments—having gone to the foremost place of Varuṇa, having sprinkled [it] with water consecrated by mantra, having performed the ritual of worship, having performed the *baddhaprakriyā*, having recited the prose (*gadya*), having offered the *bali*, and having caused [him] to enter the wind-corner, [one places] the water for the feet (*pādya*) upon the seat.

Having invoked the form of Vāyu, having sprinkled [the area] with the water from the jar, and having offered the *bali*, one should say, "I bow; may there be the fragrance-bearer," while sounding musical instruments. Having gone near the jar of Kubera, having performed the worship, the *bali*, and the *ārātrika* offerings with the water from the jar of Kubera, and having set aside the *campaka* flower at the end of the recitation of the *cetoyādi* mantra, one should go near the jar of Īśāna accompanied by music. Then the Guru, having sprinkled [the area] with the water from the jar of Īśāna using the root-mantra of Īśāna—

The meditation is on Īśāna. Having performed worship with a golden palm-tree [image], this is the eightfold invocation of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*). Having performed this either within the enclosure wall or at the site of the chariot, one should install Vatsaveśvara in the auspicious pavilion, and having offered worship, food offerings (*naivedya*), incense, lamps, and so forth—thus ends the chapter on the ritual procedure for the sacrifice of the bull. May there be auspiciousness! Salutations to the Gurus. [Blank page] If there are sugarcane stalks, small staffs, and altars, as well as cords, jewels, and garlands of *darbha* grass according to one’s preference...
I worship the deity consisting of the eight forms—from the conclusion of the worship until the conclusion of the descent:
Oṃ hām, obeisance to the Support-Power (*ādhāraśakti*). Oṃ hām, obeisance to the Seat of Ananta (*anantāsana*). Oṃ hām, obeisance to Ananta. Thus for the ritual action (*karma*).
In the center of the corners: Obeisance to Dharma. Obeisance to Jñāna. Obeisance to Vairāgya. Obeisance to Aiśvarya.

In the corners: *namaḥ* to Adharma; *namaḥ* to Ignorance (*ajñāna*); *namaḥ* to Non-sovereignty (*avairājñā*); *namaḥ* to Non-mastery (*anaiśvarya*). In the eight petals: *namaḥ* to the powers beginning with Vāmā.
In the pericarp: *namaḥ* to Manonmanī.
On the staff—salutation to Sadāśiva.
At the sacrifices—salutation to Brahmā; salutation to Viṣṇu; salutation to Rudra. On the secondary staff—salutation to Śani.
On the rope: salutation to Vāsuki. To Sadāśiva (l. 6): salutation. On the square: salutation to Jñānaśakti.
On the circle (vṛtta): salutation to Icchāśakti.
At Matme—salutation to Kriyāśakti.
At Vṛṣabha—salutation to Kṣamāmūrti. To Bhava, the lord of Kṣamāmūrti, salutation.

On the staff (*daṇḍa*): "Obeisance to the form of Fire (*vahnimūrti*); obeisance to Śarva, the lord of the form of Fire. On the secondary staff (*upadaṇḍa*): "Obeisance to the form of the Sacrificer (*yajamānamūrti*); obeisance to Īśāna, the lord of the form of the Sacrificer. On the altar (*vedikā*): "Obeisance to the form of the Sun (*arkamūrti*); obeisance to Rudra, the lord of the form of the Sun. Obeisance to the form of Water (*jalamūrti*); obeisance to Ugra, the lord of the form of Water. Obeisance to the form of Wind (*vāyumūrti*) in the cord; obeisance to Bhīma, the lord of the form of Wind. On the gem (*maṇi*).

Homage to the one whose form is the moon; homage to the great-minded lord of the one whose form is the moon. In the darbha-garland: homage to the one whose form is space; homage to Paśupati, the lord of the one whose form is space.

Having thus worshipped with the sixteen services, beginning with the invocation of the meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), one should hoist the banner. Having divided the cloth of the banner into [sections], one should place a bull in the center; above that, Kāmadeva; above him, a parasol; and two fly-whisks on both sides. In the lower portion, at the base, a full water-jar (*pūrṇakumbha*); on both sides, a lamp and an offering of a *svastika*, as well as an offering of a full water-jar and a bull.

A pair of chowries at the *śrīvatsa*, a *svastika* at the conch, a lamp at the eighth [position] for the eight auspicious signs (*aṣṭamaṅgala*), and Umādevī at the mirror; Jāhnavī at the full pitcher, Gharādevī at the bull, and Kāverī at the pair of chowries; Śrīdevī at the *śrīvatsa*, Sarasvatī at the *vāstu*, and Śaśidevī at the conch of Śaṅkara; likewise, Anala at the lamp.

One should visualize [the deity] as white in appearance like cow's milk, possessing three eyes and a bull as his mount; he has one face and four arms, holding a deer and an axe, and bearing a sword, a bow, and an arrow.

One should worship the goddess who has two eyes, two arms, is dark-complexioned, holds a sword and a shield, is vigilant, and is mounted upon a bull, using the mantras for the side-steps; having meditated upon the nature of the trident as liberation and worshipped Rudra in the center, one should immediately thereafter offer a prayer with the trident-mantra: "O Blessed One, please perform the specific worship of the Root Deity for that purpose."

"I shall perform a great festival for the God of Gods, the bestower of all fruits; be present there. Having thus made this request and received permission, the Guru—following the prayer—having adorned Caṇḍeśvara, should duly fetch the clay. Having established it with the Astra-mantra and worshipped it again, the twice-born one should collect the clay, the Goddess Earth, filling it with silk cloths and other materials.

And having covered [the vessel] again and again, one who wears new garments, being pure, should mount a bier (*mataka*) and carry the jar upon his head; he should perform the circumambulation of the village in the prescribed manner. Having entered that dwelling, in the northeast or the north, he should cause the *aṅkura* (germinating seeds) to be established according to the procedure for the offering of *aṅkuras*. May it be auspicious for Brahman; may it be auspicious for Śiva.

May these true lords of the world increase! O true lords of the world—those who sustain their bodies on roots, tubers, fruits, and vegetables, and who carry out the teachings of Śiva—may you become equal to the illustrious Nandikeśvara and Vīrabhadra! In our divine abode, may there be sandals and pavements that counteract the binding of the feet, which are exceedingly beautiful and foremost among all things; [may there be] Kumuda and Kambukaṇṭha.

The frieze, the great frieze, the lattice-vedicā, the foot-arches, the water-jars, the reed-pipes, and the vedicā ornaments; [the design] adorned with vyālas and nasalized motifs, including the Mahānāsikā class of the Drāviḍa, Vesara, Nāgara, and other styles; the auspicious pedestal, the svastika, the ploughing [motif], and the Meru, Mandara, Niṣadha, Kailāsa, elephant-back, lion, nandyāvarta, and the serpent-cluster pillar-heads.

Adorned with various ornaments, including sandalwood carvings, and featuring images of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, Nārasiṃha, Skanda, Vṛṣabha, and other forms, as well as statues of sages, Garuḍa, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Kiṃpuruṣas, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and rows of swans; endowed with a divine enclosure wall, and containing within it a central maṇḍala with inner chambers, along with five enclosure walls and gate-towers beginning with Mahāmāyī and Antarmahāmāyī—it is the abode of Sarveśvara.
May they be composed of sun-stones, moon-stones, rubies, emeralds, diamonds, lapis lazuli, gomedakas, topazes, crystals, and gold-jewels.

This is the divine abode: the half-pavilion (*ardhamaṇḍapa*), the intermediate pavilion (*antarālamaṇḍapa*), the garden pavilion (*udyānamaṇḍapa*), the bathing pavilion (*sthānamaṇḍapa*), the ablution pavilion (*snapanamaṇḍapa*), the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*), the enjoyment pavilion (*bhogamaṇḍapa*), the pavilion for enjoyments (*bhogyamaṇḍapa*), the sleeping pavilion (*śayanamaṇḍapa*), the secluded pavilion (*ekāntamaṇḍapa*), the pavilion for the Vedas, Śāstras, Purāṇas, and Āgamas, the pavilion for the offering of oblations (*ghṛtavāramaṇḍapa*), the pavilion for the sacred powder (*śrīcūrṇamaṇḍapa*), the pavilion for the festival of black fragrance (*kṛṣṇagandhotsavamaṇḍapa*), the pavilion for water-sports (*jalakrīḍāmaṇḍapa*), the forest pavilion (*vanamaṇḍapa*), and the mountain pavilion (*girimaṇḍapa*).

— may it be adorned with a *patyāgama* pavilion, a *dāna* pavilion, a *tīrtha-dīna* pavilion, a crystal pavilion, a gold-gilt pavilion, a pavilion for the installation of jewels, a four-pillared pavilion, a hundred-pillared pavilion, a thousand-pillared pavilion, and many other pavilions with numerous pillars, as well as a pavilion for mounting the chariot and a pavilion for raising the banner.

In this divine abode, may the vessels for the *arghya*, the vessels for the *ācamanīya*, the incense vessel, the lamp vessel, the conch vessel, the flower vessel, the vessel for the *nīrājana* rite, the vessel for ashes, the mirror, the parasol, the fly-whisk, and so forth, become composed of gold, red [gems], and light. In this divine abode, may the kitchen, the treasury, the clothing storehouse, the granary, the stable, the cowshed, the sacrificial hall, and all others become composed of gold and jewels. Now, in the divine abode...

May [the deities] shine with the excellence and splendor produced by the regions of white palaces, naturally radiant and free from the harshness of water made of gold. Furthermore, in the divine abode, may all things—the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, auspicious arches (*maṅgalatoraṇa*), rows of lamps, lamp-stands, flagstaffs, offering pedestals (*balipīṭha*), stepped seats (*kramāsana*), and *pālikā* vessels—be composed of gold and jewels.

In this divine temple, may all the mechanical devices—such as the water-wheel (*prabhayantra*), the water-clock (*sahmayantra*), the elephant-machine (*gajayantra*), the horse-machine (*vājiyantra*), the human-machine (*narayantra*), the *kailāsa*, the *yaśodhavimāna*, the lotus-throne (*padmapīṭha*), the lion-throne (*siṃhapīṭha*), and the palanquin (*śibikā*)—as well as the bricks and other materials, be composed entirely of gold and jewels.

In this divine abode, may all these—conchs, dundubhis, bherīs, paṭahas, maddalakas, kāṃsas, sitālas, kirīṭīs, ḍaṇḍimas, alamuravas, jhallarīs, śaṅkhas, kāhalas, kumbhas, vādyas, vaiṇavas, mahābherīs, suṣiras, ḍaḍhakās, cihnirājas, cihnidhārās, saras, maṇḍis, kinnaris, rāvaṇahastas, rudravīṇās, and so forth—be composed of gold and jewels. Dayā: May they all be composed of gold and jewels.

May this divine temple—whether with one enclosure wall, two enclosure walls, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, twelve, or more—be adorned with gate-towers (*gopura*). May this divine temple be fashioned with rows of silk cloths and banners raised high upon its peaks.

May this divine abode be adorned with festivals such as the perpetual festival, the occasional festival, the festival of faith, the festival of devotion, the spring festival, the swing festival, the festival of Madana, the campaka festival, the festival of new leaves, the pavitra festival, the lamp festival, the water-sport festival, the festival of the city of waters, the great festival of the Vedic recitation (*vedapārāyaṇa*), the hunting festival, the painting-gallery festival, and the wedding festival.

On the great festival of the Lord of Gods, for the sake of those Brahmins arriving from various regions, for the kings, lords, and men who dwell in the illustrious village, and for those eager to offer their responses—I, a learned man, perform this benediction, accompanied by the sound of the Veda: "May you be entirely pure along with Brahmā; come, O all you twice-born ones dwelling within the illustrious village!"

His body was firmly embraced by the Vedas, Vedānta, Bhāṭṭa, Prābhākara, Nyāya, Itihāsa, Purāṇa, and Vaiśeṣika. May all these groups of celibate students (*brahmacārin*) residing in this village be devoted to morning baths, the performance of twilight prayers (*sandhyā*), recitation (*japa*), libations (*tarpaṇa*), the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*), the kindling of the sacred fire (*samidhoma*), the practice of begging for alms (*bhikṣācaraṇa*), the study of the Vedas, and service to their gurus.

May all those [faults]—such as bathing in warm water, cleaning the teeth, applying collyrium, ointments, perfumes, flowers, and incense; [or perhaps] the violation of the lunar fast (*cāndrāyaṇa*); dreaming of the emission of semen; sleeping with women; physical contact; sexual intercourse; desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy, and cruelty; and the like—which are contrary to the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*)—be turned away from me.

In this [village], let those who quickly grasp the *śrī* [of the land] be devoted to the six duties (*ṣaṭkarma*)—sacrificing, officiating at sacrifices, studying, teaching, giving, and receiving—and let them all be performers of the seven *pākayajñas*: the *sthālīpāka*, the *māgrahāyaṇa*, the *aṣṭakā*, the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, the monthly *śrāddha*, the *caitra-āśvattha*, and the *vājapeya*.

May they all be performers of the seven types of *iṣṭi* sacrifices—the *Agnyādheya*, the *Agnihotra*, the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, the *Vaiśvadeva*, the *Cāturmāsya*, the *Kūrmāsyā*, and the *Rūḍapaśubandha-Sautrāmaṇī*. May they all be performers of the seven *Soma* sacrifices—the *Agniṣṭoma*, the *Atyagniṣṭoma*, the *Ukthya*, the *Ṣoḍaśin*, the *Vājapeya*, the *Atirātra*, and the *Aptoryāma*.

For all the great people residing in this village, for their performance of ritual bathing and recitation (*japa*), and for [the rites of] *garbhādhāna*, *puṃsavana*, *sīmantonnayana*, *viṣṇubali*, *jātakarman*, *nāmakaraṇa*, *annaprāśana*, *karṇavedha*, *caula*, *upanayana*, the kindling of the sacred fire (*samidādhāna*), the study of the Vedas... the fourfold [Vedic studies], *samāvartana*, *vivāha*, *aupāsana*, *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, *bhūtayajña*, *manuṣyayajña*, *brahmacarya*, *agnihotra*, *darśapūrṇamāsa*, *kṛcchra*, and *cāndrāyaṇa*— [The text continues on p. 53b, f48a.]

May they become proficient in the sixty-four arts, beginning with the Cāturmāsya, Nirūḍhapaśubandha, Sautrāmaṇi, Parvaṇāṣṭaka, Anuśrāddha, Pitṛśrāddha, Sarpabali, Īśānabali, Āyuṣyahoma, Apamṛtyuhoma, Nakṣatrahoma, Grahahoma, Vājapeya, Rājasūya, Somayāga, Aśvamedha, and so forth.

This is the ritual for the consecration and sprinkling of the establishment of Vedic Mahāśaiva Śivabrāhmaṇas in the village; it concerns the practice of the six duties—studying and teaching, giving and receiving gifts, sacrificing and officiating at sacrifices—and the performance of specific rites such as expiation (*prāyaścitta*), daily (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*) acts, as well as the various divisions of the Āgamas, the powerful methods of worship, the modes of self-oriented and other-oriented worship (*pūjā*), and the *aupāsana* fire-rituals and yantras.

The teacher of conduct—consisting of visiting temples, offering praise, circumambulation, hymns of praise, prostrations, beholding the deity, attending seats of learning (*vidyāpīṭha*), serving the guru, worshipping a tawny cow (*kapilā*), listening to the established doctrines (*siddhānta*), daily rites, the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, the offering of oblations (*bali*), initiation, eating, honoring guests, hearing the Dharma, praising the Dharma, listening to the Purāṇas, and the propitiation of the planets—says: "May there be ever-increasing prosperity; may you grant your favor."

May these ascetics dwelling within the illustrious village perform the restraint of the five senses, remain devoted to auspicious meditation, and engage in the worship of Śiva. May they become protectors of their lineage, possessing wealth and virtue.

May even the cows yield an abundance of milk that is like nectar. May this king, the lord of the land, become a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpataru*), a celestial palm tree (*tālamegha*), a red-hued cloud, a fragrant jewel (*surabhicintāmaṇi*), and so forth, adorning the crowns of the lineages of protectors of the entire world. May that king be the sovereign of all the earth, and may [all beings] possess the four faces of Brahmā, immeasurable lifespan, health, and sovereignty.

May that king—who has planted victory pillars reaching to the ends of all directions—be victorious! May he, whose fame-cloud pervades the entire universe, including the surface of the earth, the netherworld (rasātala), the subterranean realm (sutala), and the depths of the earth, as well as the worlds of the gods, humans, yakṣas, and sages, and who is a protector against the fall of the families of the *suvar*, *maha*, *jana*, *tapa*, and *satya* [worlds], be victorious!

May that king—whose royal majesty is seated upon a lion-throne resplendent with a multitude of clusters of crest-jewels from Aṅga, Vaṅga, Kaliṅga, Koṅkaṇa, Gāndhāra, Kāśmīra, Kāmbhoja, Drāviḍa, Oḍyāja, Naja, Magadha, Mālava, Kulūta, Tuṣkara, Saurāṣṭra, Mahārāṣṭra, Pāñcāla, Avantika, Ābhīra, Kuṭaja, Karṇāṭaka, Kūrjara, Siṃhala, Kerala, Kekaya, Cera, Cola, Pāṇḍya, Pāñcāla, Pramūrti, Uthika, and Makuṭa—be delightful.

May that king be as radiant as a mass of the splendor of Kauśāmbī! May that king [be equal to] Nala, Nṛga, Nahuṣa, and Nābhi; Puru, Purukutsa, Savya, Samara, and Ukta; Indradyumna, Dharmajaya, and Dharmacāritra! May all his subjects be characterized by abundant qualities equal to those of Lakṣmī, Kṣmā, Bījā, Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, and Sarasvatī!

May his princes—Viṣṇumukha, Śalilāparākrama, Kārttikeya, and Suravarasumukha—be well. May his group of princes also be well, [endowed] with knowledge of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, the six systems of philosophy, the science of yoga, the science of logic, the science of grammar, the science of archery, the practice of weapons and military camps, warfare, poetry, drama, rhetoric, composition, the playing of the vīṇā, flute, mṛdaṅga, and other instruments, calligraphy, leaf-cutting, and the arts of *indrajāla* and *mahāndrajāla*, as well as the art of making things vanish from sight.

[The knowledge of] thought, gain and loss, self-control, the examination of gems, the examination of water, the entry into the bodies of others, palmistry, the examination of various languages, the examination of horses, the examination of mantras, the examination of jewels, the examination of gold, the examination of women, the examination of wood, the examination of land, the science of spells, the science of alchemy, the science of music, and the removal of poison.

May they become skilled in the sixty-four arts (*catuḥṣaṣṭhi-kalā*), namely: counter-poisons; subjugation, attraction, paralyzing, bewildering, expelling, and killing; causing enmity; inducing disease; the power of fire, water, and armies; the paralysis of speech, wind, and hosts; and the knowledge of calculation, eloquence, valor, and the wheel. May the entire body of his servants, headed by his ministers, practice constant favor toward him.

And may those hosts of his enemies be deprived of wealth and grain by the king, and separated from their sons, friends, wives, and kinsmen, wearing only their undergarments. This king—possessed of all sciences such as the Vedas and Shastras, possessing uninterrupted prosperity, being affectionate, ethical, flourishing, renowned, radiant, steadfast, wise, and increasing in power.

May he be possessed of valor, heroism, magnanimity, profundity, and fortitude; may he be long-lived, healthy, swift, eloquent, logical, powerful, devoted, prosperous, affectionate, virtuous, compassionate, courteous, protective, and disciplined—may the great ones grant this favor.

May the great ones show their favor so that these various great gifts—including the gift of cows, land, and water-vessels (*kanikā*) composed by our king; the gift of gold; the gift of the balance (*tulādāna*); the *puruṣa*, *viśvacakra*, and *kālacakra*; the *tilaṃkṛti* and *parvata* [gifts]; the ten bows (*daśadhanus*); the images of the Śrī-deities; and on both sides, the complete forms of Śrī—all with their primary and secondary limbs—may they grant the fulfillment of all desires.

Now, may this village of Śrī—abounding in various blessings such as food, clothing, and the like; where Vaiśravaṇa resides through the performance of the Pārāyaṇa recitation—be free from disease. Now, may this village of Śrī be rich in merit, having cast aside all thieves.

May this illustrious village be adorned with gardens surrounded by numerous groves of *candana*, *campaka*, *vañjula*, *hintāla*, *tāla*, *tamāla*, *kṛtamāla*, *sarala*, *vakula*, *śakubha*, *kuṭaja*, *likuca*, *nālikera*, *āmra*, *pūga*, *punnāga*, *kadalī*, *kapittha*, *aśvattha*, *kuravaka*, *maruvaka*, *kunda*, *tinduka*, *candana*, *sahacara*, *kāyaka*, *vācāmpeya*, *canasana*, *vetasa*, *pāṭala*, and *priyālu* trees.

In this village, may there be a grove of *puluna* trees, adorned with the ornament of pairs of *cakravāka*, *kauñceya*, and *haṃsa* birds, and provided with all waters such as dug ponds. From the sowing of these seeds until the completion of the entire cycle of rites ending with the invocation—by following the instructions and receiving grace—all [the residents] attained unimpaired peace of heart.

May all the collections of rites performed during the illustrious Śaktiyātrā—from the hoisting of the banner to its lowering—result in complete peace of heart. May all those steadfast men who promote this great festival be filled with a full lifespan through the gracious glance of the venerable Ānandavallijanāyika, who resides at the foot of the glorious Kālakaṇṭha. May the illustrious Śaiva tradition flourish. Homage to the goddess Śrī Kāmākṣī! Homage to our gurus!

May this auspicious moment be favorable for the rites of instruction in the *Śivāgama* scriptures, mantras, and the Vedas pertaining to their respective lineages, performed by the Archana-ācārya, Alaṅkaraṇa-ācārya, Sthāna-ācārya, Pacana-ācārya, and Dravya-ācārya in the temple of Śiva; may they grant their grace. May [this moment] be the destroyer of all defects—the sins committed through mind, speech, and body, such as the "sins" (*pātaka*) and so forth of those receiving the instruction; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [it includes] the great sins (*mahāpātaka*), secondary sins (*upapātaka*), minor sins (*anupapātaka*), and the like.

May this instruction bring about the liberation from all fetters for the disciples. May it grant various sovereign powers and accomplishments (*siddhi*) to the disciples for as long as their lives endure. May it bestow upon the disciples longevity, health, sovereignty, and sons. May they be filled with the city of the eight great jewels, headed by *aṇimā* and the rest. May this instruction grant the accomplishment of mantra (*mantrasiddhi*).

May the knowledge of the instruction of the mantra become an illumination like a blazing light known as "knowledge" (*jñāna*). May that which is to be known be declared to be like the sun; thus may knowledge be distinguished. May the supreme mantra consisting of the *Prāsāda-mantra*, which is beyond the awakening of the disciples through the auspicious knowledge (*śivajñāna*), be most excellent. May that *Prāsāda-mantra* grant the eight supernatural powers (*aṣṭasiddhi*) to those people who have authority over its own locus.

May this [mantra] bestow all supernatural powers (*siddhi*) upon those who resort to it and recite it. Having understood this mantra, only a person who knows the Śiva-mantras and understands the subtle may be liberated from all sins; may they be so! May this seed-syllable consisting of Śiva, which is identical to the nature of Śiva—the syllable of the Prāsāda [mantra]—be supreme and free from illusion (*paramāyika*).

Just as by the very process of the sun, this [Self] is self-luminous; let it be said that this Śiva-nature alone, devoid of thought regarding the attainment of knowledge, is the Supreme. By means of the mantra of instruction, let there be the state of *sālokya*, *sāmīpya*, *sārūpya*, and *sāyujya*. At the end of the lives of the disciples, let there be supreme enjoyment, namely the attainment of the rank of *Vidyeśvara* and so forth. Let the supreme liberation for those who have attained that rank be the non-attainment of the worlds such as *Sālokya* and the cessation of the *Paramātman* and so on.

May that very attainment of qualities such as omniscience, which is equal to the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā) and the primordial Śiva, and which consists of the manifestation of the worlds following upon that [attainment], become the state of supreme liberation.

...In this monastery, let there be Archana-ācāryas, Alaṅkaraṇa-ācāryas, Sthāna-ācāryas, Pacana-ācāryas, and Dravya-ācāryas who are knowers of noble lineages, the Vedas, the Śiva-āgama scriptures, and the Purāṇas; who are devoted to the forty-four ritual acts (catuścatvāriṃśat-karman); who are proficient in the sixty-four arts (catuṣṣaṣṭhi-kalā); and who possess the power of both cursing and bestowing grace, adorned with armlets, golden earrings, and vajra ornaments.

May they be knowers of the Purāṇas, devoted to the forty [Vedic] rites, proficient in the sixty-four arts, and adorned with armlets, golden earrings, and vajra-ornaments possessing the power to both curse and bestow grace.

[The sequence consists of: a seat, a vehicle, the *arghya* offering, the placement of fragrance, and likewise a welcome; [then] the presence (*sannidhyā*), the confinement (*sannirodha*), the arrangement of the limbs (*aṅga*) and sub-limbs (*pratyaṅga*), water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and water with fragrance and flowers; incense, a lamp, and likewise bathing, clothing, and the sacred thread (*upavītaka*); fragrance, flowers, incense, a lamp, and the eye-ointment (*nīrāñjana*); the mirror, the fan, and so forth, as well as the display of the mudrās; and finally, the enclosure and the food offering (*naivedya*).

The offering of oblations through fire (*homādi-balidāna*), meditative absorption (*samādhi*), recitation (*japa*), hymns of praise (*stotra*), circumambulation and prostration (*pradakṣiṇa-namaskṛti*), the offering of water in cupped palms (*culukodaka-pradāna*), as well as the veneration of the sacred book (*pustakārādhana*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), the sipping of water (*ācamana*), and the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*)—these forty modes of service (*upacāra*) are for the worship of the deity performed for one's own sake. Salutations to Śrī Śiva. Salutations to the Gurus. To the Lord of Ekāmra, the Consort of Tuṇai. May there be auspiciousness.

Now we shall explain the procedure for festivals (*utsavapaddhati*). Regarding this, first, in the *Siddhāntaratnāvalī*: having examined the *Kāmika*, *Yoga*, *Cintya*, *Kāraṇa*, *Ajita*, *Dīpta*, *Sūkṣma*, *Suprabheda*, *Candrajñāna*, *Vīratatra*, *Sāra*, *Asahasra*, *Raurava*, *Vātula*, and other secondary scriptures (*upāgama*), [this work] contains the collection of rites—daily, occasional, optional, and expiatory—composed by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya, whose supreme name is Parameśvara and who was a teacher of two hundred thousand [verses].

Having examined the *Pratipādaka-bandha*—which covers the rites from the plowing (*karṣaṇa*) up to the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), from the consecration up to the festival (*utsava*), and from the festival up to the expiation (*prāyaścitta*)—one should, for the benefit of all, compose a *Utsava-paddhati* in the form of a compendium according to the rules therein stated. I shall now describe it: first is the sacrifice of the bull (*vṛṣabhayāga*); after that, the hoisting of the banner (*dhvajārohaṇa*).

Then follow the sounding of the drum (*bherītāḍana*) and the recollections (*smṛti*). Fourth is the offering of the sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*); fifth is the marking of the sacrificial hall (*yāgaśālā-lakṣaṇa*); and after that, the sixth is the sacrifice of the weapon (*astrayāga*).

The seventh is the ritual procedure for the offering to Bali (*balidānaka-yāgakrama*). Then, in the ninth and tenth [sections], the *nirājana* is taught; it is remembered as having the number of Rudras (eleven). After that, having bestowed the protective cord (*pratisara*), the twelfth is prescribed. Having performed the gathering of the sacred sites (*tīrthasaṅgrahaṇa*), the thirteenth is likewise established.

Having performed the powder festival (*cūrṇotsava*) after this—making it the fourteenth—one should thereafter perform the descent ritual (*avarohaṇavidhi*), making it the fifteenth. Having performed the sixteenth, known as the ablution (*snāna*), according to the sequence beginning with "whatever [is prescribed]," and so forth, one should conduct the festival according to the various divisions, such as the Śaiva and others, in the manner described in the *Siddhāntaratnāvalī*.

By means of the division of divine and human [factors], the ritual procedure for the most excellent of festivals, lasting nine days, is prescribed as follows: on the preceding night, one should commence the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*), the fire-oblation (*homa*), and the offering of sacrificial food (*bali*). Therein, beginning with the teacher and continuing through the rites from ascending to descending, [the practitioner] should first form a formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*)—observing the *nemana* vow, eating but once a day, sleeping on the ground, and abstaining from anointing with oil and the like—and having paid homage to his chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*).

On the second, third, fourth, fifth, or sixth day of the subsequent recitation (*anvāha*), at the time of morning on the tenth day, one should perform the *dvivaraṅliḥ* [rite]; on that same day, one should commence the powder festival (*cūrṇotsava*) and the ritual of the sacred ford (*tīrthakarma*).

In this festival of the new [temple], the rite must be performed prior to the hoisting of the banner: in Mārgaśīrṣa until Ārdrā; in Puṣya until Puṣya; in Māgha until Māghā; in Phālguna until Uttaraphalgunī; in Caitra until Caitrā; in Vaiśākha until Viśākhā; in Jyeṣṭha until Jyeṣṭhā; in Āṣāḍha until Uttarāṣāḍhā; in Śrāvaṇa until Śravaṇā; in Bhādra until Bhādrā; in Āśvina until Aśvinī; and in Kārttika until Kṛttikā—such are the lunar mansions for each month.

The rite for visiting sacred sites (*tīrthakārya*)—namely, bathing in the ocean or at rivers and other such places—is recommended when [the planets] are in conjunction (*yukta*) or when they are separated (*viyukta*). It should be performed in the month of Māgha until the sixth lunar day, or in the month of Jyeṣṭha until the eighth lunar day, beginning from the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*). Whether in the forenoon or the afternoon, one should select a sacred site (*tīrtha*) at a river or similar location corresponding to the lunar day (*tithi*), provided it occurs after midday. Furthermore, when two constellations (*ṛkṣa*) have arrived together and are joined by an auspicious yoga, [the rite should be done] first; likewise, this applies from the commencement of the ascent (*ārohaṇa*) up to the end of the equinox (*viṣuva*) and the solstice (*ayana*).

Or, one should begin the *tīrtha* at the conclusion of the ritual collection; for the *Śaiva* and other festivals of Śiva, one should begin the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) in the morning and the collection of earth (*mṛtsaṅgrahaṇa*) at night during the evening. If the incense is begun during the day, there is no fault in the sacrifice to Śiva. However, if it is performed in another sacrifice, there is no fruit.

One should not perform the Nṛttakalyāṇa in the midst of a festival for a deity on a single plot of land; if it is performed, a fault arises. At the time of commencing the festival, having prepared the chariots and other vehicles, having worshipped Vighneśa, having offered food offerings such as hard and soft foods, and having also worshipped Astrarāja and Caṇḍeśvara, the collection of wood [is to be done] just like the collection of stone.

One should perform the collection of wood: having offered milk-rice (*pāyasa*) alone and having adorned Caṇḍeśvara, one should perform the circumambulation of the village. Then, having worshipped Vighneśa, one should perform the collection of wood in the same manner as the collection of stone.

(1.5) Having worshipped the tip of the flagpole upon the previously mentioned trees—such as the *bilva* tree—and having performed the *bali* offering, one should block [the direction] and cut it with an axe. If it falls in the east, the north, or the northeast (*aiśānī*), it is auspicious; otherwise, one should abandon it. Having accepted that [wood], taken it along with the artisan, placed it on a chariot, tied a protective amulet (*kautuka*) to the front, bathed it with fragrant water, and again recited the *puṇyāha* formula, [one should proceed] to the assembly pavilion (*āsthānamaṇṭapa*).

Having gone [to the forest] and rubbed [the wood] with oil and other substances, one should cause betel to be offered to all. Then, having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and having placed a staff in its center—having adorned it with garments and so forth, having worshipped it with perfumes, garlands, and the like, and having honored it with incense and lamps—one should worship it starting from the portion belonging to Śiva. Having worshipped it with the *praṇava* and offered [oblations], one should establish it as prescribed in the section on general consecration (*sāmānyapratiṣṭhā*). This is the procedure for the collection of wood.

(The Ritual for the Planting of Sprouts: First is the planting of the sprout for the banner (*dhvajāṅkurārpaṇa*); second is the sprout for the festival (*mṛtsavāṅkura*); and third is what is called the sprout for the sacred ford (*tīrthāṅkura*). The sowing of seeds and the collection of earth may take place on the ninth, seventh, or third day, or even immediately. The preceptor (*ācārya*), having taken the makers of the *kundalī* and other items, and having adorned Caṇḍeśvara, [prepares] that which is accompanied by the King of Weapons (*astrarāja*), various banners, fresh coconuts, and at its conclusion, various parasols along with the *pālikā* vessels and so forth.

Having gone to the east or the north, or having gone to a riverbank, a pond, or a flower grove, one should sprinkle the ground with auspicious water (*śivatoya*). Having proclaimed an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), having worshipped [the site] with the *Hṛdaya* mantra, and having fully honored the *Kuṇḍalī* and the *Hṛdaya*, one should invoke the Earth (*bhūmi*) and worship her with perfumes and other offerings. Having worshipped the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) all around with the *Hṛdaya* mantra, one should dig with the *Astra* mantra and strew unbroken rice, parched grain, and *kuśa* grass.

Facing either east or north, one should take earth with both hands using the Tatpuruṣa mantra, place it upon *kuśa* grass in a vessel while reciting the Īśāna mantra, set it down, sprinkle it again, and offer a flower with the Hṛdaya mantra. Having thus collected the clay, having had it carried by elephants or other [vehicles], and having subsequently entered the temple, one should worship the *pālikās*, *ghaṭikās*, and *śarāvas* with offerings (*upacāras*) after presenting the food offering (*nivedya*).

One should take either a golden or an earthen [image] and place it at the front or side of the deity on a site smeared with cow dung. Having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, [one should lay out] ten threads in the eastern direction.

Having laid out ten lines on a watery area, one should decorate the center—consisting of twenty-five squares—with *śāli* rice measured by one *droṇa* and half that amount of *taṇḍula* rice. Having strewn it with *kuśa* grass and drawn an eight-petaled lotus upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), one should place a full water-jar (*pūrṇakumbha*) together with its *kūrca* grass, its lid, and its cloth and gold, as well as two *vardhanī* vessels. Having adorned them with perfumes and other offerings, one performs the meditation on the central jar:
[the deity] is white in color, has two eyes, and stands upon a white lotus.
Two-armed, accompanied by a night-lotus, and wrapped in white cloth;
(established upon a bull, p.62b, l.1) endowed with all ornaments and adorned with pearl jewelry;
equipped with a crown and tiara, and graced by a halo of light.
Kṛttikā is in the right part and Rohiṇī on the left side;
she has a face like fine silk, is red in color, and is adorned with all ornaments.

Having meditated thus and worshipped according to the ritual procedure, one should perform the rites as before: having offered milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and given betel-leaf, one should worship with the ritual services (*upacāra*). Afterwards, two squares each [should be marked] at the four doors and in the four directions. In those squares, eight water-jars (*ghaṭikā*) should be placed in the corners beginning with the northwest (*nirṛti*). In every group of four squares, eight shallow bowls (*śarāva*) should be placed for these vessels, such as the *pālikā* and so forth.

One should bind the hollow parts with *kuśa* grass or chaff; one should fill the *pālikā*s and other vessels with earth. The presiding deities (*adhidevatā*) of the *pālikā*s and others are as follows: Īśvara, Viṣṇu, and Viriñca are the deities; for the *ghaṭikā*s, the deities are Āditya, Samayī, and Vivasvat. Jalādhipa, Mitra, Soma, Pṛthivīdhara, Īśāna, and Hutāśana [are the deities] starting from the northeast. Pūṣan, Vitra, and the rest... for the sake of the [deities] beginning with Īśāna, Āpa, Apavatsa, Savitṛ, Sāvitrī, Indra, Indrajaya, Rudra, and Rudradāsaka.

Thus one should worship in the intermediate directions—having worshipped with their respective names, beginning with the seat (*āsana*) and so forth, using the root mantras—one should sow the seeds. They are as follows: barley, wild rice (*nīvāra*), mung beans, sesame, black gram (*māṣa*), peas (*śimba*), horse gram (*kulattha*), flat beans (*niṣpāva*), and mustard seeds. Having washed them with milk and established them with the *hṛdaya* mantra, one should sow the seeds with the seed-mantras of Śiva. Afterwards, having worshipped the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) at the tips of the petals, and having worshipped the eight Vasus in the middle of the petals, [one should proceed] with words proclaiming auspiciousness and well-being.

Having sprinkled [the site] with water from a jar and worshipped daily with fragrant water—having offered milk-rice (*pāyasa*) to these [deities], having presented incense and lamps, and having performed the recitation (*japa*) and the concluding offering (*nivedya*)—and having given betel-leaf to all, one should give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) by the preceptor (*ācārya*) and others. This is the procedure for the rite of sowing the germinating seeds (*aṅkurārpaṇavidhi*).
(The Ritual for the Consecration and Preliminary Rite of the Bull [Vṛṣabhapratiṣṭhādhivāsanavidhi]:

Prior to the hoisting of the banner, one should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) that night. Then, having worshipped Śiva and made a formal request, the Preceptor—having decorated the site where the bull is to be stationed with canopies, *darbha* grass garlands, and so forth—should face north. Having assumed a steady posture and performed the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and other rites as previously described, he should worship Vṛṣabheśvara with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and offer cooked mung beans (*mudgānna*). Having made a formal request, he should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) before it, measuring five spans (*tala*).

Having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with eight *droṇas* of rice and other grains, having drawn the central self-form (*madhyamātmā*) with *kuśa* grass, and having strewn it with flowers, one should worship it with the seed-syllable of the bull (*vṛṣabhabīja*). Therein, having placed nine water-filled jars—equipped with *kūrca* grass-bundles and lids—and having worshipped the sixfold seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*) of the bull in the center, one should honor the form of the seat with the root mantras. [Then one worships] in the east: "Obeisance to the Bull (*ukṣan*). In the southeast: "Obeisance to the Lord of Cattle (*gopati*)."

In the south: Oṃ, homage to Śṛṅgin. In the southwest: homage to Nandin. In the west: homage to Vṛṣapati. In the northwest: homage to Vṛṣāṇi. In the north: homage to Śaṅkukaṇṭha. In the northeast: homage to Mahodara.

Having worshipped with the root mantras beginning with *ityādhāna*, having honored them each by their respective names—or alternatively, having worshipped the world-protectors (*lokapāla*)—and having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites in their proper places, one should worship with all ritual offerings (*sarvopacāra*). Then, regarding the banner-cloth (*dhvajapaṭa*): it should be an excellent new cloth, five parts in length and one part in width; its tail should be equal in length to the [total] width, and its crest half the length of the tail. It should be white, smooth, made of cotton or similar materials, and the cloth should be divided into three parts, [with the design] in the middle part.

Having drawn a bull of white color with red horns, neck, and hooves, with a yellow tail, and having made its eyes white and black, one should thereafter draw a full water-jar, two lamps, a bell, a mirror, a śrīvatsa, and a svastika—these and other auspicious forms. Having thus prepared the banner-cloth and displayed it, one should begin the ritual of the banner (*dhvaja-yāga*).

Then, having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, having performed the offering of water for honor (*arghya*), water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth, having sprinkled [the image] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and other substances, and having offered a bull-throne (*vṛṣabhacalāsana*) and worshipped it, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) before it and perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*) according to the procedure prescribed for the fire ritual. Following the purification of the image (*beraśuddhi*), one should prepare two sacrificial mounds in another delightful location; there, having placed the cloth-painting of the bull (*vṛṣabhapaṭa*) in the center and having sprinkled it with water, [one should proceed] with a golden needle...
Having performed the opening of the eyes with the *sūryasoma* mantra, one should perform [the rite] with honey, clarified butter, gold, and *dūrvā* sprouts using the *vṛṣabhagāyatrī*:
"We know the one with sharp horns; we meditate upon the one whose feet are the Vedas; may that Bull inspire us."

[One should perform] the root mantra and the six-limbed [nyāsa], and so forth. Having performed everything beginning with the inspection of the bull (*godarśana*), one should sprinkle [the image] with the eight types of earth and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*)—without [formally] bathing it—and then sprinkle it with the water of Śiva (*śivāmbhas*). Having bathed the reflection in the mirror with the five products of the cow and other substances, one should subsequently perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) in the water. Then, having brought the banner-cloth (*dhvajapaṭa*) into the sacrificial hall (*yāgaśālā*), one should bathe it with the five products of the cow and other substances using the Vṛṣabha-gāyatrī mantra, place the seat in the middle of the footprint, and [place it] at the base of the bull.

Oṃ, homage to the Support-Power (Ādhāra-śakti). Homage to the Seat of Ananta (Anantāsana). Homage to Dharma. Homage to Jñāna. (l. 5) Homage to Vairāgya. Homage to Aiśvarya. Oṃ, homage to the Bull-Seat (Vṛṣabhāsana). Homage to the Form of the Bull (Vṛṣabhamūrti). Homage to the Bull (Vṛṣabha).

In this manner, one should fashion the form of the Bull, beginning with the syllable *praṇava* (*oṃ*) and ending with *namaḥ*. Afterwards, having performed the circumambulation of the village and brought the cloth-painting of the Bull to the western door of the sacrificial hall, one should offer the *arghya* water to the form of the Bull with the eight-limbed prostration, worship it, and install it with the mantra of the limbs of the Bull. Then, having spread [the materials] upon the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*)... having laid out the cloth-painting.

Having placed a pair of soft garments with the *vṛṣabha-gāyatrī* mantra upon the seat of Ananta, which consists of the foundational power (*ādhāra-śakti*) and so forth, and having performed the placement of the fourfold [qualities] beginning with Dharma upon the seat—having first placed the head [of the image] facing east and provided a pillow for the crest-lock—one should clothe it with a garment. Then, one should perform the placement of Brahmā’s limbs, beginning with the head, upon the form of the bull.

Having performed all [the rites] beginning with incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and collyrium (*añjana*), one should establish the household implements with the root mantra accompanied by honey and clarified butter (*madhusarpiḥ*). Having established the sleep-vessel (*nidrākumbha*) which has been struck a hundred times with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), one should worship the bull and others. Standing at the base of the bull, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the thirty-four principles (*tattva*) together with their presiding deities, from the head down to the feet, as follows: *Oṃ, obeisance to the principle of Sadāśiva; obeisance to Brahmā, the presiding deity of the principle of Sadāśiva.*

Oṃ, homage to the principle of Īśvara. Homage to Ananta, the sovereign of the principle of Īśvara. Homage to the principle of Śuddhavidyā. Homage to Śambara, the sovereign of the principle of Śuddhavidyā.

In the portion of Viṣṇu: obeisance to the principle of Māyā; obeisance to Gahaneśa, the lord of the principle of Māyā; obeisance to the principle of Kāla; obeisance to Kālana, the lord of the principle of Kāla; obeisance to Niyati, the lord of the principle of Niyati; obeisance to the principle of Vidyā; obeisance to Vedavijñāna, the lord of the principle of Vidyā; obeisance to the principle of Rāga; obeisance to Kāmadā, the lord of the principle of Rāga; obeisance to the principle of Puruṣa.

Salutation to the subtle body, the lord of the principle of the person (*puruṣa-tattva*). Salutation to the principle of primordial nature (*prakṛti-tattva*); salutation to Pradhāna, the lord of the principle of primordial nature. Salutation to the principle of the qualities (*guṇa-tattva*); salutation to the three-bodied one (*trideha*), the lord of the principle of the qualities. Salutation to the principle of intellect (*buddhi-tattva*); salutation to the Awakened One (*buddha*), the lord of the principle of intellect. Salutation to the principle of egoity (*ahaṅkāra-tattva*); salutation to the Ego-maker (*ahaṅkṛtin*), the lord of the principle of egoity. Salutation to the principle of mind (*manas-tattva*).

Homage to Saṅkalpa, the lord of the principle of mind (*manas-tattva*). Homage to the principle of hearing (*śrotra-tattva*). Homage to Vyāmacara, the lord of the principle of hearing. Homage to the principle of touch (*tvak-tattva*). Homage to Sarvāṅga, the lord of the principle of touch. Homage to the principle of sight (*cakṣus-tattva*). Homage to Prakāśaka, the lord of the principle of sight. Homage to the principle of the tongue (*jihvā-tattva*). Homage to Mahāvaktra, the lord of the principle of the tongue. Homage to the principle of the nose (*nāsā-tattva*).

Homage to Vilambaka, the sovereign of the reality of the nose. Homage to the reality of speech. Homage to Dundubhi, the sovereign of the reality of speech. Homage to the reality of the hands. Homage to [the name], the sovereign of the reality of the hands. Homage to the reality of the feet. Homage to Ramaṇa, the sovereign of the reality of the feet. Homage to the reality of the anus. Homage to Kūrṇakṛta, the sovereign of the reality of the anus. Homage to the reality of the generative organ. Homage to Ghanānanda, the sovereign of the reality of the generative organ.

Homage to the reality of sound (*śabdatattva*). Homage to the lord of the reality of sound, the subtle resonance (*sūkṣmanāda*). Homage to the reality of touch (*sparśatattva*). Homage to the lord of the reality of touch, the most powerful one (*balavattara*). Homage to the reality of form (*rūpatattva*). Homage to the lord of the reality of form, the radiant one (*bhānumat*). Homage to the reality of taste (*rasatattva*). Homage to the lord of the reality of taste, the cloud-giver (*jalada*). Homage to the reality of smell (*gandhatattva*). Homage to the lord of the reality of smell, whose limbs are fragrance (*gandhāṅga*). Homage to the reality of space (*vyomatattva*).

Salutation to the subtle *nāda*, the lord of the element of space (*vyoma-tattva*). Salutation to the element of air (*vāyu-tattva*). Salutation to Mātariśvan, the lord of the element of air. Salutation to the element of fire (*tejas-tattva*). Salutation to the storehouse of radiance, the lord of the element of fire. Salutation to the element of water (*jala-tattva*). Salutation to Jaleśa, the lord of the element of water. Salutation to the element of earth (*pṛthivī-tattva*). Salutation to Śrīkaṇṭha, the lord of the element of earth. Thus [ends] the Brahma-portion.

Having thus arranged [the deities]—having conceived the [mandala] as having three sections and having offered a flower garland and a protective cord—at the portion of Rudra, ending with the principle of Sadāśiva: *oṃ hūṃ namaḥ śivatattvāya*. *oṃ hūṃ namaḥ śivatattvādhipāya brahmaṇe*. Having thus arranged [these], at the portion of Indra, in the sequence starting from the east: *oṃ liṃ namaḥ kṣmāmūrtaye*. *oṃ lūṃ namaḥ kṣmāmūrtyadhipataye ukṣāya*. *oṃ rūṃ namaḥ agnimūrtaye*.

Salutation to the Lord of the Fire-form, the Lord of Cattle (Gopati). Oṃ Hūṃ, salutation to the Sacrificer-form. Salutation to Śṛṅgin, the Lord of the Sacrificer-form. Oṃ Ṣṭām, salutation to the Sun-form. Salutation to Nandin, the Lord of the Sun-form. Śruṃ, salutation to the Water-form. Salutation to Mahodara, the Lord of the Water-form. In the portion of Viṣṇu: Oṃ Kṣmām, salutation to the Earth-form. Salutation to Ukṣan, the Lord of the Earth-form. Salutation to the Fire-form.

Salutation to Gopati, the presiding lord of the form of Agni. Oṃ, salutation to the form of the Sacrificer. Salutation to Śṛṅgin, the presiding lord of the form of the Sacrificer. Salutation to the form of Arka. Salutation to Nandin, the presiding lord of the form of Arka. (l. 6) Salutation to the form of Water. Salutation to Vṛṣabhapati, the presiding lord of the form of Water. Salutation to the form of Pāyu. Salutation to Viṣṇu, the presiding lord of the form of Pāyu. Salutation to the form of Indu. Indu... (p. 67a, l. 1) ... [text continues]

Homage to Śaṅkukarṇa. Homage to Khamūrti. Homage to Mahodara, the lord of Khamūrti. In the Brahma-quarter: Oṃ, homage to Kṣmāmūrti. Homage to Ukṣan, the lord of Kṣmāmūrti. Oṃ, homage to Agnimūrti. Homage to Gopati, the lord of Agnimūrti. Homage to Yajamānamūrti. Homage to Śṛṅgin, the lord of Yajamānamūrti. Homage to Arkamūrti. Homage to Nandin, the lord of Arkamūrti.

Salutation to the water-form; salutation to the lord of the water-form, the lord of the bull. Salutation to the wind-form; salutation to the lord of the wind-form, Vṛṣāṇin. Salutation to the moon-form; salutation to the lord of the moon-form, Śaṅkukarṇa. Salutation to the ether-form; salutation to the lord of the ether-form, Mahodara.

Having thus assigned the forms and the lords of the forms to each respective part, one should— for the purpose of the assignment of the individual soul (*jīvanyāsa*)—invoke [the deity] with the root mantra *oṃ mama*, worship it with the ritual services such as installation (*sthāpana*), display the ritual gestures (*mudrā*), and perform the offering of water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth. Then, having protected [the area] with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), one should construct three outer enclosures outside using ashes, *darbha* grass, and sesame seeds. Afterwards, one should worship the bull (*ukṣan*) and others in the pitchers situated in the east and other directions, and for the sake of protection, worship the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) and others.

One should go to the vicinity of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*). There, in the midst of the fire upon the mound, one should perform the following: [visualize] the deity Vṛṣabha on the rim; the fourfold [powers] beginning with Nivṛtti on the girdles; and the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) at the navel. Having deposited these, one should offer "Vṛṣebhyaḥ Svāhā" to the pots and the mounds. One should then perform the conjunction of the channels (*sahanāḍī-sandhāna*) for the sake of their presence. Having offered three oblations with the root-mantra of Vṛṣabha, one should worship on the mound with: "Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti. Thus, having performed the worship.

Having offered three oblations—*oṃ ... ātmatattvāya namaḥ | oṃ hām ātmatattvādhipataye brahmaṇe namaḥ | oṃ hiṃ vidyātattvāya namaḥ | oṃ hiṃ vidyātattvādhipataye viṣṇave namaḥ | oṃ hūṃ śivatattvāya namaḥ | oṃ hūṃ śivatattvādhipataye rudrāya namaḥ*—and having thus worshipped, one should offer three oblations each to the principles of Self (*ātmatattva*), Knowledge (*vidyātattva*), and the deities Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, [saying]: *oṃ kṣmāmūrtaye namaḥ*.

Salutation to the Bull, the lord of the earth-form; salutation to the fire-form; salutation to the cowherd, the lord of the fire-form; salutation to the sacrificer-form; salutation to the horned one, the lord of the sacrificer-form; salutation to the sun-form; salutation to Nandin, the lord of the sun-form; salutation to the water-form; salutation to the lord of the bull, the lord of the water-form; salutation to the wind-form; salutation to Vṛṣāṇin, the lord of the wind-form.

"Obeisance to Indumūrti. Obeisance to Śaṅkukarṇa, the lord of Indumūrti. Obeisance to Khamūrti. Obeisance to Mahodara, the lord of Khamūrti. Having thus worshipped with mantras ending in *namaḥ*, and having offered three oblations ending in *svāhā*, one should offer either one hundred or fifty oblations each to the root mantra of Vṛṣabha and the Brahmāṅgas.

Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, the preceptor (*ācārya*), holding the *śāntikumbha* in his hand, approaches the bull. The Guru, having sprinkled [the bull] with the water from the *śāntikumbha* while reciting "O Heart of the Guru, *namaḥ*," establishes the presence of these [deities]. Having concealed [the bull] with the *varma* mantra and restrained it, he should cause the lords of the *tattvas* to hear: "O Brahmā, lord of the *ātmatattva*, for as long as any defect arises regarding the cloth, you must remain right here in person."

Oṃ hāṃ hiṃ(hīṃ), homage to the two principles of the Self and Knowledge (ātmatattva-vidyātattvābhyāṃ). One should worship by reciting [the mantras] ending with Māyā and Anādā: Oṃ lūṃ, homage to the two forms of Earth (kṣmāmūrtibhyāṃ). Homage to the two forms of Earth, the two Bulls (ukṣābhyāṃ). Homage to the two forms of Fire, Rūpa and Vahni (rapavahnimūrtibhyāṃ). Homage to Gopati, the lord of the two forms of Fire (vahnimūrtyadhipābhyāṃ). Oṃ śrā(śrūṃ) śrā(śrūṃ), homage to the two forms of the Sacrificer (yajamānamūrtibhyāṃ). Homage to Śr̥ṅgin, the two forms of the Sacrificer (yajamānamūrtibhyāṃ).

Oṃ ṣṭraṃ ṣṭram, homage to the two Sun-forms (*arkamūrti*). Homage to the two Nandis of the Sun-forms. Oṃ vraṃ, homage to the two Water-forms (*jalamūrti*). [Homage] to the two Vṛṣabhas of the Water-forms. Oṃ pūṃ yūṃ, homage to the two Wind-forms (*vāyumūrti*). Homage to the two Vṛṣāṇis of the Wind-forms. Oṃ sūṃ sūm, homage to the two Moon-forms (*indumūrti*). Homage to the two Śaṅkukaṇṭhas of the Moon-forms. Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ, homage to the two Space-forms (*khamūrti*). Homage to the two Mahodaras.

Thus the forms and the lords of the forms should perform the conjunction (*sandhāna*). Then, having gone to the edge of the sacrificial mound (*sthāṇḍila*) and having worshipped in this manner—having performed the conjunction—one should offer oblations. In the portion belonging to Viṣṇu, for the sake of purification: *oṃ hiṃ vidyā-tattvāya namaḥ |* "Obeisance to the principle of knowledge (*vidyā-tattva*); obeisance to Viṣṇu, the lord of the principle of knowledge. Having thus worshipped and caused [the deity] to be present (*sannidhāpya*): *oṃ kṣmā-mūrtaye namaḥ |* "Obeisance to the form of the Earth"; *ukṣāya namaḥ |* "Obeisance to the Bull"; *rūṃ vahnimūrtaye namaḥ |* "Obeisance to the form of Fire"; *adhipataye gopataye namaḥ |* "Obeisance to the Lord, the Protector of Cattle."

Oṃ śūṃ, homage to the form of the sacrificer. Oṃ śūṃ, homage to the form of the sacrificer. Homage to Śṛṅgin, the lord of the form of the sacrificer. Oṃ ṣṭām, homage to the form of the Sun. Homage to Nandin, the lord of the form of the Sun. Oṃ ṣṭrāṃ, homage to the form of the Root of Water. Homage to Vṛṣabhapati, the lord of the form of Water. Oṃ yūṃ, homage to the form of Wind. Homage to Vṛṣāṇin, the lord of the form of Wind.
Hrām! Homage to Indumūrti. Homage to Śaṅkukaṇṭha, the lord of Indumūrti. Oṃ hūṃ! Homage to Khamūrti. Homage to Mahodara, the lord of Khamūrti.

Having worshipped [the deity] ending with *namaḥ*, and having offered three oblations ending with *svāhā*, one should offer either fifty or a hundred oblations each for the root mantra of the bull (*vṛṣabha*) and the Brahma-limbs (*brahmāṅga*). Then, having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should go near the cloth-painting (*paṭa*) of the bull; as before, having sprinkled it with water from the pacification-vessel (*śāntikumbha*), and having touched the portion belonging to Viṣṇu in the middle of the *kuśa* grass while reciting the root mantra of the bull, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) according to the number of oblations. Again, one should sprinkle it with the water of pacification.

Having performed the *avakuṇṭhana* (sealing) with the presence of the heart-mantra, and having performed the *arghya* (offering of water) and the *nirodhana* (confinement), one should cause Viṣṇu to hear this command: “O Viṣṇu, Lord of the *vidyā-tattva*, as long as any evil has arisen, you must remain right here by your very presence. Then: *oṃ hūṃ hūṃ namaḥ to the *vidyā-tattva* and the *śiva-tattva*. Namaḥ to Viṣṇu and Śiva, the Lords of the *vidyā-tattva* and the *śiva-tattva*.*

Having thus worshipped up to Sadāśiva, one should perform worship by uttering "namaḥ" at the end [of each name]. Oṃ lūṃ lūṃ, obeisance to the two forms of Earth (Kṣmāmūrti). Rūṃ rūṃ, obeisance to the two forms of Fire (Vahnimūrti). Oṃ śrūṃ śrūṃ, obeisance to the two forms of the Sacrificer (Yajamānamūrti). Oṃ ṣūṃ ṣūṃ, obeisance to the two forms of the Sun (Arkamūrti). Oṃ pūṃ pūṃ, obeisance to the two forms of Water (Jalamūrti). Yūṃ yūṃ, obeisance to the two forms of Wind (Vāyumūrti). Sūṃ sūṃ, obeisance to the two forms of the Moon (Indumūrti). Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ, obeisance to the two forms of Space (Khamūrti).

One should offer [the oblation] with the *iḍā*, the *mūrti*, and so forth, whether pure or impure. Oṃ hāṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the bull (*ukṣan*) for the lord of the earth-form (*kṣmāmūrti*). Oṃ hiṃ, obeisance to the bull (*gopati*) for the lord of the fire-form (*vahnimūrti*). Obeisance to the horned one (*śṛṅgin*) for the lord of the sacrificer-form (*yajamānamūrti*). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Nandin for the lord of the sun-form (*arkamūrti*). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the lord of bulls (*vṛṣabhapati*) for the lord of the water-form (*jalamūrti*). Oṃ pūṃ, obeisance to the testicles (*vṛṣaṇa*) for the lord of the wind-form (*vāyumūrti*).

"Oṃ, salutation to Śaṅkukarṇa, the lord of the Moon-form; oṃ, salutation to Mahodara, the lord of the Ether-form. Thus one should perform the conjunction with the lords of the forms (*mūrtyādhipas*). Then, having gone near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*): "Oṃ huṃ, salutation to the Śiva-principle (*śivatattva*); oṃ hūṃ, salutation to Rudra, the lord of the Śiva-principle. Having thus worshipped and caused [the deity] to be present, [one offers]: "Salutation to the bull for the lord of the Earth-form; oṃ, salutation to the Fire-form."

Salutation to Gopati, the lord of the fire-form; salutation to the sacrificer-form; salutation to Śṛṅgin, the lord of the sacrificer-form; salutation to the sun-form; salutation to Nandin, the lord of the sun-form; salutation to the water-form; salutation to Vṛṣabhapati, the lord of the water-form; salutation to the wind-form; salutation to Vṛṣāṇin, the lord of the wind-form; salutation to the moon-form.

"Obeisance to Śaṅkukarṇa, the lord of the moon-form. Obeisance to the ether-form. Obeisance to Mahodara, the lord of the ether-form. Having thus worshipped with these [mantras] ending in *namaḥ*, and having offered three oblations ending in *svāhā*, one should offer either one hundred or fifty oblations each to the Vṛṣabha-mūla-mantra and the Brahmāṅgas. Afterwards, having gone near the cloth-painting (*paṭa*) of the bull, having sprinkled it with water for pacification (*śāntijala*), [one should perform the rite] in the portion of Rudra with the tip of a *kuśa* blade using the Vṛṣabha-mūla-mantra.

Having touched [the object] and recited [the mantra] as many times as the number of oblations (*homa*), having again sprinkled it with water empowered by the *śakti* [mantra], and having effected its presence with "Oṃ, *hṛdayāya* namaḥ" (*hṛdayāya namaḥ*), he should seal it with the *avakuṇṭhana* [mudrā]. Then he should proclaim the command of Rudra: "O Rudra, O Lord, as long as the cloth arising from faults has not been stolen by you from this state of the realized reality of Śiva (*jñātaśivatatvapada*), so long [must you remain] here. Thus he should inform him.

Then, for the purpose of removing defects from the root onwards, one should offer a hundred *pūrṇāhuti*s with the sword [mantra] of Śiva-Aghora. Afterwards, having offered the *caru*, performed the *pūrṇāhuti*, given water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*) and betel, having tethered the bull, offered the *vyāhṛti* oblations, presented the internal *bali*, and performed the salutation to the ears, one should perform the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*). Having approached the bull, having circumambulated the bull to the right, [one should act] at the ear.

"O Blessed One, Lord of Bulls, whatever has been deficient through ignorance or delusion in this sacrifice here, may all that be made complete by your grace. Om! Salutations to the Blessed One, the Bull, whose form is Dharma; salutations be to you! Whether the rite was complete or incomplete, may it be accepted according to one’s own capacity. Having thus made this petition and applied the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), one should conclude [the ritual] with oblations, or with Vedic chants, or with great festivals of dance and song performed with devotion, and observe a vigil for one night.

The consecration of the bull (*vṛṣādhivāsana*). One should offer oblations every day, reciting one hundred repetitions each of their respective root mantras; one should present worship, offerings (*bali*), and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth to the bull, the water-jar, and the other [implements], together with the preceptor, disciples, and others—[and then] sleep. Thus ends the ritual procedure for the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the bull installation.
(The Ritual for Hoisting the Banner:

On the following day, having performed the ritual bathing and other preliminaries, having performed the *sakalīkaraṇa*, having prepared the general *arghya* offering, and having carried out everything including the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and the inner sacrifice (*antaryajana*), one should worship the cloth and the jar with perfumes and other offerings in their proper order, and [worship] the bull in the navel.

Having worshipped the Bull in the fire—having performed one hundred and eight oblations with sacrificial fuel (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and cooked rice (*caru*)—and having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root mantra of the Bull and performed the ritual confinement (*niruddhya*), one should thereafter prepare the ground for the temple. Having smeared the area with cow dung and constructed a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) on that site, one should perform the consecration of the pavilion and other rites, sprinkling it with water while reciting the *tatpuruṣa* mantra. Then, having prepared three altars (*sthaṇḍila*) and drawn the [mandala] lines, one should summon the attendants.

Having sprinkled [the image] with the *astra* mantra and donned the turban and upper garment, one should go near the bull-cloth (*vṛṣapaṭa*). Having lifted it up, saying "the seed-receptacle," together with the jar and the rest, and accompanied by the deity of the *astra*, as well as Soma and Skanda, and all musical instruments, one should perform a circumambulation of the village. Then, entering the temple to the accompaniment of the sounding of conchs and drums and the chanting of Brahmins, one should place that cloth upon the ground (*sthaṇḍila*) with the *hṛdaya* mantra. With the single *astrarāja* mantra, one should place it on the ground in front of that [image].

Having placed the bull-pitcher (*vṛṣabhakumbha*) surrounded by the pitchers of the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*) upon a single sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in front of that [bull], and having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) there, one should bathe [the bull] with the water from the bull-pitcher—[located] in the middle of the stream of banners—after having deposited the seed-syllable of the bull (*vṛṣabhabīja*). Then, having sprinkled the pitchers of the Lords of Knowledge with the *Vṛṣabhagāyatrī* mantra, and having bathed the bull with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and so forth, and having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should prepare a sacrificial mound in front of it with eight *droṇas* of rice.

Having prepared nine jars, having taken them along with tufts of grass, lids, gold, garments, and other ornaments, and having adorned them, one who is surrounded by the retinue of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvara) and others should invoke the deity Vṛṣabha; having invoked the bull and the other [deities] with their respective mantras, one should perform worship with perfumes and other offerings, present the sacrificial oblation, and complete the worship ending with recitation.

Having bathed the king of weapons, the Trident (śūla), with the water from that jar, having adorned and worshipped it, and having offered [oblations], one should worship the banner of the Vṛṣabha-gāyatrī; then, having offered rice mixed with jaggery and curds, as well as rice with mung beans, one should cause the consecration thread (kautuka) to be tied to the king of weapons with the Heart-mantra.
