Having offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the *Bṛhatsāman*, one should cause it to be given to the devotees and attendants. Then, having adorned the flagpole and provided garlands, ornaments, garments, and so forth—

One should fasten the bell with the *vṛṣabha-gāyatrī* mantra; having mounted another pole onto the flagstaff, one should cause it to be carried to the front of the temple. The preceptor should go in front, the sacrificer behind the bull, and they should present offerings to the guardians of the directions, from Brahmā to Īśāna. Then, together with the devotees, having performed a circumambulation of the village, they should enter the temple. Having brought it to the place of the staff, accompanied by all musical instruments and joined with auspicious sprouts—

Accompanied by full water-pots and various lamps, adorned in the four directions with song and dance—having had the *puṇyāha* (day of merit) proclaimed at the site of the banner, having sprinkled the altar (*vedikā*) with water, having worshipped the seat beginning with Ādhāraśakti and ending with Śakti, having meditated upon Sadāśiva on the staff, and having invoked and worshipped him; [one should worship] Soma, Sūrya, and Agni on the joints of the staff, Anila on the staff, the presiding deity of the carpenter on the rope, and the deity Vāyu on the cloth of the banner.

Having invoked the deity Vṛṣabha and worshipped him in due order, having offered green-gram rice (*mudgānna*) and milk-rice (*pāyasānna*) to the bull and presented betel leaves and other offerings, and having given betel leaves to the devotees and offered incense and lamps, the preceptor (*deśika*) should then raise the banner and fasten it with a rope. Having informed Śiva, at an auspicious moment and a favorable conjunction (*sulagna*), he should conduct the supreme festival accompanied by the sounding of musical instruments.

Standing at the base of the bull, having first touched it oneself—or having another attendant speak the words for the purpose of mounting—one should quickly mount it. Having handed over the staff, one should gradually fasten the root-rope. From that point until the end of the ritual site, one should worship the deity of the bull three times, twice, or once a day, up until the time of the conclusion of the mounting.

Having thus worshipped [the deity], one should cause [the recipient] to be given food of mung beans mixed with molasses. Afterwards, having offered the recitation (*japa*) one hundred and eight times with the mantra "Oṃ Vṛṣabhāya Namaḥ," one should perform the recitation for a tenth part of that—namely, one hundred times—with the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*): *Praṃ Hṛdayāya Namaḥ*; *Hrīṃ Śirase Namaḥ*; *Oṃ Prarūṃ Śikhāya Namaḥ*; *Oṃ Vraiṃ Kavacāya Namaḥ*; *Oṃ Vrauṃ Netrebhyo Namaḥ*.

Saying "Oṃ vruḥ, obeisance to the weapon (*astra*)," one should go from the altar (*vedi*) to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and food, and having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root-mantra of the Bull (*Vṛṣabha*), one should dismiss the Bull-fire in the four directions. A pure dance should be performed; such is the procedure for hoisting the banner (*dhvajārohaṇavidhi*). According to the *Vātula*, a woman should consume that [remnant] of the bull's mass; she shall obtain a son of Atri, who destroys disease and removes all defects. O Śikhidhvaja, this is the desired [fruit] of the Bull in the venerable *Mṛgendra*.

(The Ritual Procedure for the Procession) In whatever kingdom this installation of the flagstaff is performed, there Lakṣmī shall abide at all times, even in the midst of calamities. No portents, misfortunes, or delusions caused by hostile forces shall occur there, provided one has adorned [the site] according to the previously mentioned ritual. [The deity] should be placed upon a chariot, a stage, a shield, a palanquin, or similar vehicle, endowed with the radiance of various ornaments and flowers.

Having brought [the deity] to the root shrine accompanied by the divine power (*devaśakti*), having invoked [him], and having offered incense and lamps, he should worship with a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). Then, together with the stationary image (*bera*) ending with the portion for peace (*śānti*) and so forth, he should begin the circumambulation. In front, accompanied by various ornaments and the sounds of drums (*berī*) and other instruments, [he proceeds]. Vināyaka and Subrahmaṇya are in the middle; Soma and Skanda are in front with the Goddess; behind them are the various *bherīs*; and after that, the preceptor (*deśika*) places Caṇḍeśvara on his left side.

Having stood at the base, one should mutter either the *aghora* mantra; the king [stands] in front and the patron (*yajamāna*) behind. Behind them follow temple-servants, dancers, lute-players, singers, drummers, and great Śaivas, accompanied by the sounds of the Vedas and other scriptures. Following after them, people of the four castes, like a lunar orb, proceed toward Maheśvara; such a person obtains the fruit of an *aśvamedha* sacrifice. Having thus satisfied [the deities], on the first day, [one worships] Raṅga in the morning and Haṃsa at night.

On the second day—at night, the moon’s orb. On the third day—at night, a *bhūta* [spirit] joined with a peak; on the fourth day, a palanquin; at night, a serpent-machine (*nāgayantra*). On the fifth day, a shield; at night, a bull. After the circumambulation, one should perform the serving of food. In gardens and such places, there is the recitation of Vedic hymns at every moment.

Accompanied by singers playing the *vīṇā* and flute according to the Vedas (*śruti*), and by dancers and the attendants of Rudra, one should gratify the Lord at every step with offerings of fruit and such, as well as betel-leaf and other items. Then, having entered the temple on the sixth day, having placed the deity upon a palanquin or a litter, and having performed the *cūrṇotsava* as will be described below, one should worship the deities with water mixed with saffron, safflower, turmeric, and so forth; having sprinkled them and smeared the Lord with saffron paste using the *astra-mantra*, one should sprinkle everyone during the night, [mounted] upon an elephant.

On the seventh [day] the chariot, and on the eighth having mounted the horses— at the time of departure, those mounted on horses, such as Kunda and others, equipped with weapons like the *keṭaka*, and accompanied by all ornaments, should proceed surrounded by the retinue of Rudra’s courtesans.

In the meantime—having performed the suppression of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous, and having proclaimed all that is lawful and unlawful—he should afterwards enter his residence. On the ninth day, accompanied by a palanquin yoked with human figures and carrying a skull-bowl, he should place the deity upon a lion-throne scented with black incense on the tenth day. Having circumambulated the city and other sites, and having paraded the deformed food atop a palace or a flagstaff, he should cast it at a crossroads.

Having offered the *nīrāñjana* rite with a cloth lamp, Śailādi, Nandin, Vināyaka, and Caṇḍeśvara should circumambulate the temple. Then, for the purpose of the removal [of obstacles], having offered the essence of coconuts, green gram soup, and fruits appropriate to the season, and having adorned the Brahmins with perfumes and flowers, he should feed the Brahmins who are poor, blind, and miserable; or else he may act in another manner—this is the procedure for the sequence of the procession (*yānakrama*).

(The Worship in the Sacrificial Hall—) The Guru, having performed his ablutions and so forth, having washed his feet, and having sipped water (*ācamana*), performs the *puṇyāha* rite beginning with the worship of Vighneśvara in the sacrificial hall; then, having sprinkled [the area], and having performed the ritualization of the body (*sakalīkaraṇa*), the worship of the door, the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*), and so on, he performs the worship of the door and the propitiation of the pitcher (*kalaśārādhana*) as before, and having offered the food oblation (*naivedya*) and other items, he subsequently goes near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and, having carried out the rites up to the waving of the mirror and lamp, [he recites] the root mantra one hundred and eight times.

Having offered oblations with fuel-sticks (*samidh*), rice, and clarified butter (*ājya*), and having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the nine grains beginning with parched rice (*lāja*) using the five Brahmans and the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), and having given the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should worship [the deity] with food offerings (*naivedya*) and so forth. Then, for the sake of warding off all obstacles, one should worship the trident (*triśūla*) prepared for Īśāna, adorning it with worship and other rites; having worshipped it with food offerings and so forth, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the seed-syllable of fire (*agnibīja*), and having offered with the *Vṛṣakāya* mantra and its root mantra, one should give the final full oblation—the inner offering (*antarbali*) and the outer offering (*bahirbali*).

Having fashioned two bulls, worshipped them with fragrant substances such as oil and the like, adorned them, and offered food offerings (*naivedya*) and so forth, one should present the final oblation (*pūrṇā*). At the base of the flagpole, having worshipped a lotus with oil and other substances, and having presented food offerings with perfumes and the like, one should perform the worship of the flagpole. Having performed the *puṇyāha* rite at the top of the pole and having performed the ritual of the limbs (*sakalīkaraṇa*), one should prepare the water for respectful offering (*arghya*).

Having sprinkled the staff with water for purification (*arghya*) and protected it with the *kavaca* mantra, one should worship [the deities] from Śakti up to the final Śakti in their proper order. Then, preceded by the syllable *Oṃ*, one worships Brahmā at the base of the staff, Viṣṇu in the middle of the staff, and Rudra at the top. Having worshipped the three principles (*tattva*)—the principle of the self (*ātmatattva*) and its presiding lord—one worships Skanda on the handle and the seven Mothers, beginning with Brāhmī and Māheśvarī. Finally, one worships Daṇḍin on the two side-staffs (*upadaṇḍa*).

On the left side—*namas* to Muṇḍin. Having worshipped the eight great nāgas, beginning with Ananta and Vāsuki, upon the garland of darbha grass; and having honored the nine Śaktis, beginning with Vāmā, within the circle of the bell and Sadāśiva—at the tips of the petals of the pedestal: [worship] Indra and the other world-protectors (*lokapālas*).
On the secondary petals: "The bull Ukṣa and Gopati, likewise Śaṅkukarṇa, Tiṣṇaśṛṅga, Nandin, and the bull Vṛṣa, as well as Paśupati."
One should worship Mahodara and [the others] each by their own names.

Having worshipped [them] on the banner-cloth with the Vṛṣagāyatrī mantra—having thus offered boiled rice mixed with curd, honey, and ghee, and having worshipped them with incense, lamps, and so forth—one should worship Ananta and the other eight Vidyeśvaras upon the main altar (daṇḍavedikā) amidst the sounds of all auspicious musical instruments. Then, having worshipped the twelve Ādityas, beginning with Vaikartana, upon the secondary altar (upavedikā)—having offered them ghee, jaggery, and milk-rice (pāyasa), and having presented incense and lamps and worshipped them—the meditation [is as follows]:

And one attendant: two-faced, six-eyed, with a garland of darbha grass and ropes, having the form of a servant’s body, two-armed, two-nosed, and possessing the form of a staff while seated upon a lotus posture.

Having meditated thus, and having offered milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with ghee and molasses, one should present the *bali* offering at the places of Brahmā, Indra, and the others upon the base of the banner, amidst the sounding of conchs and auspicious musical instruments, using the names of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) in the dative case followed by *svāhā*. One should perform this every day, morning and evening. Then, having circumambulated the village accompanied by dance, song, and all ornaments for the Lord of the Festival, wherever there is an invocation of the deities of the junctions, there one should do likewise.

Having performed the incense, lamps, food offerings, dance, music, and so forth for the deity, and having entered the temple, one should perform the sixteen services, beginning with the food offering, for the Lord of the Festival in the pavilion of the sacred site; thus [it is done] in the evening and in the morning.
(The sequence of festivals: First there shall be Vighnarātri; second, Paiśāca;
third, Brahmarātri; and fourth, Gandharva.
The fifth shall be Bhūtarātri, the sixth Guharātraka;
the seventh shall be Ṛṣirātra, and the eighth Nāgarātraka.
The ninth should be the Indrarātra, and the tenth the Viṣṇurātraka;
the eleventh should be the Rudra, and the twelfth the Śivarātraka.
The *gaṇarātra* is on the thirteenth day, while the *rākṣasa* is the fourteenth.
The *candrarātra* is the fifteenth, and the *śaktirātra* is the sixteenth.
From Vighna up to Canda, there is indeed a festival of bliss.
From Vighna (Gaṇeśa) up to Śiva, as well as the festival of the ancestors (Pitṛs).
From Vighna up to Indra during festivals and the like,
and likewise from Vighna up to the Ṛṣis during the Śrīkara festival.
Then, one should perform the terrestrial festival beginning with Vighna and ending with Bhūta;
likewise, in due order, the sattvic festival beginning with Vighna and ending with Brahmā.
One should perform the Śiva-festival, which consists of the Vighna, the Vighnātirātra, and [the others].
The characteristics of the bali offering: Listen to the sequence for the consumption of the bali by these deities,
beginning from the start of the festival and continuing in order from morning until evening.
In this way, the night should be understood; such is the sequence of the ritual for Puṣkala.
For festivals and the like, however, it is proclaimed that [the ritual] should be performed either in the evening or during the night itself.

One should not perform [the ritual] for anyone other than a festival; the best of teachers should arrange the great night (*mahārātri*) for the gods in the intervals between festivals, and the night-rite (*rātrika*) for Vijaya according to the proper sequence. (Balilakṣaṇa, p. 78a, l. 1)
Mudga-rice, sweetmeat balls, ghee, and plantains combined with sugar-cane juice.
On the first day, one should offer [the oblation] while recollecting the Vighnas:
pure rice and *kṛsarā* rice soaked in curd mixed with black gram (*māṣa*).
On the second day, one should offer [the oblation] while reciting the Paiśāca mantra:
milk-rice mixed with ghee, along with cakes accompanied by lotuses.
On the third day, one should give [the offering] while recollecting the Brahma-mantra:
kṛsarā-rice and meat together with ghee and combined with mung beans.
On the fourth day, one should give [the offering] while reciting the mantra of the Gandharvas:
parched grain (*lāja*) mixed with milk, ending with *indravallī* and turmeric (*haridrā*).
On the fifth day, one should give it while recollecting the mantra of the Bhūtas.
Food with ghee, combined with jaggery and accompanied by coconut fruit.
And on the sixth day, one should give [the offering] while recollecting the mantra of Skanda:
tips of kuśa grass mixed with curd, as well as the fruit of the bṛhatī plant.
On the seventh day, while reciting the mantra of the Ṛṣis,
one should offer pure food consisting of milk-rice enriched with *śāli* rice and accompanied by pieces of sugarcane.
On the eighth day, while reciting the mantra of the Nāgas, [the same] should be given.
One should offer curd-rice mixed with jaggery and combined with the fruits of the citron tree.
On the ninth day, recollecting the Aindra mantra,
one should offer food made of *gulā* mixed with ghee and combined with plantain fruit.
On the tenth day, one should give [the offering] while recollecting the Viṣṇu mantra:
red rice combined with meat, along with cakes and sesame seeds.
On the eleventh day, it should be given while recollecting the Raudra mantra.
On the twelfth day, while recollecting the mantra of Śiva, one should offer wheat flour, curd-rice mixed with jaggery and sugar-candy,
as well as milk-rice combined with wood-apple fruit and parched grain.
On the thirteenth day, one should give [the offering] while recollecting the *gaṇa-mantra*:
red food mixed with molasses, along with an *āḍhaka* measure of flour.
On the fourteenth day, one should offer [the oblation] while reciting the Rākṣasa mantra:
milk-rice mixed with ghee, together with a jackfruit.
On the fifteenth day, it should be performed while recollecting the Candra mantra.
On the sixteenth day, rice mixed with molasses and combined with pieces of *kūśmāṇḍa* gourd, along with curd, should be offered while reciting the *kapardhaphala* mantra.
(The mounting of the chariot:)

Thus is the *bali* offering proclaimed. Even in the absence of [the usual] materials, one should offer a *bali* of curd-rice. Having offered the *bali* from Brahmā to Īśāna, the wise practitioner, having worshipped according to the ritual procedure all the locations and so forth with the mantras of Vighnarāja and the others, should cast the *bali* with the appropriate materials. One should employ the formula for the assignment of the *bali*: beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ), followed by the name of the deity in the dative case, and ending with *svāhā*. For example: "Oṃ, [Name], svāhā! (or "Oṃ, [Name], balaye svāhā!").

One should especially offer the *bali* offering at the foremost part of all the temples. Having thus performed the sequence of the *bali*, one should cast the *bali* upon the *balipīṭha*. Then, having entered the sacrificial hall (*yāgaśālā*), one should install the *vajra* and other implements in their proper order. Then, having dismissed the *liṅgamūrti*, one should likewise set aside the *liṅga*.

One should perform the circumambulation of the village—having performed the ritual cleansing at the end of the child’s [initiation] according to the rules—one should sprinkle it with pure waters. One should adorn each house with plantains, betel-nut trees, full water-pots containing fruits, strings of pearls, and flowers.

Adorned with various banners, chowries, and fans, having placed the images upon a chariot or even on a stage, covered with new cloth, accompanied by dance and song, endowed with the radiance of flowers, and decorated with all ornaments—one or two of the eighteen types of images should be made to ascend the chariot for seven or nine days; prior to that, the chariot [should be prepared] together with the artisans.

Having thoroughly examined each major and minor limb and having made it firm, and having carefully inspected the components of the chariot, when the workmanship was completed, on the eve preceding the mounting of the chariot, [he performed] the binding of the chariot... (Note: The ellipsis "tu bandhanam" suggests the completion of the preparatory rites for the chariot's harnessing or stabilization.)

Having prepared the chariot, having purified it by sprinkling it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), clay, cow dung, water infused with *kāṣāya* dye, the *arghya* offering, and pure water, while reciting the *astra-mantra*; and having performed the purification once more by sprinkling it with the *pañcagavya* and the *arghya* offering; and having constructed a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) according to the prescribed characteristics either at the front of the temple or at the front of the chariot; and having smeared it with cow dung; and having sprinkled both the pavilion and the chariot with the water from the *puṇyāha* ceremony following the worship of Vighneśvara; and having sprinkled them again with the *pañcagavya* and the *arghya* offering— (p. 80a)

The procedure for hoisting the banner: having adorned [the chariot] with perfumes and other offerings, having bound the *kautuka* (protective thread) upon the two chariots according to the prescribed method, and having offered incense and lamps—having decorated the chariot with various cloths and the like, and having adorned it with plantains, betel-nut trees, pillars, coconuts, fruits, and so forth—one should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) marked with the proper characteristics upon the altar in the sacrificial hall; this [mound], together with gold and jewels, is to be covered with threads, cloth, and tufts of grass (*kūrca*).

Having established the central jar and the others—having consecrated the eight jars in the eight directions beginning with the east—and having then performed the worship of the doors and so forth, the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), and the internal sacrifice (antaryāga) with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should worship Śiva, from Śakti down to the final Śakti, in the central jar.

Having performed the placement of the thirty-eight *kalās*, namely Daṇḍabhaṅgī and Muṇḍabhaṅgī, and having executed the meditation (*dhyāna*), the invocation (*āvāhana*), and all other ritual services (*upacāra*), one should then, in the pitchers starting from the east, invoke in due order by their respective names using the seat-mantra (*āsana-mantra*) and the root-mantras of the forms (*mūrti*): Bhānu in the east, Indu in the southeast, Hari in the south, Gaṇapati in the southwest, Vṛṣabha in the west, Ananta in the northwest, Dharmapati in the north, and Dharādhara in the northeast; and having performed the invocation and all other ritual services.

Having thus offered milk-rice (*pāyasa*) to these [deities] and completed the worship up to the end of the recitation (*japa*), one should go to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Following the procedure taught for the fire-rite (*agnikārya*), one should perform the purifications of the pit (*kuṇḍasaṃskāra*) as before, ending with the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the kindling (*dīpana*). Having consecrated the Śiva-fire, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations for each substance—namely fuel-sticks (*samidh*), rice, and clarified butter (*ājya*)—with the root mantra. Then, having offered oblations with the nine grains (*navadhānya*) and with the Brahma-mantras and the limbs (*aṅga*) mantras, and having offered the *vyāhṛti* at the conclusion of the substances, one should present the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and the inner and outer offerings (*antarbali* and *bahirbali*).

In the morning, the Guru, having performed the fourfold [rite] beginning with bathing, and having performed—as before—the preparation of the *kalaśa* and the *homa*, goes near the chariot; having performed the ritual placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*), having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and having consecrated it through the rites of inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and so forth.

Having touched the chariot with the tips of *darbha* grass, or having recited the five *śānti* mantras or the *vyomavyāpin* mantra, and having performed [the preliminary rites] beginning with ..., one should worship all the deities upon the chariot as follows: "Homage to the Bull" on the two *vajradaṇḍas*; "Homage to the Sun" and "Homage to the Moon" on the wheels; "Homage to Hari" and "Homage to the Wielder of the Thunderbolt" (*vajrin*) in the portions of Viṣṇu on the central shaft; and "Homage to the One with Two Shafts" on the single seat (*ekapīṭha*).

On the banners: "Salutation to Śatarudra. Having worshipped Dharma and the others on the limbs—on the cooking vessel: "Salutation to Sadāśiva"; on the joints: "Salutation to Dakṣiṇāmūrti"; "Salutation to Viṣṇu"; "Salutation to Brahmā"; "Salutation to Skanda. Having worshipped the world-protectors at the edge of the chariot: on the ropes: "Salutation to the Serpents"; on the umbrella: "Salutation to the Pāśupata weapon"; on the banner: "Salutation to the Bull."

Mukhabhadra—having conceived Brahmā as the charioteer—at the top of the peak, [one should say] "Obeisance to Īśāna. Having worshipped Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta in the four directions starting from the east, and having worshipped the *japa* on both sides, one should meditate upon the horse-form of the Four Vedas at its tip and complete the deposition of the six objects (*ṣaḍarthanyāsa*). The path of the worlds (*bhuvādhvā*) is in the foundation; the path of the arts (*kalādhvā*) and the path of principles (*tattvādhvā*) are in the range of the feet and the pedestal; and the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvā*) is in the region of the throat.

The preceptor, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *śikhara-mantra* and the path (*adhvan*) with the syllable *nyau*, and having worshipped them in due order, should place [the mantras] residing in their respective locations— starting from the *mūlādhāra*, *svādhiṣṭhāna*, *maṇipūra*, *anāhata*, *viśuddhi*, *ājñā*, and *ājñāpāya*— while meditating on [the deity] as follows:
"Having five colors and great radiance, bestowing fearlessness and granting boons,
six-footed, possessing a belly, a trident, and a noose, and four-armed."
It has one face, three eyes, six parts, and is endowed with auspiciousness;
its foot is joined with a wheel, and its nose is the support of the elements.
The mature stage is called Sujānu; the upper stage is Ūraka. The belly is declared to be Devāsana, and the heart is indeed Stambha.
The immovable form is declared to be the throat, and it is remembered as the throat;
the head, the crest, and the top-knot are to be worshipped as the essence, ordained by the ritual rule.
This meditation on the chariot is proclaimed as the cause of all auspiciousness.

Having meditated thus, and having worshipped Devī, Skanda, Vināyaka, and Caṇḍeśvara in their respective hearts, one should thereafter perform the service of offering food (*naivedya*) and other offerings to the pitchers on the altar. Then, having performed the circumambulation of the temple accompanied by all auspicious rites, and having bathed [the deity] at the front of the chariot, one should offer incense and lamps to the chariot. At an auspicious moment, one should consecrate [the deity] in those respective locations.

Having offered incense and lamps, and having paid homage to the deity, one should request, "Let the mounting upon the chariot be performed. Then, with the permission of Śiva, having placed [the image] upon the chariot at an auspicious moment and a favorable conjunction accompanied by all musical instruments, one should present a full water-pot, a vessel of sesame seeds, and a cow with its calf to the Brahmins. One should give garments, gold, fruits, betel, and other gifts to the devotees beginning with the preceptor, extending to the common people. Having satisfied everyone, one should afterwards prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) before the deity.

Having prepared a vessel made of gold or other materials with gold, saffron, agallochum, camphor, sandalwood, turmeric, and so forth; having placed within it a paste of *pāṭala*, blue lotus, cumin, *puṇnāga*, and fresh *campaka* flowers; having surrounded the cauldron with saffron-colored cloth and the like; having set it upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*); having performed the ritual of the limbs (*sakalīkṛtya*); having sprinkled it with the water of the *arghya* offering using the weapon-mantra (*astra*) and having consecrated it with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*); having worshipped the cauldron with the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*); and having worshipped even the liquid [within] with the root-mantra (*mūla*), [one worships] from Śakti up to the end of Śakti.

Having worshipped—having purified [the object] by means of the *nirīkṣaṇa* and other rites—he should display the *amṛtamudrā*. Having offered incense and lamps, and having taken hold of the primary liṅga, the pedestal, and so forth, as well as the wet clay and saffron turban, the preceptor himself, together with the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), having likewise taken hold of the wet clay and the saffron turban, should cause the patron (*yajamāna*) and all the people, including the devotees, to receive them.

Having placed the images of Vighneśvara upon their respective seats, and at an auspicious moment determined by the moon and the stars, having performed a circumambulation of the village preceded by the recitation of *svasti* and accompanied by all musical instruments, and having placed [the deity] in a chariot starting from the preceptor (*ācārya*) down to the devotees (*bhakta*), and having circumambulated the village, one should descend the deity from the chariot, enter the temple, perform the expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) and so forth, gratify the preceptor with garments and other gifts, offer the great oblation (*mahāhavis*), and cause [these gifts] to be distributed to everyone; such is the procedure for the mounting of the chariot (*rathārohaṇa-vidhi*).
(The Procedure for the Black Incense: *kṛṣṇagandhavidhi*)
Listen now to the procedure for black fragrances on the eighth and ninth days,
which serves to accomplish desired goals and is the cause for obtaining sons, grandsons, and so forth.
It destroys the faults such as the killing of a Brahmin, wards off all enemies,
brings victory and good fortune to the king, ensures an abundance of food, and increases the harvest of grain.
Or he who, by the mere sight of his form dancing in wrath, obtains the fruit [of his desires],
and who, when moving to another place, binds himself with the curiosity of creation and maintenance,
as well as the heavy dissolution and the concealment that is like an application of camphor.
At dawn, there is likewise grace in the service of dance.

Having spoken thus, having brought the Dancing Form (nṛttamūrti) into the assembly pavilion (āsthānamaṇṭapa), and having performed its installation and so forth—having worshipped the Dancing Form, having performed the binding of the protective thread (rakṣābandhana) according to the previously mentioned method, having tied the auspicious thread (kautuka) on the night following the eighth day at the conclusion of the festival of the procession of offerings (balibhramaṇotsava), having presented the offerings of food (naivedya) and other services, having adorned both [the deity and the image], and having circumambulated the temple to the accompaniment of all auspicious musical instruments, one should bathe [the deity] in the assembly pavilion.

One should pass the remainder of the night by means of diversions such as dancing, singing, and hymns. One should strew it with *darbha* grass and flowers; having bathed Kālakaṇṭha in the center of this [site], and having performed the *puṇyāha* ceremony preceded by the worship of Vighneśvara, one should prepare thirty-one *śānti*-vases according to the previously mentioned procedure. Having performed the fire-rite (*agnikārya*) up to the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should worship Maheśa therein and offer, in sequence: *śamī*, *bilva*, *avaṭa*, pure mustard seeds, barley, sesame, bamboo, rice, and black gram.
Having offered the vyāhṛtis at the end of each substance, one should offer the pūrṇāhuti again and again.

One should perform one hundred and eight oblations—with clarified butter using the root mantra one hundred and eight times; having offered oblations with the three principles (*tattva*) of the *bilva* fruit, plantain, breadfruit, and so forth, and having given the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should place a vessel containing black fragrant substances upon a tripod (*tripādī*) on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) situated around the rice; having wrapped it with a cloth, mixed it with camphor and other perfumes, performed the ritual of "totalization" (*sakalīkaraṇa*) and the rest, sprinkled it with the *aghora* mantra, and concealed it with the *varman* mantra.

Having consecrated [the offerings] with the Brahmāṅgas and the Mūla-mantra, having displayed the *dhenumudrā*, and having offered water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth, as well as incense and lamps, one should perform the *sampātābhihuta* oblation and the *pūrṇāhuti*. Then, having worshipped the black fragrance from the power (*śakti*) up to the end of the powers (*śaktyanta*), and having recited the *naivedya* mantra and the Mūla-mantra one hundred and eight times, one should dismiss the fire. Having performed a circumambulation of the temple to the accompaniment of auspicious sounds, and having placed [the deity] before the *liṅga* in the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*), one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the thirty-eight *kalās*, beginning with *daṇḍabhāgyā*.

Having performed [the preliminary rites] and worshipped [the deity] from Śakti up to Śakti, having applied black sandalwood paste (*kṛṣṇagandha*) to the five faces of the God with the mantras of the Five Brahmans, and having offered the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) beginning with food offerings (*naivedya*), one should thereafter place the black sandalwood paste before Naṭeśa. Having worshipped Naṭeśa from Śakti up to Śakti, and having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the thirty-one digits (*kalā*)—consisting of the seat (*āsana*), the image (*mūrti*), the staff-break (*daṇḍabhaṅgi*), and the skull-break (*muṇḍabhaṅgi*)—as well as the placement on the neck (*śrīkhaṇṭhanyāsa*), one should perform the meditation (*dhyāna*).

[He is] amidst a mass of matted hair, with a *muṇḍu* drum and a mirror; he wears a garland of skulls, bones, celestial rivers, and the severed head of the King of Demons (*Cetātman*); he has the feet of the Goddess as his garment; he holds a snake in his right hand and a *ḍamaru* drum in his left, which is extended; he stands upon the back of the Smara who is smeared with ashes and possesses a green luster; having made his own right foot into a thunderbolt and raised it, he stands with his left foot placed between the two, reaching the tip of the banner, the small bells, and the jeweled bank.

I bow to Naṭeśa Śiva, who is three-eyed, smeared with ashes, accompanied by Umā, and saluted; he who wears a garland of skulls, holds a staff in his right hand, a earring upon his ear-lobes, and is adorned with side-locks on the left, joined with Umā.

Having thus invoked—having worshipped both [deities] with the meditation on the Goddess and the mantra *śyāmāṃ paramiścariṃ ca*—and having offered incense and lamps, one should perform the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), including the food offering (*naivedya*) consisting of flour-cakes, milk-rice, fruits, sweetmeats, and so forth, along with betel and other items. One should apply black fragrant paste; one should apply it on the forehead with the *aghora* mantra and everywhere else with the *sadyojāta* mantra. Afterwards, immediately following [the offering to] Umāmaheśvara, one should cause it to be given for all the images; and for female images, [it should be applied] on the forehead and the neck.

One should hold [the vessel] with the root-mantra or with the heart-mantra; thereafter, one should cause the disciples and other devotees to smell the Kṛṣṇa-fragrance. Having placed the Lord upon a jeweled lion-throne, with Gaurī to His left, and having ascended [the throne] together with the preceptor on the right side—one should arrange kings, female dancers, and male dancers to the left and in front, and male dancers on both sides, performing their dance toward the temple.

Accompanied by musicians, having gone as far as seven houses and entered the temple, one should perform the offering of food and other rites as before; thereafter, having established [the image] in the assembly hall, one should offer the *arghya* with the eightfold flowers and worship it with the eye-anointing rite (*nīrāñjana*) and so forth.

Thereafter, having bathed [the image] with *gavya* (cow-products), *tapada*, and so forth, and having consecrated pure camphor as before, having anointed it, and having adorned it by clothing it in white garments, placing bright garlands, and white ornaments—having offered milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and the like, and having presented incense and lamps—at the time of the procession, the wife should be made to proceed slowly on the vehicle. There, as before, with Vedic recitations, dance, song, and so forth, having had the wife mount the vehicle, and having performed all the rites such as the waving of lights (*nīrājana*), one should enter the temple with all the ritual offerings (*upacāra*).

Having performed the worship, he should spend the remainder of the night without departing; at dawn, having worshipped Narteśa and prepared the sanctuary, [he should go] to a river or similar place... having established a sacred bathing site (*tīrtha*), having removed the protective amulet (*kautuka*), and having circumambulated the city and other sites accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments, [he should perform] the subduing of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous in a pure location...

Having caused the recitation of the *vācaka* at the marketplace and having resolved the amorous quarrel with the Goddess, one should enter the inner sanctum (*vinālaya*) without a surrounding enclosure, establish her in her own place, and after consecrating her with [water] for drinking and so forth, one should cause a pure dance to be performed with offerings such as *nivedya*; this is the ritual procedure for black incense.

(The Ritual for Collecting the Tīrtha—) According to the former view regarding the Great Tīrtha (*mahātīrtha*), after the festival consisting of the regular offerings, circumambulations, and so forth, the collection of the *tīrtha* should be performed at night. Having performed the protection (*rakṣā*) as before and having uttered the benedictions (*āśiṣaḥ*), one should prepare a single sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in the middle of the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*) as before. Having strewn it with *darbha* grass and flowers, one should place within it a water-pot (*kumbha*) endowed with all ornaments, which brings about the state of *Manonmanī*.

Having placed eight water-jars (*kalaśa*) beginning with that of Gaṅgā all around it, and having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa; having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*), and having fashioned the staff-bending (*daṇḍabhaṅgi*) within the jar; having performed the deposition of the Gaurī-kalās, [saying] "I bow to the beloved of Bandhūbhāṇaka"; and having worshipped her with all the services beginning with perfume (*gandha*); and having worshipped the eight goddesses beginning with Gaṅgā in all eight jars with all the services beginning with invocation (*āvāhana*); and having performed the fire-rite (*agnikārya*) ending with the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).

Having offered one hundred and eight oblations into the fire for each respective name according to the sequence of invocation, and having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should circumambulate the jars along with the trident and the city and so forth, accompanied by all musical instruments; then, having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) that they should be led into river-banks and other sacred sites (*tīrtha*) for the purpose of bathing, and having performed the rite for an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should worship the eight sacred sites beginning with the Gaṅgā in a single water-pot (*karaka*), and fasten a protective thread (*kautuka*) around its neck for the sake of the consecration of the sacred site.
Having cast that into the water of the jar and entered the temple, [this concludes] the ritual for collecting the sacred waters (*tīrthasaṃgrahaṇavidhi*).
Now, the ritual for the powder festival (*cūrṇotsavavidhi*):

On the following day, one should begin the powder festival (*cūrṇotsava*) after [the ritual for] Bali. Having bathed the two sacrificial altars (*sthaṇḍila*) at the top of the temple with turmeric, oil, ghee, betel, perfumes, flowers, and ashes, and having consecrated them with the four purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), one should worship the mortar (*ulūkhala*) as Pradhi and the pestle (*musala*) as Meru—the forms of the seats—using the root mantras. Then, having placed one *droṇa* or half a *droṇa* of turmeric powder in the mortar, and having also placed the husk within it, one should draw a lotus.

Having performed the auspicious rite (*puṇyāha*) consisting of the worship of Vināyaka and other deities, one should set up a trident upon a single [stand], and having placed a mortar and pestle made of sacrificial wood (*yājñīyavṛkṣa*) and endowed with the proper characteristics, one should wrap them with a cloth.

Having taken up a long beard [of grass] and sprinkled it with *arghya* water while reciting the *astra-mantra*, one should perform the four purificatory rites beginning with inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*). Then, having worshipped the *rudrakumbha* upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) situated between those two, as well as the eight pitchers of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) surrounding it—one should likewise place *dūrvā* grass together with the goddesses upon the petals starting from the east around the mortar.

Having cast [the image] with the *padamantra*, or with a hymn of devotion, or with a Drāviḍa hymn, and having reduced it to powder, one should perform the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) before it, ending with the *pūrṇāhuti*. Then, having offered oblations of sacrificial wood, clarified butter, and parched grain with the five Brahmans and the six limbs according to one's capacity—and having performed the *pūrṇāhuti*—thereafter the Moon, Sun, Fire, the Vasus, Vāsava, the seven Mothers, Nandin... Bhṛṅgin, Gajavaktra, Ṣaḍānana, and all the sages of the seven principal mountain ranges attend upon [it].

Of the Supreme Lord Sāmbaśiva—(l. 5) ...the foremost gods such as Brahmā and Viṣṇu, the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Suras, Kinnaras, and the wise ones of the oceans—the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) and the leaders of the hosts of all the Rudras—crush [themselves] in service at the festival of the Supreme Lord. ॥ 2 ॥ The fourteen worlds and all the directions, the months, the seasons, the ages, and the entire host of his progeny dance at the festival of the powder-offering for the sake of serving Śiva.

The stars repeatedly perform the dissolution, the cosmic age, and the eon; all the great wonders such as the dancing Gaṅgā and other sacred fords, and the preeminent mantras of all the Vedas and entire scriptures, serve [the Lord] during the powder festival, the auspicious time of Śiva’s great festival, manifesting as the great forms of the lords of the hosts of Siddhas. (4)

Moving through the ether and the wind, they traverse the divine realm; all objects of the senses, such as sounds and so forth, which are enchanting to the mind—O Lord of all, for the sake of the festival of powder, you cause Pārvatī’s husband to enjoy the delight of his service for a month. 5.

Vīreśa, Kālī, Madhusūdanavallabhā, Vāgīśvarī, all the Yoginīs, the seats of yoga (yogapīṭhas), and the Bhairava deities on earth—[they] take delight; their qualities, which are fond of the festival of powder (cūrṇotsava), captivate and become [manifest]. 6.

The preceptors of Śiva, the lords of brahmins, manifest the festival of Śiva, which is illuminated by the waving of lights from the crest-jewels of the seven serpent-kings of the netherworld; it is perfected by the recitation of all mantras during the powder-festival.

(7) Thus the sages, the ancestral deities, the Vidyādharas, and the sixty-four specialized arts rejoiced: "We are meritorious, having attained the fruits of all our actions, dwelling here through the boundless grace of Śiva. (8)

If you are unable to describe the greatness of the Cūrṇotsava festival right here, then let the entire collection of Śiva’s scriptures do so; if not, then my own intuition prompts me to praise them. (9)

Then, having mixed [the powder] with oil in a vessel of gold or other precious metal, and having worshipped it with the five Brahmans, the six limbs, and the root mantra—having offered incense and lamps; having circumambulated the temple accompanied by all musical instruments; having worshipped from Śakti up to Īśāna-Śakti upon the root-liṅga; having caused [the powder] to be applied along with the ashes and the Brahma-limbs; having placed a turban of saffron; having smeared it with its paste; and having adorned it with its perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and having presented the food offering—

Having offered incense and lamps, and having smeared all the *beras* with those [same] powders, he displays the lotus mudrā (*padmamudrā*). Then, having sprinkled ghee mixed with *dūrvā* grass upon the heads of all the *beras*, having dismissed the fire, having worshipped the *astra* [mantra] with water from that [consecration] jar, having offered incense and lamps, and having himself taken hold [of them], he offers turbans, betel-leaf, and other items to all of them.
Having circumambulated all [the deities] together with the trident and the *pu...* [vessel], and having entered the temple—this is the ritual procedure for the powder festival (*cūrṇotsava*).
(The Ritual for Great Pilgrimage Sites—*mahātīrthavidhiḥ*):

At the pilgrimage sites along a river, as far as possible on its bank—having first prepared a water-shed (*prapā*) and subsequently performed the *aṅkura* rite as before—one should perform the ritual bath at the sacred site (*tīrthasnāna*). This is for the purpose of removing all uncontacted defects, for the attainment of the grace of the sacred site, for the accomplishment of fruits such as dharma which bring pleasure to all the gods, and for the attainment of states such as *sāloka*. On the bank of the sacred site, according to one’s capacity, [one should worship] with weapons, the king of mantras, Soma, Skanda, sprouts, umbrellas, chowries, and so forth.

Having established the *prapādika* [water-offering pit] together with various musical instruments and pitchers for the Tīrthas, and having installed the gods before it; then, in the center of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), one should place the eight pitchers of Gaṅgā and the others starting from the east, as well as the *pālikās*, and worship them all without exception. Then, one should invoke Durgā in the northeast.

In the vicinity of the trident, having performed the *ālāganam* for the thirty-eight deities, the eighteen *gaṇas*, and the world-protectors (*lokapālas*), and having released the festive thread (*kautuka*) of the deities beginning with the Weapon (*astra*), one should release it into the midst of the sacred water—from Śiva down to the Weapon—along with the earthen vessels (*pālikās*). Having consecrated [the deity] with their cloths, one should perform the ritual bath together with all the people. Then the Preceptor (*ācārya*), having removed the festive thread from the sacred water and entered the temple.

Having consecrated each deity’s own vessel, offered the food-offering (*naivedya*), incense, and lamps, and entered the temple—while all [the officiants] remain in the assembly hall accompanied by the chanting of the *brahmaghoṣa*—the preceptor (*ācārya*) receives [the offerings] into his hand from them. Then, the instructor (*deśika*), preceded by a benediction with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), gives the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), betel, and other gifts to all the Brahmins. The best of men performs the ritual bath together with the trident; he is liberated from all sins, and the serpents... [are pacified].
Thus concludes the procedure for the sacred sites (*tīrthavidhi*).
Now follows the ritual bath with the jar (*ghaṭasnāna*, also known as *ghaṭābhiṣeka*).

For the sake of the completion of the festival of Vidhihara, for the sake of the stability of those who seek the fulfillment of their goals, for the sake of attaining the grace of the gods, and for the sake of attaining proximity to the deities such as Indra, one should perform the ritual bathing with the water-pot (*ghaṭasnāna*). Having specifically performed the fire-oblation (*homa*) in the *uṇḍa* pit and offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), having united [the fires] from each respective direction into the principal *kuṇḍa*, and having worshipped Śiva—having offered the final oblation and having specifically worshipped the Śiva-pitcher and the other vessels—one should worship the deities residing in the fire.

Having joined [the vessels] to the *kumbha*, having offered incense and lamps, one should give the prescribed sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor and others; having given clothing and other fees to the attendants and others, one should lift the *kumbhas*, perform a circumambulation of the temple, and place them in the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*). Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) and so forth upon the primary *liṅga*, one should consecrate it. Having consecrated the *vardhanī* on the pedestal and the *vidyeśa-kalaśas* in their respective places, one should consecrate the Goddess with the *śrīkaṇṭha-nyāsa* using the *kalaśa* as before.

Having offered incense and lamps for the presentation of the great sacrificial oblation (*mahāhavis*), one should proceed to the fire-sanctuary (*agni-sadana*). Having offered one hundred and eight oblations into the Śiva-fire with the *mūla-mantra* and the *aghora-mantra*, reciting them while holding the head [of the vessel], and having given the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should unite the fire with the Lord of the Sacrifice (*yāgeśa*). Then, according to the method taught by the Guru, one should unite the deities of the five enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇa*)—the Kumbha, Vardhanī, and so forth—with their respective locations.
Having also dismissed that [fire], one should present abundant sacrificial food and cause the bathing of the image (*biṃba*). Thus ends the procedure for the pot-consecration (*ghaṭābhiṣeka-vidhi*).
(The Ritual of Descent:

For the purpose of suppressing the wicked and protecting the virtuous, on an auspicious day, in the forenoon, or at night, one should perform the descent (*avarohaṇa*) preceded by the *brahma-tāla* and the water-pot (*ghaṭa*). Having joined [the deity] residing in the three worlds to the bull in the most excellent manner, and having placed the bull upon the form situated before Śiva, and having joined the deities of the enclosure (*āvaraṇa*) to their respective enclosures, one should worship according to the ritual rule. On that day, after the silent offering (*mauna-bali*) and the fire-oblation (*homa*), [one should offer] a portion of the sacrificial food (*havirbhāga*).

Having said "to the deity," and having made that [the deity] the object [of his focus], the teacher should begin the silent offering (*maunabali*). Having adorned *Somāskanda* with the worship beginning with the ritual bathing (*snāna*) and so forth, and having fully worshipped [the deities] from Śakti up to Śakti, he should perform the deposition (*nyāsa*) of the thirty-one digits (*kalā*)—namely the *daṇḍabhaṅgi*, *muṇḍabhagnī*, and the *śrīkaṇṭha*—and then meditate: "I worship Guheśa, whose right and left [hands] are extended... Thus, having worshipped him together with his limbs and the fivefold enclosure (*pañcāvaraṇa*).

Having meditated upon and worshipped that deity as will be described hereafter, and having prayed for the welfare of the world, and having received permission from him, one who observes the vow of silence, with palms joined in *añjali*, having understood [the ritual] together with its ancillaries, and having mounted the deities of the *astra* and others upon their respective vehicles—[visualizing them] endowed with many forms together with the weapons such as the *kheta* and *astras* accompanied by perfumes and other offerings—one should, while observing the vow of silence, [proceed] with the sound of musical instruments and the like, [placing] the *kukkuṭā* [seals] at the junctions beginning with the station of Brahmā (*brahmasthāna*) in those respective locations.

Accompanied by the sound of musical instruments and preceded by the lowering of the banner, having performed the bali offering as before and having stationed the deities of the junctions, one should dismiss them in sequence, circumambulate the temple, and enter it. Then, having lowered [the image] in due order with the mantra as before and having placed it in its former location, one should release all [offerings] into food, a liṅga, or water; such is the procedure for the descent.
(The Ritual for the Caṇḍotsava:

After the hoisting of the banner, one should place a bull upon [another] bull—having performed the ceremonial bathing of the bull, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth. One should offer as a food-offering (*naivedya*) mung-bean rice mixed with ghee and plantain fruit; having worshipped it with incense, lamps, and the like, one should present these while being liberated [from bonds]. Then, having worshipped with the sixteen types of service (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), one should bring the image of Caṇḍa into the sacrificial hall, place the Caṇḍa-vessel (*caṇḍakumbha*) upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), worship it, and sprinkle [the deity] with the water from that vessel.

Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite and adorned [the deity] with the remains of the offerings (*nirmālya*) and so forth, one performs the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*): having offered oblations ending with the *pūrṇāhuti*, one offers one hundred and eight oblations separately with fuel-sticks (*samid*), rice, clarified butter (*ājya*), and the mantras of Brahmā and the limbs (*aṅga*). Having offered as many oblations as possible with the root-mantra of Caṇḍa and given the *pūrṇāhuti*, one offers the *vyāhṛti* at the conclusion of the substances. Then, having dismissed both [the deity and the fire], and having performed a circumambulation of the temple accompanied by all auspicious rites, one should install [the deity] in its place. This is the procedure for the festival of Caṇḍa.
The Ritual for the Festival of the Preceptor (*ācāryotsavavidhi*):

Having adorned the preceptor with perfumes, garments, earrings, and other ornaments, one should cause the prescribed sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to be given. Thinking, "The preceptor is [my] mental satisfaction; therefore, Śiva is intent on his satisfaction," one should worship him together with the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) just like Śiva. Then, having placed him upon a chariot or a palanquin, [The text continues...]

Accompanied by various musical instruments, the sounds of dancing, singing, and the Vedas, as well as umbrellas, chowries, and diverse lamps, and together with the king, the patron, and all the people, he should circumambulate the city and cause [the image] to enter his own home in a vehicle; he should give the prescribed sacrificial fees to the attendants and others—this is the procedure for the festival of the Ācārya.

(The Festival of the Auspicious Vow)— On the tenth, seventh, or fifth day, one should perform the festival of the auspicious vow (*kalyāṇavratotsava*) according to the rules for the marriage ceremony (*vivāhavidhi*) with the appropriate ritual honors.
(The Festival of the Goddess)—

Then, one should cause a festival for the Goddess to be held for nine days, seven days, five days, three days, or even a single day. On the eleventh day and night, having performed all the mantras beginning with the Indra-vimāna [and others], having sprinkled [the deity] with consecrated water, having bathed the God preceded by the ritual ablution, and having adorned Him, one should bring Śiva, seated within that *vimāna*, into the center. Having had Him perform three circumambulations together with the Goddess, starting from Caṇḍeśa, accompanied by ornaments, the sacrificer, and musical instruments—at the time of entering the temple, at the front of the *gopura*—

Having dispelled the quarrel over the leading [of the image] at the peak of the Vindhya mountains and having caused the vision [of the deity] to be granted, one should cause [the image] to enter according to the ritual rules; this is the procedure for the festival of the Goddess.
(Description of the Festival:

Either in front of the assembly pavilion (*āsthānamaṇḍapa*) or even at the front of the temple (*prāsāda*), having smeared [the ground] with cow dung, prepare two sacrificial altars (*sthaṇḍila*). Having strewn [them] with *darbha* grass and flowers, one should fashion tufts of grass (*kūrca*) upon the altar with the heart-mantra. If there are two altars, one should place three tridents (*śūla*) upon them. One should place a drum (*bherī*) in front of that, and then have the proclamation of the "Auspicious Day" (*puṇyāha*) made. After worshipping the "Weapon-drum" (*astrabherī*), the wise practitioner should beat the drum.
Namely: then the Guru—having performed his ablutions and other rites, and having sat down with a serene countenance—makes this formal resolve: "On this auspicious lunar day..."

For the purpose of serving the auspicious occasion of the hoisting of the new banner for the illustrious Supreme Lord (*śrīmatparameśvara*), for the sake of [invoking] the vehicles of all the deities, and for the attainment of security, health, victory, and success for all humans, beasts, cattle, and birds, I shall strike the drum (*bherī*). Having sprinkled [it] with the water of the *puṇyāha* rite... having performed the ritual integration of the limbs (*sakalīkṛtya*), having sprinkled the trident (*triśūla*) with the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*) using the weapon-mantra (*astra*), and having bathed it with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), [I recite]: *huṃ phaṭ namaḥ* for the dismissal of the weapon.

"Huṃ phaṭ namaḥ to the one whose form is the weapon"—having thus worshipped the Lord of the Weapon (*astreśa*) upon his seat arising from the six syllables, and having invoked him with "Oṃ hāṃ astrāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ," one should install the deities of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*): on the central petal—"Oṃ hāṃ rudrāya namaḥ"; on the southern petal—"to Brahmā, namaḥ"; on the northern petal—"to Viṣṇu, namaḥ"; in the center of the vessel (*pālikā*)—"Oṃ devyai namaḥ"; to the south of the vessel—"to Sarasvatī, namaḥ."

On the left side of the *pālikā*, salutation to Mahālakṣmī. At the front of the *kumbha*, salutation to Gaṇapati. In the middle of the *kumbha*, salutation to Skanda. At the tip of the staff, salutation to Śāstra. In the middle of the staff, salutation to Bhāskara. On the lotus of the staff, salutation to Candra. At the base of the staff, salutation to Caṇḍa. At the tips of the petals starting from the east, salutation to Indra; salutation to Mātṛ; salutation to Vīrabhadra; salutation to Durgā; salutation to Kṣetrapāla; salutation to Vasu.

"Salutation to the Gaṇas; salutation to the Nakṣatras. Having thus worshipped the Lord of the Weapon (Astreśa) according to the sequence of worship by offering perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and betel, and having offered water for sipping and the arghya libation, one should then perform the worship of the drum (bherī).

Having rendered it pure with the general *arghya* water, having sprinkled the drum (*bherī*) [with that], having offered the seat of the *praṇava*, and having covered the drum with a new cloth, one should worship it with perfumes and other offerings. Because of the statement, "The two deities are in the middle and on the right and left sides of the drum," one should offer: "Obeisance to Śambhu in the middle of the drum; obeisance to Viṣṇu on the right; obeisance to Brahmā on the left; obeisance to Brāhmī at the [right] peg; obeisance to Māheśvarī; obeisance to Kaumārī; obeisance to Vaiṣṇavī."

Salutation to Vārāhī. Salutation to Māhendrī. (l. 2) Salutation to Cāmuṇḍā. On the shield, salutation to Anantā. Salutation to Vāsukī. Salutation to Tārkṣya. Salutation to Kārkoṭaka. Salutation to Padma. Salutation to Mahāpadma. (l. 3) Salutation to Kha(ka)pāla. Salutation to Gulikā. On the right side, salutation to Candra. On the left side, salutation to Sūrya. On the striking-staff, salutation to Skanda. Salutation to the reality of the sound of the kettle-drum. (l. 4) Salutation.

Salutation to Sarasvatī, the presiding deity of the principle of power (*śakti-tattva*). Having thus performed the worship in the prescribed order, beginning with the offering of fragrance and so forth, the preceptor should thereafter strike the drum (*bherī*). Having struck the drum according to the rule—one, two, or three times in succession—he should first strike it once, then twice, and then three times. Recalling the *astra-mantra* during the first watch (*prahara*), he should strike it for the first time with the *tryambaka* mantra; he should strike it once for the second [watch].

These two [verses] are from the *Śāntyadhyāya*; the third is by means of the mantra *brahmajajñānam*, recited three times for the sake of filling the sky and the earth—the source of all worlds—for the pleasure of the foremost among the gods, headed by Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu, and for the prosperity of the people who are the kings of the world. This is the consecration (*adhivāsa*) of the Supreme Lord for the specific procession (*yātrā*). One should strike the drum (*bherī*); in the ritual application at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), it should be struck; for the eighteen [villages], it should be struck.

On this very night, during the great festival of the illustrious *Yatra*, all that was offered to the Great Lord (*Maheśvara*) by those performing the rites—may it be for the invocation of all the gods. Come quickly! O Śrī Padmodbhava... [with] Vārtāka... with the sound of the *kautika* drum, with the *tthallima* and *dalā* drums, we perform the *kūrma* and the *vināyaka-tāla*. We praise the elephant-faced one, the son of the daughter of the mountain (*Girisutā*), the one fashioned by the *Gaṇas*, Gaṇapati, the beloved...

Bow down to that God who holds an axe in his hand, whose wrists are adorned with bracelets, who has swallowed the splendor of the sun, who is beautifully fashioned and worthy of worship, and who performs a graceful dance. He wears a crown set with well-fashioned jewels, reveals the rhythmic beat (*tāla*), and is the essence of the mountain (*giri-tattva*). He is the beloved of Lambodara and Varakuñja, anointed with the saffron of the gods' artistic grace. He is white and possesses a horn, holds sweetmeats in his hand, and carries a jackfruit. He is the Lord of the Gaṇas, adorned by the excellent three eyes and various serpents; bow to him, the truth itself.

[He] who is adorned by various hosts of serpents serving as ornaments; who has whitened the moon with clouds that have been whitened [by his radiance]; who has adorned the sky with the rays from the jewels on his hoods; whose body... [is marked by] the trident, skull, and the hand-gesture of fearlessness belonging to Hara, Hara, Śiva, and Gaṇapati.

(The Ritual for the Festival of the Devotees—*bhaktotsavavidhiḥ*) Now, having bathed the devotees’ *bherā*-drums and other instruments before Śiva in the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*), and having consecrated the previously brought *bherā*-drums, one should perform the powder festival (*cūrṇotsava*) as before. Having taken up the devotees’ *bherā*-drums and so forth, and having given saffron turbans, sacred threads (*pavitra*), garlands, and the like to the preceptor (*ācārya*) and all the people, one should offer a hymn of praise to the devotees.

Having given betel leaves and other offerings to the devotees of Śiva, having circumambulated the city, and having entered it, one should establish all [the images] in their respective places; having offered [food], and having presented incense and lamps, one should cause garments and other gifts to be bestowed upon the devotees of Śiva. This is the procedure for the festival of devotion. (The end of the section on affectionate play?)

On the following day, having performed in sequence the great ablution (*mahāsnāna*), the *śāntihoma*, the *mūrtihoma*, the *diśāhoma*, and so forth, and having consecrated [the deity], one should cause the removal of fatigue to be performed—at the end of the day of the *tīrtha*. Regarding the "quarrel of affection" (*praṇayakalaha*): it is said that when the seed-field is fully joined, the five [elements] beginning with creation... [are established]. First is the installation of the *kṣetrapāla* (guardian of the field). When the time for the city... has arrived, even if [the deity] has perished, there should indeed be a festival.

One should perform the rite of expiation (*prāyaścitta*); one should carry out the *śānti*-oblation. Thereafter, one should conduct the festival according to the path prescribed by the rules. Even when Jupiter and Venus are in conjunction, one should perform the festival during that month; however, the preceptor should avoid the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) there and instead cause the festival to be performed. Or, even during the heliacal setting of Jupiter and Venus, or when the lunar day (*tithi*) and so forth, the ascendant (*lagna*), and the month are void, or in other such cases, for one who is pregnant, or for the rites of shaving, sowing seeds, re-initiation, binding, and likewise for internal purification, the *śānti*-oblation must be performed. That preceptor is honored.

(The Ritual of the Field Protector—) Hereafter, I shall proclaim the sequence of the ritual for the Field Protector (kṣetrapāla), including the Field Protector himself, the mantra, the placement of the mudrā, the worship, the festival, the bath, and [the rite] for Vidā... Vanīśvara. Īśvara said:

The field-protector (*kṣetrapāla*) is that which has been vomited forth; it is joined with the seed-syllable and the sixth vowel, conjoined with the thirteenth [consonant], and endowed with the *bindu* and *nāda*. This is declared to be the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). One should arrange the [six] limbs (*aṅga*) as follows: one should place [the syllables] accompanied by *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, and *phaṭ*, joined with *bindu* and *nāda*, ending in the *visarga*. Among all these, the weapon (*astra*) is said to be the *visarga* in sequence. In the eastern direction, shaped like a lamp, one should employ the entire mantra;
this is known as the "Great Mantra" (*mahāmantra*), and the characteristics of the mudrās are now described.
(The characteristics of the mudrās: One should conquer the foot, the trident, the bud, and the harsh [mudrās] with the two conchs.
At the end of the mantra, the application should be performed by means of the mudrā; one should employ the ritual applications.
Three-eyed, six-armed, and fierce, with hair standing erect and excellent fangs; with a wrathful gaze and a dark body, bearing a plow as his crest;
adorned with human heads and a garland of serpents around his neck; with leaf-clusters at his ears and earrings of skulls.

In his right hands he holds a khaṭvāṅga, a serpent, and a noose with a trident; in his left hands, a skull-cup, a hand-drum, and a sword. He is adorned with all ornaments and endowed with a garland of heads; he is joined with various radiant colors and accompanied by the tinkling sound of small bells—napu...

One should fashion a sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*) attached to the foot [of the image], endowed with a circle of light (*prabhāmaṇḍala*), and made of clay, in the eastern part of the village, or likewise in the north... in the forest, at a hamlet, a lotus-pool, on a riverbank, in a field, or in the northeast portion of the temple; one should construct it in front of the temple, measuring seven cubits...
[with] four archways (*toraṇa*), provided with four doors, equipped with canopies and banners, and adorned with strings of pearls.
Having divided the pavilion into three parts, one should arrange an altar in the center.
Having made two [sections] measuring one palm-span each, they should be smeared with cow dung.
It is provided with sixteen pillars and adorned with door-arches.
To the east, however, that [fire-pit] is square; to the south, it is a circular pit;
to the west, it is five-cornered; and to the north, it is triangular.
It is endowed with three girdles, or indeed with a single girdle;
it is provided with a navel and a womb, and in the center, it is provided with a lotus.
Having performed the inspection and the sprinkling, one should sprinkle [the site] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*);
one should sprinkle it with water from *kuśa* grass using the Heart-mantra and the Weapon-mantra.
There, one should cause the Brahmins to pronounce a "holy day" (*puṇyāha*) and then feed them;
thereafter, having performed the deposition of jewels (*ratnanyāsa*) with the Heart-mantra itself.
The opening of the eyes should be performed; one should apply the eye-mantra...
[with] ghee, honey, and curds, [offering them] with the heart-mantra itself.
One should cause all the Brahmins to see [the site] with five cows;
having performed purification with the primary seed-mantra once for each,
one should wash it with water, clay, cow-dung, sprouts, ashes, and bilva-water.
Having performed a circumambulation of the village while reciting the *Pañcabrahma*,
one should wash [the site] with the *Pañcabrahma* and sprinkle it with scented water;
and one should offer perfume, flowers, and incense, accompanied by the mantras.
One should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) in water together with a pair of garments,
either for three nights at the confluence of three rivers or for a single watch (*yāma*) in a reservoir of water.
Then, having emerged from the water and removed the garments and the tuft of grass (*kūrca*) from the Lord of Gods (*Deveśa*), [one should proceed].
Having brought [the deity] to the bathing pavilion and performed purification in the proper sequence,
having worshipped with scents, flowers, and so forth, one should consecrate [the deity] together with the pedestal;
having established [it] with the five Brahmans, one should offer water for the feet and water for sipping.
One should place there water-pots provided with cloths and gold;
one should worship [the deities] from Indra up to Īśāna with their respective mantras.
According to the procedure prescribed for the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), one should consecrate the *śivāgni* fire.

With fuel-sticks (*samid*), clarified butter (*ājya*), sacrificial porridge (*caru*), parched grain (*lāja*), uncooked cakes (*apūpa*), barley, and sesame seeds— along with the five Brahmans and the six limbs— one should offer a hundred oblations of the root mantra;
likewise, with the *kṣurikā* weapon-mantra and others, twenty oblations for each.

At the clear dawn, having bathed and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) according to the rules, the wise one— having first purified himself through the application of *bhasman* on his limbs and other means of self-purification—
should worship with perfumes, flowers, incense, the five lamps, and the *arghya* offering.
Having meditated upon the form of the image preceded by the consecration of the mantra— [the practitioner],
adorned with the Śivadharmas, mantras, and Śiva-śāstras,
should place the seed-syllable *saṃ* at the heart by means of the rite of *prāṇapratiṣṭhā*.
One should install all the deities who have been established by their own names alone.
At the conclusion of that, one should consecrate them with the fivefold Brahma-mantra;
one should offer incense, flowers, and incense smoke.
One should offer the mudrās conjoined with the word "namas" at the end;
then, one should arrange them all around, starting from Indra and ending with Īśāna:
Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, and Mattabhairava.
Kapālabhiṣa and Sahara—these are the eight Bhairavas.
One should worship Kumbhaka and the guardian of the door;
then, one should sacrifice the bali-offering and the peacock-feather fan in the east and all around.
...and having performed [the rites], one should worship each with its own respective mantra;
one should especially offer bali-offerings to the Piśācas of the great seats (mahāpīṭha);
at the conclusion of the food offering, one should also present betel leaves.

And having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) before that [image], one should offer a *bali* in the middle of the night, consisting of sugar-candy, clarified butter, cakes, along with parched grain flour and parched rice; the water for the feet (*pādya*) should be offered with the *Sadyojāta* mantra, and the water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamanīyaka*) with the foot-mantra (*pāda*).

Having placed the *arghya* on the head, one should perform the consecration with the *hṛdaya* mantra. One should offer flowers with the *Īśāna* mantra, fragrance with the *Tatpuruṣa* mantra, the lamp with the *Netra* mantra, and the water for sipping (*ācamanīyaka*) with the *Vāma* mantra.
One should offer the food offering with the Heart mantra and the betel-leaf with the Armor mantra;
one should worship the Kṣetrapāla with the Weapon mantra.
Thus... [as before] ... thereafter, worship should be performed, which bestows both success and the supreme goal.
One should perform the consecration and hold a festival there for seven days,
or alternatively, one should perform the festival for a single day. Beginning the recitation of the mantra on the seventh day, one should visit the sacred bathing site at dawn.
The first has the elements as its deity; the second has the Gaṇas as its deity;
the third has the Piśācas as its deity; the fourth has the Mantras as its deity;
the fifth has Rati as its deity; and the sixth indeed has the Rākṣasas as its deity.
One should offer oblations of cooked rice, mung beans, and parched grain in the evening and in the morning to the seventh field-protector, who is the deity of the days.
One should perform one hundred oblations for each [mantra], beginning with the heart-mantra and ending with the weapon-mantra.
Likewise, the divine full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) should be performed by the Puruṣa-mantra;

one should offer the bali-offering in the evening and morning, and then, at the conclusion of the fire-sacrifice (*homa*), hold a festival. Then, during the seven-day period, one should perform the fourth auspicious day (*puṇyāha*).

And a great oblation (mahāhavis) must be performed, especially until the conclusion of the festival. Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with rice grains, one should perform the installation of the water-jars (kumbha).
[One should offer] water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamanīya), the respectful offering (arghya), the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and water with kuśa grass.
One should arrange it there as before and place the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*):
milk, curd, and ghee, [using] the mantras of Indra and the others up to Īśāna;
then, having meditated upon Kṣetrapāla with the Śaiva mantra, one should perform the ritual placement of the self.
One should consecrate the jars with the respective seed-syllable mantras.

Having established the great banner (*mahādhvaja*) in the east, one should worship the *arghya* offering at the site. At the conclusion of the festival, one should offer the great oblation (*mahāhavi*) to the Lord of the Field (*kṣetreśa*).
One should honor the teacher there with garments, gold, and finger-rings.
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual for propitiating the Kṣetrapāla in the Kriyāpāda of the Raurava. May there be auspiciousness.
